About the Open Logic Project
This words-only view expands the abbreviation “i.e.” for smoother browser read-aloud.

The Open Logic Text is an open-source, collaborative textbook of formal meta-logic and formal methods, starting at an intermediate level (that is, after an introductory formal logic course). Though aimed at a non-mathematical audience (in particular, students of philosophy and computer science), it is rigorous.

Coverage of some topics currently included may not yet be complete, and many sections still require substantial revision. We plan to expand the text to cover more topics in the future. We also plan to add features to the text, such as a glossary, a list of further reading, historical notes, pictures, better explanations, sections explaining the relevance of results to philosophy, computer science, and mathematics, and more problems and examples. If you find an error, or have a suggestion, please let the project team know.

The project operates in the spirit of open source. Not only is the text freely available, we provide the LaTeX source under the Creative Commons Attribution license, which gives anyone the right to download, use, modify, re-arrange, convert, and re-distribute our work, as long as they give appropriate credit. Please see the Open Logic Project website at openlogicproject.org for additional information.

Extensionality

A set is a collection of objects, considered as a single object. The objects making up the set are called elements or members of the set. If x is an element of a set A, we write x is an element of A; if not, we write x is not an element of A. The set which has no elements is called the empty set and denoted “the empty set”.
Explanation

It does not matter how we specify the set, or how we order its elements, or indeed how many times we count its elements. All that matters are what its elements are. We codify this in the following principle.
Definition: Extensionality
If A and B are sets, then A equals B if and only if every element of A is also an element of B, and vice versa.

Extensionality licenses some notation. In general, when we have some objects a sub 1, and so on, a sub n, then the set containing a sub 1 through a sub n is the set whose elements are a sub 1, through a sub n. We emphasise the word “the”, since extensionality tells us that there can be only one such set. Indeed, extensionality also licenses the following: the set a, a, b equals the set a, b equals the set b, a This delivers on the point that, when we consider sets, we don't care about the order of their elements, or how many times they are specified.
Example 1

Whenever you have a bunch of objects, you can collect them together in a set. The set of Richard's siblings, for instance, is a set that contains one person, and we could write it as S equals the singleton set containing Ruth. The set of positive integers less than 4 is the set containing 1, 2, and 3, but it can also be written as the set containing 3, 2, and 1 or even as the set containing 1, 2, 1, 2, and 3. These are all the same set, by extensionality. For every element of the set containing 1, 2, and 3 is also an element of the set containing 3, 2, and 1 (and of the set containing 1, 2, 1, 2, and 3), and vice versa.

Frequently we'll specify a set by some property that its elements share. We'll use the following shorthand notation for that: the set of x such that phi of x, where the phi of x stands for the property that x has to have in order to be counted among the elements of the set.
Example 2
In our example, we could have specified S also as S equals the set of x such that x is a sibling of Richard
Example 3

A number is called perfect if and only if it is equal to the sum of its proper divisors (i.e., numbers that evenly divide it but aren't identical to the number). For instance, 6 is perfect because its proper divisors are 1, 2, and 3, and 6 equals 1 plus 2 plus 3. In fact, 6 is the only positive integer less than 10 that is perfect. So, using extensionality, we can say: the singleton set containing 6 equals the set of x such that x is perfect and 0 is less than or equal to x, which is less than or equal to 10 We read the notation on the right as “the set of x's such that x is perfect and 0 is less than or equal to x, which is less than or equal to 10”. The identity here confirms that, when we consider sets, we don't care about how they are specified. And, more generally, extensionality guarantees that there is always only one set of x's such that phi of x. So, extensionality justifies calling the set of x such that phi of x the set of x's such that phi of x.

Extensionality gives us a way for showing that sets are identical: to show that A equals B, show that whenever x is an element of A then also x is an element of B, and whenever y is an element of B then also y is an element of A.
Exercise 1
Prove that there is at most one empty set, i.e., show that if A and B are sets without elements, then A equals B.
Subsets and Power Sets
Explanation

We will often want to compare sets. And one obvious kind of comparison one might make is as follows: everything in one set is in the other too. This situation is sufficiently important for us to introduce some new notation.
Definition: Subset

If every element of a set A is also an element of B, then we say that A is a subset of B, and write A is a subset of B. If A is not a subset of B we write A is not a subset of B. If A is a subset of B but A is not equal to B, we write A is a proper subset of B and say that A is a proper subset of B.
Example 4

Every set is a subset of itself, and the empty set is a subset of every set. The set of natural even numbers is a subset of the set of natural numbers. Also, the set a, b is a subset of the set a, b, c. But the set containing a, b, and e is not a subset of the set containing a, b, and c.
Example 5

The number 2 is an element of the set of integers, whereas the set of even numbers is a subset of the set of integers. However, a set may happen to both be an element and a subset of some other set, e.g., the singleton set containing 0 is an element of the set containing 0 and the singleton set containing 0 and also the singleton set containing 0 is a subset of the set containing 0 and the singleton set containing 0.

Extensionality gives a criterion of identity for sets: A equals B if and only if every element of A is also an element of B and vice versa. The definition of “subset” defines A is a subset of B precisely as the first half of this criterion: every element of A is also an element of B. Of course the definition also applies if we switch A and B: that is, B is a subset of A if and only if every element of B is also an element of A. And that, in turn, is exactly the “vice versa” part of extensionality. In other words, extensionality entails that sets are equal if and only if they are subsets of one another.
Proposition
A equals B if and only if both A is a subset of B and B is a subset of A.

Now is also a good opportunity to introduce some further bits of helpful notation. In defining when A is a subset of B we said that “every element of A is and so on,” and filled the “and so on” with “an element of B”. But this is such a common shape of expression that it will be helpful to introduce some formal notation for it.
Definition
for every x in A, phi abbreviates for every x, if x is in A then phi. Similarly, there exists an x in A such that phi abbreviates there exists an x such that x is in A and phi.
Using this notation, we can say that A is a subset of B if and only if for every x in A, x is in B.
Now we move on to considering a certain kind of set: the set of all subsets of a given set.
Definition: Power Set
The set consisting of all subsets of a set A is called the power set of A, written the power set of A. the power set of A equals the set of B such that B is a subset of A
Example 6

What are all the possible subsets of the set containing a, b, and c? They are: the empty set, the singleton set containing a, the singleton set containing b, the singleton set containing c, the set containing a and b, the set containing a and c, the set containing b and c, the set containing a, b, and c. The set of all these subsets is the power set of the set a, b, c: the power set of the set a, b, c equals the set containing the empty set; the singleton a; the singleton b; the singleton c; the sets a,b; b,c; a,c; and a,b,c
Exercise 2
List all subsets of the set containing a, b, c, and d.
Exercise 3
Show that if A has n elements, then the power set of A has 2 to the n power elements.
Some Important Sets
Example 7

We will mostly be dealing with sets whose elements are mathematical objects. Four such sets are important enough to have specific names: the natural numbers equal 0, 1, 2, 3, and so on; the integers equal the negative whole numbers, zero, and the positive whole numbers; the rational numbers are fractions m over n with integers m and n and nonzero n; the real numbers run from negative infinity to infinity These are all infinite sets, that is, they each have infinitely many elements.

As we move through these sets, we are adding more numbers to our stock. Indeed, it should be clear that the natural numbers are a subset of the integers, which are a subset of the rational numbers, which are a subset of the real numbers: after all, every natural number is an integer; every integer is a rational; and every rational is a real. Equally, it should be clear that the natural numbers are a proper subset of the integers, which are a proper subset of the rational numbers, since negative 1 is an integer but not a natural number, and one half is rational but not integer. It is less obvious that the rational numbers are a proper subset of the real numbers, i.e., that there are some real numbers which are not rational.

We'll sometimes also use the set of positive integers the positive integers equal the set 1, 2, 3, and so on and the set containing just the first two natural numbers the binary alphabet B equals the set containing zero and one.
Example 8: Strings

Another interesting example is the set A star of finite strings over an alphabet A: any finite sequence of elements of A is a string over A. We include the empty string the empty string among the strings over A, for every alphabet A. For instance, the binary alphabet B star equals the set of all finite binary strings: the empty string; zero; one; zero zero; zero one; one zero; one one; then all longer binary strings If x equals x sub 1 through x sub n and is an element of A star is a stringReader correction: the source has no space between the displayed formula and ‘is’. Example 9: Infinite sequences

For any set A we may also consider the set A to the omega power of infinite sequences of elements of A. An infinite sequence a sub 1, a sub 2, a sub 3, a sub 4, and so on consists of a one-way infinite list of objects, each one of which is an element of A.
Unions and Intersections
Explanation

In the Extensionality section, we introduced definitions of sets by abstraction, i.e., definitions of the form the set of x such that phi of x. Here, we invoke some property phi, and this property can mention sets we've already defined. So for instance, if A and B are sets, the set the set of x such that x is in A or x is in B consists of all those objects which are elements of either A or B, i.e., it's the set that combines the elements of A and B. We can visualize this as in the union diagram, where the highlighted area indicates the elements of the two sets A and B together.

The union A union B of two sets is the set of elementsReader correction: the source omits ‘the’ before ‘set’ in this caption. This reader supplies it; the source file is unchanged. of A together with those of B.
Union of A and B: elements in A or B. The highlighted region contains every element in A or B, including elements in both sets.
Set A
The left boundary.
Set B
The right boundary.
Highlighted region
The highlighted region contains every element in A or B, including elements in both sets.
This operation on sets—combining them—is very useful and common, and so we give it a formal name and a symbol.
Definition: Union
The union of two sets A and B, written A union B, is the set of all things which are elements of A, B, or both. A union B equals the set of x such that x is in A or x is in B
Example 10

Since the multiplicity of elements doesn't matter, the union of two sets which have an element in common contains that element only once, e.g., the set a, b, c union the set a, 0, 1 equals the set a, b, c, 0, 1.
The union of a set and one of its subsets is just the bigger set: the set a, b, c union the singleton a equals the set a, b, c.
The union of a set with the empty set is identical to the set: the set a, b, c union the empty set equals the set a, b, c.
Exercise 4
Prove that if A is a subset of B, then A union B equals B.
Explanation

We can also consider a “dual” operation to union. This is the operation that forms the set of all elements that are elements of A and are also elements of B. This operation is called intersection, and can be depicted as in the intersection diagram.
The intersection A intersect B of two sets is the set of elements they have in common.
Intersection of A and B: elements common to both. The highlighted region is the overlap containing the elements that belong to both A and B.
Set A
The left boundary.
Set B
The right boundary.
Highlighted region
The highlighted region is the overlap containing the elements that belong to both A and B.
Definition: Intersection

The intersection of two sets A and B, written A intersect B, is the set of all things which are elements of both A and B. A intersect B equals the set of x such that x is in A and x is in B Two sets are called disjoint if their intersection is empty. This means they have no elements in common.
Example 11
If two sets have no elements in common, their intersection is empty: the set a, b, c intersect the set 0, 1 equals the empty set.
If two sets do have elements in common, their intersection is the set of all those: the set a, b, c intersect the set a, b, d equals the set a, b.
The intersection of a set with one of its subsets is just the smaller set: the set a, b, c intersect the set a, b equals the set a, b.
The intersection of any set with the empty set is empty: the set a, b, c intersect the empty set equals the empty set.
Exercise 5
Prove rigorously that if A is a subset of B, then A intersect B equals A.
Explanation

We can also form the union or intersection of more than two sets. An elegant way of dealing with this in general is the following: suppose you collect all the sets you want to form the union (or intersection) of into a single set. Then we can define the union of all our original sets as the set of all objects which belong to at least one element of the set, and the intersection as the set of all objects which belong to every element of the set.
Definition

If A is a set of sets, then the union of A is the set of elements of elements of A: the union of A equals the set of x belonging to an element of A; that is, the set of x for which there is a B in A with x in B
Definition

If A is a set of sets, then the intersection of A is the set of objects which all elements of A have in common: the intersection of A equals the set of x belonging to every element of A; that is, the set of x such that for every B in A, x is in B
Example 12

Suppose A equals the set whose elements are the set a, b; the set a, d, e; and the set a, d. Then the union of A equals the set containing a, b, d, and e and the intersection of A equals the singleton set containing a.
Exercise 6
Show that if A is a set and A is an element of B, then A is a subset of the union of B.

We could also do the same for a sequence of sets A sub 1, A sub 2, and so on the union over i of A sub i equals the set of x belonging to at least one A sub i; the intersection over i of A sub i equals the set of x belonging to every A sub i

When we have an index of sets, i.e., some set I such that we are considering A sub i for each i is an element of I, we may also use these abbreviations: the union over i in I of A sub i equals the union of the set of A sub i for i in I; the intersection over i in I of A sub i equals the intersection of the set of A sub i for i in I
Finally, we may want to think about the set of all elements in A which are not in B. We can depict this as in the difference diagram.
The difference A set minus B of two sets is the set of those elements of A which are not also elements of B.
Difference A minus B: elements in A but not B. The highlighted region is the part of A outside B, containing elements in A that are not in B.
Set A
The left boundary.
Set B
The right boundary.
Highlighted region
The highlighted region is the part of A outside B, containing elements in A that are not in B.
Definition: Difference
The set difference A set minus B is the set of all elements of A which are not also elements of B, i.e., A set minus B equals the set of x such that x is in A and x is not in B
Exercise 7
Prove that if A is a proper subset of B, then B set minus A is not the empty set.
Pairs, Tuples, Cartesian Products
Explanation

It follows from extensionality that sets have no order to their elements. So if we want to represent order, we use ordered pairs the ordered pair x, y. In an unordered pair the set containing x and y, the order does not matter: the set x, y equals the set y, x. In an ordered pair, it does: if x is not equal to y, then the ordered pair x, y is not equal to the ordered pair y, x.

How should we think about ordered pairs in set theory? Crucially, we want to preserve the idea that ordered pairs are identical if and only if they share the same first element and share the same second element, i.e.: the ordered pair a, b equals the ordered pair c, d if and only if a equals c and b equals d We can define ordered pairs in set theory using the Wiener–Kuratowski definition.
Definition: Ordered pair
the ordered pair a, b equals the set containing the singleton a and the set a, b.
Exercise 8
Using the ordered-pair definition, prove that the ordered pair a, b equals the ordered pair c, d if and only if both a equals c and b equals d.
Explanation

Having fixed a definition of an ordered pair, we can use it to define further sets. For example, sometimes we also want ordered sequences of more than two objects, e.g., triples the ordered triple x, y, z, quadruples the ordered quadruple x, y, z, u, and so on. We can think of triples as special ordered pairs, where the first element is itself an ordered pair: the ordered triple x, y, z is the ordered pair whose first coordinate is the ordered pair x, y and whose second coordinate is z. The same is true for quadruples: the ordered quadruple x, y, z, u is the ordered pair whose first coordinate is the ordered pair whose first coordinate is the ordered pair x, y and second coordinate z, and whose second coordinate is u, and so on. In general, we talk of ordered n-tuples the ordered n tuple x sub 1 through x sub n.
Certain sets of ordered pairs, or other ordered n-tuples, will be useful.
Definition: Cartesian product
Given sets A and B, their Cartesian product A cross B is defined by A cross B equals the set of ordered pairs x, y such that x is in A and y is in B
Example 13
If A equals the set containing 0 and 1, and B equals the set containing 1, a, and b, then their product is A cross B equals the set of ordered pairs 0,1; 0,a; 0,b; 1,1; 1,a; and 1,b
Example 14

If A is a set, the product of A with itself, A cross A, is also written A squared. It is the set of all pairs the ordered pair x, y with x and y are elements of A. The set of all triples the ordered triple x, y, z is A cubed, and so on. We can give a recursive definition: A to the first power equals A; A to the k plus 1 power equals A to the k power cross A
Exercise 9
List all elements of the set 1, 2, 3 cubed.
Proposition
If A has n elements and B has m elements, then A cross B has n times m elements.
Proof

For every element x in A, there are m elements of the form the ordered pair x, y is an element of A cross B. Let B sub x equals the set of ordered pairs x, y such that y is in B. Since whenever x sub 1 is not equal to x sub 2, the ordered pair x sub 1, y is not equal to the ordered pair x sub 2, y, B sub x sub 1 intersect B sub x sub 2 equals the empty set. But if A equals the set containing x sub 1 through x sub n, then A cross B equals B sub x sub 1 union through B sub x sub n, and so has n times m elements.

To visualize this, arrange the elements of A cross B in a grid: array of Cartesian-product rows: B sub x sub 1 equals the set of ordered pairs x sub 1, y sub 1 through x sub 1, y sub m; B sub x sub 2 equals the set of ordered pairs x sub 2, y sub 1 through x sub 2, y sub m; the pattern continues; B sub x sub n equals the set of ordered pairs x sub n, y sub 1 through x sub n, y sub m Since the x sub i are all different, and the y sub j are all different, no two of the pairs in this grid are the same, and there are n times m of them.
End of proof.
Exercise 10
Show, by induction on k, that for all k is greater than or equal to 1, if A has n elements, then A to the k power has n to the k power elements.
Example 15

If A is a set, a word over A is any sequence of elements of A. A sequence can be thought of as an n-tuple of elements of A. For instance, if A equals the set containing a, b, and c, then the sequence “the string b a c” can be thought of as the triple the ordered triple b, a, c. Words, i.e., sequences of symbols, are of crucial importance in computer science. By convention, we count elements of A as sequences of length 1, and the empty sequence as the sequence of length 0. The set of all words over A then is A star equals the union of the singleton set containing the empty sequence, A, A squared, A cubed, and so on.
Russell's Paradox

Extensionality licenses the notation the set of x such that phi of x, for the set of x's such that phi of x. However, all that extensionality really licenses is the following thought. If there is a set whose members are all and only the phi's, then there is only one such set. Otherwise put: having fixed some phi, the set the set of x such that phi of x is unique, if it exists.

But this conditional is important Crucially, not every property lends itself to comprehension. That is, some properties do not define sets. If they all did, then we would run into outright contradictions. The most famous example of this is Russell's Paradox.

Sets may be elements of other sets—for instance, the power set of a set A is made up of sets. And so it makes sense to ask or investigate whether a set is an element of another set. Can a set be a member of itself? Nothing about the idea of a set seems to rule this out. For instance, if all sets form a collection of objects, one might think that they can be collected into a single set—the set of all sets. And it, being a set, would be an element of the set of all sets.

Russell's Paradox arises when we consider the property of not having itself as an element, of being non-self-membered. What if we suppose that there is a set of all sets that do not have themselves as an element? Does R equals the set of x such that x is not an element of itself exist? It turns out that we can prove that it does not.
Theorem: Russell's Paradox
There is no set R equals the set of x such that x is not an element of itself.
Proof
If R equals the set of x such that x is not an element of itself exists, then R is an element of R if and only if R is not an element of R, which is a contradiction.
End of proof.
Explanation

Let's run through this proof more slowly. If R exists, it makes sense to ask whether R is an element of R or not. Suppose that indeed R is an element of R. Now, R was defined as the set of all sets that are not elements of themselves. So, if R is an element of R, then R does not itself have R's defining property. But only sets that have this property are in R, hence, R cannot be an element of R, i.e., R is not an element of R. But R can't both be and not be an element of R, so we have a contradiction.

Since the assumption that R is an element of R leads to a contradiction, we have R is not an element of R. But this also leads to a contradiction For if R is not an element of R, then R itself does have R's defining property, and so R would be an element of R just like all the other non-self-membered sets. And again, it can't both not be and be an element of R.
Further note

How do we set up a set theory which avoids falling into Russell's Paradox, i.e., which avoids making the inconsistent claim that R equals the set of x such that x is not an element of itself exists? Well, we would need to lay down axioms which give us very precise conditions for stating when sets exist (and when they don't).

The set theory sketched in this chapter doesn't do this. It's genuinely naïve. It tells you only that sets obey extensionality and that, if you have some sets, you can form their union, intersection, etc. It is possible to develop set theory more rigorously than this.

Relations as Sets
Explanation

In the Some Important Sets section, we mentioned some important sets: the natural numbers, the integers, the rational numbers, the real numbers. You will no doubt remember some interesting relations between the elements of some of these sets. For instance, each of these sets has a completely standard order relation on it. There is also the relation is identical with that every object bears to itself and to no other thing. There are many more interesting relations that we'll encounter, and even more possible relations. Before we review them, though, we will start by pointing out that we can look at relations as a special sort of set.

For this, recall two things from the Pairs, Tuples, Cartesian Products section. First, recall the notion of an ordered pair: given a and b, we can form the ordered pair a, b. Importantly, the order of elements does matter here. So if a is not equal to b then the ordered pair a, b is not equal to the ordered pair b, a. (Contrast this with unordered pairs, i.e., 2-element sets, where the set a, b equals the set b, a.) Second, recall the notion of a Cartesian product: if A and B are sets, then we can form A cross B, the set of all pairs the ordered pair x, y with x is an element of A and y is an element of B. In particular, A squared equals A cross A is the set of all ordered pairs from A.

Now we will consider a particular relation on a set: the less than-relation on the set the natural numbers of natural numbers. Consider the set of all pairs of numbers the ordered pair n, m where n is less than m, i.e., R equals the set of ordered pairs n, m of natural numbers with n less than m There is a close connection between n being less than m, and the pair the ordered pair n, m being a member of R, namely: n is less than m if and only if the ordered pair n, m is in R Indeed, without any loss of information, we can consider the set R to be the less than-relation on the natural numbers.

In the same way we can construct a subset of the natural numbers squared for any relation between numbers. Conversely, given any set of pairs of numbers S is a subset of the natural numbers squared, there is a corresponding relation between numbers, namely, the relationship n bears to m if and only if the ordered pair n, m is in S. This justifies the following definition:
Definition: Binary relation

A binary relation on a set A is a subset of A squared. If R is a subset of A squared is a binary relation on A and x and y are elements of A, we sometimes write R relates x to y (or x is R-related to y) for the ordered pair x, y is in R.
Example: Relations on the natural numbers

The set the natural numbers squared of pairs of natural numbers can be listed in a 2-dimensional matrix like this: an infinite array of ordered pairs of natural numbers, with the diagonal pairs zero zero, one one, two two, three three, and so on emphasized We have put the diagonal, here, in bold, since the subset of the natural numbers squared consisting of the pairs lying on the diagonal, i.e., the set containing the ordered pairs zero zero, one one, two two, and so on is the identity relation on the natural numbers. (Since the identity relation is popular, let's define the identity relation on A equals the set of ordered pairs x, x such that x is in A for any set A.) The subset of all pairs lying above the diagonal, i.e., L equals the ordered pairs zero one, zero two, and so on; one two, one three, and so on; two three, two four, and so on is the less than relation, i.e., L relates n to m if and only if n is less than m. The subset of pairs below the diagonal, i.e., G equals the ordered pairs one zero, two zero, two one, three zero, three one, three two, and so on is the greater than relation, i.e., G relates n to m if and only if n is greater than m. The union of L with I, which we might call K equals L union I, is the less than or equal to relation: K relates n to m if and only if n is less than or equal to m. Similarly, H equals G union I is the greater than or equal to relation. These relations L, G, K, and H are special kinds of relations called orders. L and G have the property that no number bears L or G to itself (i.e., for all n, neither L relates n to itself nor G relates n to itself). Relations with this property are called irreflexive, and, if they also happen to be orders, they are called strict orders.
Explanation

Although orders and identity are important and natural relations, it should be emphasized that according to our definition any subset of A squared is a relation on A, regardless of how unnatural or contrived it seems. In particular, the empty set is a relation on any set (the empty relation, which no pair of elements bears), and A squared itself is a relation on A as well (one which every pair bears), called the universal relation. But also something like E equals the set of ordered pairs n, m such that n is greater than 5 or m times n is at least 34 counts as a relation.

Philosophical Reflections

In the Relations as Sets section, we defined relations as certain sets. We should pause and ask a quick philosophical question: what is such a definition doing? It is extremely doubtful that we should want to say that we have discovered some metaphysical identity facts; that, for example, the order relation on the natural numbers turned out to be the set R equals the set of ordered pairs n, m of natural numbers with n less than m that we defined in the Relations as Sets section. Here are three reasons why.

First: in the ordered-pair definition, we defined the ordered pair a, b equals the set containing the singleton a and the set a, b. Consider instead the definition the alternate ordered pair a, b equals the set containing the singleton b and the set a, b, which equals the ordered pair b, a. When a is not equal to b, we have that the ordered pair a, b is not equal to the alternate ordered pair a, b. But we could equally have regarded the alternate ordered pair a, b as our definition of an ordered pair, rather than the ordered pair a, b. Both definitions would have worked equally well. So now we have two equally good candidates to “be” the order relation on the natural numbers, namely: R is the set of ordered pairs n, m of natural numbers with n less than m; S is the set of alternate ordered pairs n, m of natural numbers with n less than m Since R is not equal to S, by extensionality, it is clear that they cannot both be identical to the order relation on the natural numbers. But it would just be arbitrary, and hence a bit embarrassing, to claim that R rather than S (or vice versa) is the ordering relation, as a matter of fact. (This is a very simple instance of an argument against set-theoretic reductionism which Benacerraf made famous in one thousand nine hundred sixty five. We will revisit it several times.)

Second: if we think that every relation should be identified with a set, then the relation of set-membership itself, is an element of, should be a particular set. Indeed, it would have to be the set the set of ordered pairs x, y such that x is an element of y. But does this set exist? Given Russell's Paradox, it is a non-trivial claim that such a set exists. In fact, it is possible to develop set theory in a rigorous way as an axiomatic theory, and that theory will indeed deny the existence of this set. So, even if some relations can be treated as sets, the relation of set-membership will have to be a special case.

Third: when we “identify” relations with sets, we said that we would allow ourselves to write R relates x to y for the ordered pair x, y is in R. This is fine, provided that the membership relation, “is an element of”, is treated as a predicate. But if we think that “is an element of” stands for a certain kind of set, then the expression “the ordered pair x, y is in R” just consists of three singular terms which stand for sets: “the ordered pair x, y”, “is an element of”, and “R”. And such a list of names is no more capable of expressing a proposition than the nonsense string: “the cup penholder the table”. Again, even if some relations can be treated as sets, the relation of set-membership must be a special case. (This rolls together a simple version of Frege's concept horse paradox, and a famous objection that Wittgenstein once raised against Russell.)

So where does this leave us? Well, there is nothing wrong with our saying that the relations on the numbers are sets. We just have to understand the spirit in which that remark is made. We are not stating a metaphysical identity fact. We are simply noting that, in certain contexts, we can (and will) treat (certain) relations as certain sets.
Special Properties of Relations
Introduction

Some kinds of relations turn out to be so common that they have been given special names. For instance, less than or equal to and is a subset of both relate their respective domains (say, the natural numbers in the case of less than or equal to and the power set of A in the case of is a subset of) in similar ways. To get at exactly how these relations are similar, and how they differ, we categorize them according to some special properties that relations can have. It turns out that (combinations of) some of these special properties are especially important: orders and equivalence relations.
Definition: Reflexivity
A relation R is a subset of A squared is reflexive if and only if, for every x is an element of A, R relates x to itself.
Definition: Transitivity
A relation R is a subset of A squared is transitive if and only if, whenever R relates x to y and R relates y to z, then also R relates x to z.
Definition: Symmetry
A relation R is a subset of A squared is symmetric if and only if, whenever R relates x to y, then also R relates y to x.
Definition: Anti-symmetry

A relation R is a subset of A squared is anti-symmetric if and only if, whenever both R relates x to y and R relates y to x, then x equals y (or, in other words: if x is not equal to y then either R does not relate x to y or R does not relate y to x).
Explanation

In a symmetric relation, R relates x to y and R relates y to x always hold together, or neither holds. In an anti-symmetric relation, the only way for R relates x to y and R relates y to x to hold together is if x equals y. Note that this does not require that R relates x to y and R relates y to x holds when x equals y, only that it isn't ruled out. So an anti-symmetric relation can be reflexive, but it is not the case that every anti-symmetric relation is reflexive. Also note that being anti-symmetric and merely not being symmetric are different conditions. In fact, a relation can be both symmetric and anti-symmetric at the same time (e.g., the identity relation is).
Definition: Connectivity
A relation R is a subset of A squared is connected if for all x and y are elements of A, if x is not equal to y, then either R relates x to y or R relates y to x.

Definition: Irreflexivity
A relation R is a subset of A squared is called irreflexive if, for all x is an element of A, not R relates x to itself.
Definition: Asymmetry
A relation R is a subset of A squared is called asymmetric if for no pair x and y are elements of A we have both R relates x to y and R relates y to x.

Note that if A is not the empty set, then no irreflexive relation on A is reflexive and every asymmetric relation on A is also anti-symmetric. However, there are R is a subset of A squared that are not reflexive and also not irreflexive, and there are anti-symmetric relations that are not asymmetric.
Equivalence Relations
The identity relation on a set is reflexive, symmetric, and transitive. Relations R that have all three of these properties are very common.
Definition: Equivalence relation
A relation R is a subset of A squared that is reflexive, symmetric, and transitive is called an equivalence relation. elements x and y of A are said to be R-equivalent if R relates x to y.

Equivalence relations give rise to the notion of an equivalence class. An equivalence relation “chunks up” the domain into different partitions. Within each partition, all the objects are related to one another; and no objects from different partitions relate to one another. Sometimes, it's helpful just to talk about these partitions directly. To that end, we introduce a definition:
Definition: Equivalence classes and quotient

Let R is a subset of A squared be an equivalence relation. For each x is an element of A, the equivalence class of x in A is the set the R equivalence class of x equals the set of y in A such that R relates x to y. The quotient of A under R is A modulo R equals the set of R equivalence classes of x for x in A, i.e., the set of these equivalence classes.
The next result vindicates the definition of an equivalence class, in proving that the equivalence classes are indeed the partitions of A:
Proposition: Equality of equivalence classes
If R is a subset of A squared is an equivalence relation, then R relates x to y if and only if the R equivalence class of x equals the R equivalence class of y.
Proof

For the left-to-right direction, suppose R relates x to y, and let z is in the R equivalence class of x. By definition, then, R relates x to z. Since R is an equivalence relation, R relates y to z. (Spelling this out: as R relates x to y and R is symmetric we have R relates y to x, and as R relates x to z and R is transitive we have R relates y to z.) So z is in the R equivalence class of y. Generalising, the R equivalence class of x is a subset of the R equivalence class of y. But exactly similarly, the R equivalence class of y is a subset of the R equivalence class of x. So the R equivalence class of x equals the R equivalence class of y, by extensionality.

For the right-to-left direction, suppose the R equivalence class of x equals the R equivalence class of y. Since R is reflexive, R relates y to itself, so y is in its own R equivalence class. Thus also y is in the R equivalence class of x by the assumption that the R equivalence class of x equals the R equivalence class of y. So R relates x to y.
End of proof.
Example: Congruence modulo n

A nice example of equivalence relations comes from modular arithmetic. For any a, b, and n is a positive integer, say that a is congruent to b modulo n if and only if dividing a by n gives the same remainder as dividing b by n. (Somewhat more symbolically: a is congruent to b modulo n if and only if, for some k is an integer, a minus b equals k times n.) Now, congruence modulo n is an equivalence relation, for any n. And there are exactly n distinct equivalence classes generated by congruence modulo n; that is, the quotient of the natural numbers by congruence modulo n has n elements. These are: the set of numbers divisible by n without remainder, i.e., the equivalence class of 0 modulo n; the set of numbers divisible by n with remainder 1, i.e., the equivalence class of 1 modulo n; and so on; and the set of numbers divisible by n with remainder n minus 1, i.e., the equivalence class of n minus 1 modulo n.

Orders
Explanation

Many of our comparisons involve describing some objects as being “less than”, “equal to”, or “greater than” other objects, in a certain respect. These involve order relations. But there are different kinds of order relations. For instance, some require that any two objects be comparable, others don't. Some include identity (like less than or equal to) and some exclude it (like less than). It will help us to have a taxonomy here.
Definition: Preorder
A relation which is both reflexive and transitive is called a preorder.
Definition: Partial order
A preorder which is also anti-symmetric is called a partial order.
Definition: Linear order
A partial order which is also connected is called a total order or linear order.
Example: Hierarchy of order types

Every linear order is also a partial order, and every partial order is also a preorder, but the converses don't hold. The universal relation on A is a preorder, since it is reflexive and transitive. But, if A has more than one element, the universal relation is not anti-symmetric, and so not a partial order.
Example: No-longer-than preorder

Consider the no longer than relation precedes or is equal to on the set of finite binary sequences: x precedes or equals y if and only if the length of x is less than or equal to the length of y. This is a preorder (reflexive and transitive), and even connected, but not a partial order, since it is not anti-symmetric. For instance, zero one is no longer than one zero and one zero is no longer than zero one, but zero one is not equal to one zero.
Example: Subset partial order

An important partial order is the relation is a subset of on a set of sets. This is not in general a linear order, since if a is not equal to b and we consider the power set of a, b equals the set containing the empty set, the singleton a, the singleton b, and the set a, b, we see that the singleton a is not a subset of the singleton b and the singleton a is not equal to the singleton b and the singleton b is not a subset of the singleton a.
Example: Divisibility as an order

The relation of divisibility without remainder gives us a partial order which isn't a linear order. For integers n and m, we write n divides m to mean n (evenly) divides m, i.e., if and only if there is some integer k so that m equals k times n. On the natural numbers, this is a partial order, but not a linear order: for instance, 2 does not divide 3 and also 3 does not divide 2. Considered as a relation on the integers, divisibility is only a preorder since it is not anti-symmetric: 1 divides negative 1 and negative 1 divides 1 but 1 is not equal to negative 1.
Example: Extension order on finite sequences

The extension relation on a set of sequences the set of finite sequences over A is the following: s is an initial segment of s prime if and only if s equals the empty sequence (the empty sequence), s equals s prime, or s equals the sequence s sub 1 through s sub n and s prime equals the sequence s sub 1 through s sub n, followed by s sub n plus 1 through s sub m. If s is an initial segment of s prime we also say that s is an initial segment of s prime. The extension relation on the set of finite sequences over A is a partial order but not a linear order, e.g., if a is not equal to b, then a b is not an initial segment of b a and b a is not an initial segment of a b.
Definition: Strict order
A strict order is a relation which is irreflexive, asymmetric, and transitive.
Definition: Strict linear order
A strict order which is also connected is called a strict total order or strict linear order.
Example: Strict and non-strict orders

Any strict order R on A can be turned into a partial order by adding the diagonal the identity relation on A, i.e., adding all the pairs the ordered pair x, x. (This is called the reflexive closure of R.) Conversely, starting from a partial order, one can get a strict order by removing the identity relation on A. These next two results make this precise.
Proposition: Add identity to a strict order
If R is a strict order on A, then R plus equals R union the identity relation on A is a partial order. Moreover, if R is a strict linear order, then R plus is a linear order.
Proof

Suppose R is a strict order, i.e., R is a subset of A squared and R is irreflexive, asymmetric, and transitive. Let R plus equals R union the identity relation on A. We have to show that R plus is reflexive, anti-symmetric, and transitive.
R plus is clearly reflexive, since the ordered pair x, x is in the identity relation on A, which is a subset of R plus for all x is an element of A.

To show R plus is anti-symmetric, suppose for reductio that R plus relates x to y and R plus relates y to x but x is not equal to y. Since the ordered pair x, y is in R union the identity relation on A, but the ordered pair x, y is not in the identity relation on A, we must have the ordered pair x, y is in R, i.e., R relates x to y. Similarly, R relates y to x. But this contradicts the assumption that R is asymmetric.

To establish transitivity, suppose that R plus relates x to y and R plus relates y to z. If both the ordered pair x, y is in R and the ordered pair y, z is in R, then the ordered pair x, z is in R since R is transitive. Otherwise, either the ordered pair x, y is in the identity relation on A, i.e., x equals y, or the ordered pair y, z is in the identity relation on A, i.e., y equals z. In the first case, we have that R plus relates y to z by assumption, x equals y, hence R plus relates x to z. Similarly in the second case. In either case, R plus relates x to z, thus, R plus is also transitive.

Concerning the “moreover” clause, suppose that R is also connected. So for all x is not equal to y, either R relates x to y or R relates y to x, i.e., either the ordered pair x, y is in R or the ordered pair y, x is in R. Since R is a subset of R plus, this remains true of R plus, so R plus is connected as well.
End of proof.
Proposition: Remove identity from a partial order
If R is a partial order on A, then R minus equals R set minus the identity relation on A is a strict order. Moreover, if R is a linear order, then R minus is a strict linear order.
Proof
This is left as an exercise.
End of proof.

The following simple result establishes that strict linear orders satisfy an extensionality-like property:
Proposition: Strict orders determined by predecessors
If less than is a strict linear order on A, then: for all a and b in A, if every x in A is less than a if and only if it is less than b, then a equals b
Proof

Suppose for every x in A, x is less than a if and only if x is less than b. If a is less than b, then a is less than itself, contradicting the fact that less than is irreflexive; so a is not less than b. Exactly similarly, b is not less than a. So a equals b, as less than is connected.
End of proof.
Graphs

A graph is a diagram in which points—called “nodes” or “vertices” (plural of “vertex”)—are connected by edges. Graphs are a ubiquitous tool in discrete mathematics and in computer science. They are incredibly useful for representing, and visualizing, relationships and structures, from concrete things like networks of various kinds to abstract structures such as the possible outcomes of decisions. There are many different kinds of graphs in the literature which differ, e.g., according to whether the edges are directed or not, have labels or not, whether there can be edges from a node to the same node, multiple edges between the same nodes, etc. Directed graphs have a special connection to relations.
Definition: Directed graph
A directed graph G equals the ordered pair V, E is a set of vertices V and a set of edges E is a subset of V squared.
Explanation

According to our definition, a graph just is a set together with a relation on that set. Of course, when talking about graphs, it's only natural to expect that they are graphically represented: we can draw a graph by connecting two vertices v sub 1 and v sub 2 by an arrow if and only if the ordered pair v sub 1, v sub 2 is in E. The only difference between a relation by itself and a graph is that a graph specifies the set of vertices, i.e., a graph may have isolated vertices. The important point, however, is that every relation R on a set X can be seen as a directed graph the ordered pair X, R, and conversely, a directed graph the ordered pair V, E can be seen as a relation E is a subset of V squared with the set V explicitly specified.

Trees

A particular kind of partial order which plays an important role in all parts of logic is a tree. Finite trees occur in elementary parts of logic: for example, formulas can be understood in terms of their decomposition into a syntax tree, while derivations in many derivation systems also take the form of finite trees.
Infinite trees appear already in the proof of the completeness theorems for propositional and first-order logic, and are used throughout mathematical logic.
The set-theoretic concept of a tree is closely related to the notion of a tree in graph theory. Here is a picture of a (finite) tree:
Finite rooted tree with root r
The lowermost root r has children a and b. Node a has children c, d, and e. Nodes b, c, d, and e are leaves.
Edges: r to a; r to b; a to c; a to d; a to e.
r — root.
a — child of r; parent of c, d, and e.
c — leaf; child of a.
d — leaf; child of a.
e — leaf; child of a.
b — leaf; child of r.

The lowermost node r is the root. Every node other than r has exactly one parent node immediately below it. We can think of the relation a node x stands in to a node y if y can be reached from x by following edges upwards as x being an ancestor of y.

The ancestor relation in a tree is a strict partial order. This motivates the set-theoretic definition. To state it we need two concepts. A least element in a set A partially ordered by less than or equal to is an element x is an element of A such that for all y is an element of A we have that x is less than or equal to y. A set is well-ordered by less than or equal to if every one of its non-empty subsets has a least element.
Definition: Tree

A tree is a pair T equals the ordered pair consisting of A and the less-than-or-equal relation such that A is a set and less than or equal to is a partial order on A with a unique least element r is an element of A (called the root) such that for all x is an element of A, the set the set of y such that y is less than or equal to x is well-ordered by less than or equal to.
Definition: Successors

Suppose T equals the ordered pair consisting of A and the less-than-or-equal relation is a tree. If x and y are elements of A, x is less than y, and there is no z is an element of A such that x is less than z, which is less than y, then we say that y is a successor of x.
The successors of x is an element of A are also called its children. If y is a successor of x, then we call x the predecessor or parent of y.
Proposition: A tree node has at most one predecessor
If the ordered pair consisting of A and the less-than-or-equal relation is a tree, then every x is an element of A other than the root has at most one predecessor.
Proof

Suppose y sub 1 is less than x and y sub 2 is less than x and y sub 1 is not equal to y sub 2. Then the set containing y sub 1 and y sub 2 is a subset of the set of z such that z is less than x. Since the set of z such that z is less than x is well-ordered by less than or equal to, its subset the set containing y sub 1 and y sub 2 has a least element, which obviously must be either y sub 1 or y sub 2. So either y sub 1 is less than or equal to y sub 2 or y sub 2 is less than or equal to y sub 1. We assumed that y sub 1 is not equal to y sub 2, so actually either y sub 1 is less than y sub 2 or y sub 2 is less than y sub 1. Since we assumed that y sub 1 is less than x and y sub 2 is less than x, we furthermore have that either y sub 1 is less than y sub 2, which is less than x or y sub 2 is less than y sub 1, which is less than x. So y sub 1 and y sub 2 cannot both be predecessors of x.
End of proof.
Definition: Finite and finitely branching trees

A tree T equals the ordered pair consisting of A and the less-than-or-equal relation is said to be infinite if A is an infinite set, and finite otherwise. If T is such that every x is an element of A has only finitely many successors, then we say that T is finitely branching.
Definition: Branches

Given a tree T equals the ordered pair consisting of A and the less-than-or-equal relation, a branch of T is a maximal chain in T, i.e., a set B is a subset of A such that for any x and y are elements of B either x is less than or equal to y or y is less than or equal to x, and for any z is an element of X set minus B there exists u is an element of B such that neither z is less than or equal to u nor u is less than or equal to z.
We use the set of branches of T to denote the set of all branches of T.
Example: Infinite binary tree

A classic example of a finitely branching tree is the infinite binary tree of finite sequences of 0s and 1s, sometimes denoted the set of finite binary sequences or the set of finite binary sequences, ordered by the extension relation is an initial segment of (e.g., one zero one is an initial segment of one zero one one zero one). Since any binary string can always be extended by adding a 0 or a 1 on the end, this tree contains infinitely many elements: every element s has exactly two successors, s followed by 0 and s followed by 1. Its root is the empty sequence the empty sequence.
Example: Tree of finite natural-number sequences

Slightly more generally, the set of finite sequences of natural numbers the set of finite sequences of natural numbers with the extension relation is an initial segment of is also a tree. It is obviously not finitely branching: every s is a finite sequence of natural numbers has infinitely many successors s followed by n, one for every n is a natural number. Every A is a subset of the set of finite natural-number sequences which is closed under is an initial segment of is a subtree of the set of finite sequences of natural numbers. (That is, A is such that if s is an element of A and s prime is an initial segment of s, then also s prime is an element of A.) All finite trees can be represented as finite subtrees of the set of finite sequences of natural numbers.
Proposition: König's lemma
If T equals the ordered pair consisting of A and the less-than-or-equal relation is a finitely branching infinite tree, then T has an infinite branch.
A special case of König's lemma widely used in computability theory, known as weak König's lemma, is the following: any infinite subtree of the set of finite binary sequences has an infinite branch.
Operations on Relations

It is often useful to modify or combine relations. In the proposition turning a strict order into a partial order, we considered the union of relations, which is just the union of two relations considered as sets of pairs. Similarly, in the proposition turning a partial order into a strict order, we considered the relative difference of relations. Here are some other operations we can perform on relations.
Definition: Inverse, product, restriction, and application
Let R, S be relations, and A be any set.
The inverse of R is R inverse equals the set of ordered pairs y, x such that the ordered pair x, y is in R.
The relative product of R and S is R relative product S equals the set of ordered pairs x, z such that there exists y with R relating x to y and S relating y to z.
The restriction of R to A is the restriction of R to A equals R intersect A squared.
The application of R to A is the image of A under R equals the set of y such that there exists x in A with R relating x to y
Example: Operations on the integer successor relation

Let S is a subset of the integers squared be the successor relation on the integers, i.e., S equals the set of integer pairs x, y such that x plus 1 equals y, so that S relates x to y if and only if x plus 1 equals y.
S inverse is the predecessor relation on the integers, i.e., the set of ordered pairs x, y in the integers squared such that x minus 1 equals y.
S relative product S is the set of integer pairs x, y such that x plus 2 equals y
the restriction of S to the natural numbers is the successor relation on the natural numbers.
the image of the set 1, 2, 3 under S is the set containing 2, 3, and 4.
Definition: Transitive closure
Let R is a subset of A squared be a binary relation.

The transitive closure of R is R plus equals the union over positive natural numbers n of R to the n power, where we recursively define R to the first power equals R and R to the power open parenthesis n plus 1 close parenthesis equals R to the power n relative product R.
The reflexive transitive closure of R is R star equals R plus union the identity relation on A.
Example: Closure of the integer successor relation

Take the successor relation S is a subset of the integers squared. S squared relates x to y if and only if x plus 2 equals y, S cubed relates x to y if and only if x plus 3 equals y, etc. So S plus relates x to y if and only if x plus n equals y for some n is greater than or equal to 1. In other words, S plus relates x to y if and only if x is less than y, and S star relates x to y if and only if x is less than or equal to y.

Basics
Explanation

A function is a map which sends each element of a given set to a specific element in some (other) given set. For instance, the operation of adding one defines a function: each number n is mapped to a unique number n plus one.

More generally, functions may take pairs, triples, etc., as inputs and return some kind of output. Many functions are familiar to us from basic arithmetic. For instance, addition and multiplication are functions. They take in two numbers and return a third.
In this mathematical, abstract sense, a function is a black box: what matters is only what output is paired with what input, not the method for calculating the output.
Definition: Function
A function f is a function from A to B is a mapping of each element of A to an element of B.

We call A the domain of f and B the codomain of f. The elements of A are called inputs or arguments of f, and the element of B that is paired with an argument x by f is called the value of f for argument x, written f of x.
The range the range of f of f is the subset of the codomain consisting of the values of f for some argument; the range of f equals the set of values f of x for x in A.

The diagram in Figure: Function from a three-element domain to a four-element codomain may help to think about functions. The ellipse on the left represents the function's domain; the ellipse on the right represents the function's codomain; and an arrow points from an argument in the domain to the corresponding value in the codomain.
Function from a three-element domain to a four-element codomain
Three domain elements each have exactly one outgoing arrow. The arrows end at three of the four codomain elements, leaving one codomain element unused.
Domain: three elements.
Codomain: four elements.
Mapping: three arrows, one from each domain element; three codomain elements receive an arrow and one does not.
Example: Multiplication on natural numbers

Multiplication takes pairs of natural numbers as inputs and maps them to natural numbers as outputs, so goes from the natural numbers cross the natural numbers (the domain) to the natural numbers (the codomain). As it turns out, the range is also the natural numbers, since every n is a natural number is n times one.
Example: Multiplication and square-root mappings

Multiplication is a function because it pairs each input—each pair of natural numbers—with a single output: multiplication is a function from pairs of natural numbers to the natural numbers. By contrast, mapping a natural number n to a real x such that x squared equals n is not functional, since each positive integer n has two square roots: the square root of n and negative the square root of n. We can make it functional by only returning the positive square root: the square-root function is a function from the natural numbers to the real numbers.
Example: Student grades and parents

The relation that pairs each student in a class with their final grade is a function—no student can get two different final grades in the same class. The relation that pairs each student in a class with their parents is not a function: students can have zero, or two, or more parents.
Explanation

We can define functions by specifying in some precise way what the value of the function is for every possible argument. Different ways of doing this are by giving a formula, describing a method for computing the value, or listing the values for each argument. However functions are defined, we must make sure that for each argument we specify one, and only one, value.
Example: Successor function and its range

Let f is a function from the natural numbers to the natural numbers be defined such that f of x equals x plus one. This is a definition that specifies f as a function which takes in natural numbers and outputs natural numbers. It tells us that, given a natural number x, f will output its successor x plus one. In this case, the codomain the natural numbers is not the range of f, since the natural number zero is not the successor of any natural number. The range of f is the set of all positive integers, the positive integers.
Example: Extensionally equal successor functions

Let g is a function from the natural numbers to the natural numbers be defined such that g of x equals x plus two minus one. This tells us that g is a function which takes in natural numbers and outputs natural numbers. Given a natural number n, g will output the predecessor of the successor of the successor of x, i.e., x plus one.
Explanation

We just considered two functions, f and g, with different definitions. However, these are the same function. After all, for any natural number n, we have that f of n equals n plus one, which equals n plus two minus one, which equals g of n. Otherwise put: our definitions for f and g specify the same mapping by means of different equations. Implicitly, then, we are relying upon a principle of extensionality for functions, if f of x equals g of x for every x, then f equals g provided that f and g share the same domain and codomain.
Example: Function defined by even and odd cases

We can also define functions by cases. For instance, we could define h is a function from the natural numbers to the natural numbers by h of x equals x divided by two if x is even, and the quantity x plus one, divided by two, if x is odd Since every natural number is either even or odd, the output of this function will always be a natural number. Just remember that if you define a function by cases, every possible input must fall into exactly one case. In some cases, this will require a proof that the cases are exhaustive and exclusive.
Kinds of Functions
Explanation
It will be useful to introduce a kind of taxonomy for some of the kinds of functions which we encounter most frequently.

To start, we might want to consider functions which have the property that every member of the codomain is a value of the function. Such functions are called surjective, and can be pictured as in Figure: Surjective function from three domain elements onto two codomain elements.
Surjective function from three domain elements onto two codomain elements
Each of the three domain elements has one outgoing arrow, and both codomain elements receive at least one arrow.
Domain: three elements.
Codomain: two elements.
Mapping: three arrows; every codomain element is a value, so the function is surjective.
Definition: Surjective function

A function f is a function from A to B is surjective if and only if B is also the range of f, i.e., for every y is an element of B there is at least one x is an element of A such that f of x equals y, or in symbols: for every y in B, there exists an x in A such that f of x equals y We call such a function a surjection from A to B.
Explanation
If you want to show that f is a surjection, then you need to show that every object in f's codomain is the value of f of x for some input x.

Note that any function induces a surjection. After all, given a function f is a function from A to B, let f prime is a function from A onto the range of f be defined by f prime of x equals f of x. Since the range of f is defined as the set of values f of x in B for x in A, this function f prime is guaranteed to be a surjection
Explanation

Now, any function maps each possible input to a unique output. But there are also functions which never map different inputs to the same outputs. Such functions are called injective, and can be pictured as in Figure: Injective function from three domain elements into a seven-element codomain.
Injective function from three domain elements into a seven-element codomain
The three domain elements point to three distinct codomain elements. Four codomain elements receive no arrow.
Domain: three elements.
Codomain: seven elements.
Mapping: three arrows with distinct targets, so no two arguments have the same value.
Definition: Injective function

A function f is a function from A to B is injective if and only if for each y is an element of B there is at most one x is an element of A such that f of x equals y. We call such a function a injection from A to B.
Explanation
If you want to show that f is a injection, you need to show that for any elements x and y of f's domain, if f of x equals f of y, then x equals y.
Example: Injective and surjective combinations
The constant function f is a function from the natural numbers to the natural numbers given by f of x equals one is neither injective, nor surjective.
The identity function f is a function from the natural numbers to the natural numbers given by f of x equals x is both injective and surjective.
The successor function f is a function from the natural numbers to the natural numbers given by f of x equals x plus one is injective but not surjective.

The function f is a function from the natural numbers to the natural numbers defined by: f of x equals x divided by two if x is even, and the quantity x plus one, divided by two, if x is odd is surjective, but not injective.
Explanation

Often enough, we want to consider functions which are both injective and surjective. We call such functions bijective. They look like the function pictured in Figure: Bijective function pairing three domain elements with three codomain elements. Bijections are also sometimes called one-to-one correspondences, since they uniquely pair elements of the codomain with elements of the domain.
Bijective function pairing three domain elements with three codomain elements
Three arrows pair the three domain elements one-to-one with the three codomain elements; every codomain element is used exactly once.
Domain: three elements.
Codomain: three elements.
Mapping: three one-to-one arrows covering the codomain, so the function is both injective and surjective.
Definition: Bijection
A function f is a function from A to B is bijective if and only if it is both surjective and injective. We call such a function a bijection from A to B (or between A and B).
Functions as Relations
Explanation

A function which maps elements of A to elements of B obviously defines a relation between A and B, namely the relation which holds between x and y if and only if f of x equals y. In fact, we might even—if we are interested in reducing the building blocks of mathematics for instance—identify the function f with this relation, i.e., with a set of pairs. This then raises the question: which relations define functions in this way?
Definition: Graph of a function

Let f is a function from A to B be a function. The graph of f is the relation the graph R sub f is a subset of A cross B defined by the graph R sub f is the set of ordered pairs x, y such that f of x equals y
Explanation

The graph of a function is uniquely determined, by extensionality. Moreover, extensionality (on sets) will immediately vindicate the implicit principle of extensionality for functions, whereby if f and g share a domain and codomain then they are identical if they agree on all values.
Similarly, if a relation is “functional”, then it is the graph of a function.
Proposition: Relations that are function graphs
Let R is a subset of A cross B be such that:
If R relates x to y and R relates x to z then y equals z; and
for every x is an element of A there is some y is an element of B such that the ordered pair x, y is in R.
Then R is the graph of the function f is a function from A to B defined by f of x equals y if and only if R relates x to y.
Proof

Suppose there is a y such that R relates x to y. If there were another z is not equal to y such that R relates x to z, the condition on R would be violated. Hence, if there is a y such that R relates x to y, this y is unique, and so f is well-defined. Obviously, R sub f equals R.
End of proof.
Explanation

Every function f is a function from A to B has a graph, i.e., a relation on A cross B defined by f of x equals y. On the other hand, every relation R is a subset of A cross B with the properties given in Proposition: Relations that are function graphs is the graph of a function f is a function from A to B. Because of this close connection between functions and their graphs, we can think of a function simply as its graph. In other words, functions can be identified with certain relations, i.e., with certain sets of tuples. Note, though, that the spirit of this “identification” is as in Philosophical Reflections: it is not a claim about the metaphysics of functions, but an observation that it is convenient to treat functions as certain sets. One reason that this is so convenient, is that we can now consider performing similar operations on functions as we performed on relations (see Operations on Relations). In particular:
Definition: Function restriction and image
Let f is a function from A to B be a function with C is a subset of A.

The restriction of f to C is the function the restriction of f to C, from C to B defined by the restriction of f to C, evaluated at x, equals f of x for all x is an element of C. In other words, the restriction of f to C equals the ordered pairs x, y in the graph of f whose first coordinate is in C.
The application of f to C is the image of C under f equals the set of values f of x for x in C. We also call this the image of C under f.
Explanation

It follows from these definitions that the range of f equals the image of the domain of f under f, for any function f. These notions are exactly as one would expect, given the definitions in Operations on Relations and our identification of functions with relations. But two other operations—inverses and relative products—require a little more detail. We will provide that in Inverses of Functions and Composition of Functions.
Inverses of Functions
Explanation

We think of functions as maps. An obvious question to ask about functions, then, is whether the mapping can be “reversed.” For instance, the successor function f of x equals x plus one can be reversed, in the sense that the function g of y equals y minus one “undoes” what f does.

But we must be careful. Although the definition of g defines a function from the integers to the integers, it does not define a function from the natural numbers to the natural numbers, since g of zero is not a natural number. So even in simple cases, it is not quite obvious whether a function can be reversed; it may depend on the domain and codomain.
This is made more precise by the notion of an inverse of a function.
Definition: Inverse function
A function g is a function from B to A is an inverse of a function f is a function from A to B if f of g of y equals y and g of f of x equals x for all x is an element of A and y is an element of B.
If f has an inverse g, we often write f inverse instead of g.
Explanation

Now we will determine when functions have inverses. A good candidate for an inverse of f is a function from A to B is g is a function from B to A “defined by” g of y equals the x such that f of x equals y But the scare quotes around “defined by” (and “the”) suggest that this is not a definition. At least, it will not always work, with complete generality. For, in order for this definition to specify a function, there has to be one and only one x such that f of x equals y—the output of g has to be uniquely specified. Moreover, it has to be specified for every y is an element of B. If there are x sub one and x sub two is an element of A with x sub one is not equal to x sub two but f of x sub one equals f of x sub two, then g of y would not be uniquely specified for y equals f of x sub one, which equals f of x sub two. And if there is no x at all such that f of x equals y, then g of y is not specified at all. In other words, for g to be defined, f must be both injective and surjective.

Let's go slowly. We'll divide the question into two: Given a function f is a function from A to B, when is there a function g is a function from B to A so that g of f of x equals x? Such a g “undoes” what f does, and is called a left inverse of f. Secondly, when is there a function h is a function from B to A so that f of h of y equals y? Such an h is called a right inverse of f—f “undoes” what h does.
Proposition: Injective functions have left inverses
If f is a function from A to B is injective, then there is a left inverse g is a function from B to A of f so that g of f of x equals x for all x is an element of A.
Proof

Suppose that f is a function from A to B is injective. Consider a y is an element of B. If y is in the range of f, there is an x is an element of A so that f of x equals y. Because f is injective, there is only one such x is an element of A. Then we can define: g of y equals x, i.e., g of y is “the” x is an element of A such that f of x equals y. If y is not in the range of f, we can map it to any a is an element of A. So, we can pick an a is an element of A and define g is a function from B to A by: g of y equals x when f of x equals y, and equals a when y is not in the range of f It is defined for all y is an element of B, since for each such y is in the range of f there is exactly one x is an element of A such that f of x equals y. By definition, if y equals f of x, then g of y equals x, i.e., g of f of x equals x.
End of proof.
