Chapter. Incompleteness and Provability.

Section. Introduction. Hilbert thought that a system of axioms for a mathematical structure, such as the natural numbers, is inadequate unless it allows one to derive all true statements about the structure. Combined with his later interest in formal systems of deduction, this suggests that he thought that we should guarantee that, say, the formal systems we are using to reason about the natural numbers is not only consistent, but also complete, that is, every statement in its language is either derivable or its negation is. Goedel's first incompleteness theorem shows that no such system of axioms exists: there is no complete, consistent, axiomatizable formal system for arithmetic. In fact, no “sufficiently strong,” consistent, axiomatizable mathematical theory is complete. A more important goal of Hilbert's, the centerpiece of his program for the justification of modern (“classical”) mathematics, was to find finitary consistency proofs for formal systems representing classical reasoning. With regard to Hilbert's program, then, Goedel's second incompleteness theorem was a much bigger blow. The second incompleteness theorem can be stated in vague terms, like the first incompleteness theorem. Roughly speaking, it says that no sufficiently strong theory of arithmetic can prove its own consistency. We will have to take “sufficiently strong” to include a little bit more than Q . The idea behind Goedel's original proof of the incompleteness theorem can be found in the Epimenides paradox. Epimenides, a Cretan, asserted that all Cretans are liars; a more direct form of the paradox is the assertion “this sentence is false.” Essentially, by replacing truth with derivability, Goedel was able to formalize a sentence which, in a roundabout way, asserts that it itself is not derivable. If that sentence were derivable, the theory would then be inconsistent. Goedel showed that the negation of that sentence is also not derivable from the system of axioms he was considering. (For this second part, Goedel had to assume that the theory T is what's called “ omega -consistent.” omega -Consistency is related to consistency, but is a stronger property. Footnote. That is, any omega -consistent theory is consistent, but not vice versa. End footnote. A few years after Goedel, Rosser showed that assuming simple consistency of T is enough.) The first challenge is to understand how one can construct a sentence that refers to itself. For every formula A in the language of Q , let the numeral naming A denote the numeral corresponding to the Goedel number of A . Think about what this means: A is a formula in the language of Q , the Goedel number of A is a natural number, and the numeral naming A is a term in the language of Q . So every formula A in the language of Q has a name, the numeral naming A , which is a term in the language of Q ; this provides us with a conceptual framework in which formulas in the language of Q can “say” things about other formulas. The following lemma is known as the fixed-point lemma. Lemma. Let T be any theory extending Q , and let B of x be any formula with only the variable x free. Then there is a sentence A such that T proves that A is equivalent to B of the numeral naming A . End lemma. The lemma asserts that given any property B of x , there is a sentence A that asserts “ B of x is true of me,” and T “knows” this. How can we construct such a sentence? Consider the following version of the Epimenides paradox, due to Quine: Quotation. “Yields falsehood when preceded by its quotation” yields falsehood when preceded by its quotation. End quotation. This sentence is not directly self-referential. It simply makes an assertion about the syntactic objects between quotes, and, in doing so, it is on par with sentences like List. Next item. “Robert” is a nice name. Next item. “I ran.” is a short sentence. Next item. “Has three words” has three words. End list. But what happens when one takes the phrase “yields falsehood when preceded by its quotation,” and precedes it with a quoted version of itself? Then one has the original sentence! In short, the sentence asserts that it is false. End section.

Section. The Fixed-Point Lemma. Section. The First Incompleteness Theorem. We can now describe Goedel's original proof of the first incompleteness theorem. Let T be any computably axiomatized theory in a language extending the language of arithmetic, such that T includes the axioms of Q . This means that, in particular, T represents computable functions and relations. We have argued that, given a reasonable coding of formulas and proofs as numbers, the relation the external proof coding relation for T applied to x and y is computable, where the external proof coding relation for T applied to x and y holds if and only if x is the Goedel number of a derivation of the formula with Goedel number y in T . In fact, for the particular theory that Goedel had in mind, Goedel was able to show that this relation is primitive recursive, using the list of forty five functions and relations in his paper. The forty fiveth relation, x B y , is just the external proof coding relation for T applied to x and y for his particular choice of T . Remember that where Goedel uses the word “recursive” in his paper, we would now use the phrase “primitive recursive.” Since the external proof coding relation for T applied to x and y is computable, it is representable in T . We will use the arithmetic proof formula for T applied to x and y to refer to the formula that represents it. Let the arithmetic provability formula for T applied to y be the formula there exists x such that the arithmetic proof formula for T holds of x and y . This describes the forty sixth relation, Bew of y , on Goedel's list. As Goedel notes, this is the only relation that “cannot be asserted to be recursive.” What he probably meant is this: from the definition, it is not clear that it is computable; and later developments, in fact, show that it isn't. Let T be an axiomatizable theory containing Q . Then the external proof coding relation for T applied to x and y is decidable, hence representable in Q by a formula the arithmetic proof formula for T applied to x and y . Let the arithmetic provability formula for T applied to y be the formula we described above. By the fixed-point lemma, there is a formula G subscript T such that Q (and hence T ) derives Displayed expression. G subscript T is equivalent to the negation of the arithmetic provability formula for T at the numeral naming G subscript T. End displayed expression. Note that G subscript T says, in essence, “ G subscript T is not derivable in T .” Lemma. If T is a consistent, axiomatizable theory extending Q , then T does not prove G subscript T . End lemma. Section. Comparison with Goedel's Original Paper. It is worthwhile to spend some time with Goedel's one thousand nine hundred thirty one paper. The introduction sketches the ideas we have just discussed. Even if you just skim through the paper, it is easy to see what is going on at each stage: first Goedel describes the formal system P (syntax, axioms, proof rules); then he defines the primitive recursive functions and relations; then he shows that x B y is primitive recursive, and argues that the primitive recursive functions and relations are represented in theory P . He then goes on to prove the incompleteness theorem, as above. In Section three, he shows that one can take the unprovable assertion to be a sentence in the language of arithmetic. This is the origin of the beta -lemma, which is what we also used to handle sequences in showing that the recursive functions are representable in Q . Goedel doesn't go so far to isolate a minimal set of axioms that suffice, but we now know that Q will do the trick. Finally, in Section four, he sketches a proof of the second incompleteness theorem. End section.

Section. The Derivability Conditions for P A . Peano arithmetic, or P A , is the theory extending Q with induction axioms for all formulas. In other words, one adds to Q axioms of the form Displayed expression. if A holds of zero and, for every x, A of x implies A of the successor of x, then A holds of every x. End displayed expression. for every formula A . Notice that this is really a schema, which is to say, infinitely many axioms (and it turns out that P A is not finitely axiomatizable). But since one can effectively determine whether or not a string of symbols is an instance of an induction axiom, the set of axioms for P A is computable. P A is a much more robust theory than Q . For example, one can easily prove that addition and multiplication are commutative, using induction in the usual way. In fact, most finitary number-theoretic and combinatorial arguments can be carried out in P A . Since P A is computably axiomatized, the derivability predicate the external proof coding relation for P A applied to x and y is computable and hence represented in Q (and so, in P A ). As before, we will take the arithmetic proof formula for P A applied to x and y to denote the formula representing the relation. Let the arithmetic provability formula for P A applied to y be the formula there exists x such that the external proof coding relation for P A holds of x and y , which, intuitively says, “ y is derivable from the axioms of P A .” The reason we need a little bit more than the axioms of Q is we need to know that the theory we are using is strong enough to derive a few basic facts about this derivability predicate. This exercise remains unsolved. Digression. The moral of the story is that no “reasonable” consistent theory for mathematics can derive its own consistency statement. Suppose T is a theory of mathematics that includes Q and Hilbert's “finitary” reasoning (whatever that may be). Then, the whole of T cannot derive the consistency statement of T , and so, a fortiori, the finitary fragment can't derive the consistency statement of T either. In that sense, there cannot be a finitary consistency proof for “all of mathematics.” There is some leeway in interpreting the term “finitary,” and Goedel, in the one thousand nine hundred thirty one paper, grants the possibility that something we may consider “finitary” may lie outside the kinds of mathematics Hilbert wanted to formalize. But Goedel was being charitable; today, it is hard to see how we might find something that can reasonably be called finitary but is not formalizable in, say, Z F C , Zermelo—Fraenkel set theory with the axiom of choice. End digression. End section.

Section. Loeb's Theorem. The Goedel sentence for a theory T is a fixed point of the negation of the arithmetic provability formula for T at y , that is, a sentence G such that Displayed expression. T proves that the negation of its arithmetic provability formula at the numeral naming G is equivalent to G. End displayed expression. It is not derivable, because if T proves G , (a) by derivability condition (one), T proves that its arithmetic provability formula holds of the numeral naming G , and (b) T proves G together with T proves that the negation of its arithmetic provability formula at the numeral naming G is equivalent to G gives T proves the negation of its arithmetic provability formula at the numeral naming G , and so T would be inconsistent. Now it is natural to ask about the status of a fixed point of the arithmetic provability formula for T applied to y , that is, a sentence H such that Displayed expression. T proves that its arithmetic provability formula at the numeral naming H is equivalent to H. End displayed expression. If it were derivable, T proves that its arithmetic provability formula holds of the numeral naming H by condition (one), but the same conclusion follows if we apply modus ponens to the equivalence above. Hence, we don't get that T is inconsistent, at least not by the same argument as in the case of the Goedel sentence. This of course does not show that T does derive H . We can make headway on this question if we generalize it a bit. The left-to-right direction of the fixed point equivalence, if the arithmetic provability formula for T holds of the numeral naming H, then H , is an instance of a general schema called a reflection principle: if the arithmetic provability formula for T holds of the numeral naming A, then A . It is called that because it expresses, in a sense, that T can “reflect” about what it can derive; basically it says, “If T can derive A , then A is true,” for any A . This is true for sound theories only, of course, and this suggests that theories will in general not derive every instance of it. So which instances can a theory (strong enough, and satisfying the derivability conditions) derive? Certainly all those where A itself is derivable. And that's it, as the next result shows. Theorem. If T derives if the arithmetic provability formula for T holds of the numeral naming A, then A , then in fact T derives A . End theorem. Put differently, if T does not prove A , then T does not prove the implication: if its arithmetic provability formula holds of the numeral naming A, then A . This result is known as Loeb's theorem. Section. The Undefinability of Truth. The notion of definability depends on having a formal semantics for the language of arithmetic. We have described a set of formulas and sentences in the language of arithmetic. The “intended interpretation” is to read such sentences as making assertions about the natural numbers, and such an assertion can be true or false. Let the standard natural number structure N be the structure with domain the natural numbers and the standard interpretation for the symbols in the language of arithmetic. Then A is true in the standard natural number structure N means “ A is true in the standard interpretation.” Definition. Section. Introduction. In first-order logic, we combine the non-logical symbols of a given language, that is, its constant symbols, function symbols, and predicate symbols, with the logical symbols to express things about first-order structures. This is done using the notion of satisfaction, which relates a structure the structure M , together with a variable assignment s , and a formula A : the statement that structure M under assignment s satisfies A holds if and only if what A expresses when its constant symbols, function symbols, and predicate symbols are interpreted as the structure M says, and its free variables are interpreted as s says, is true. The interpretation of the identity predicate the equality symbol is built into the definition of structure M under assignment s satisfies the following: A , as is the interpretation of the universal quantifier and the existential quantifier . The former is always interpreted as the identity relation on the domain the domain of structure M of the structure, and the quantifiers are always interpreted as ranging over the entire domain. But, crucially, quantification is only allowed over elements of the domain, and so only object variables are allowed to follow a quantifier. In second-order logic, both the language and the definition of satisfaction are extended to include free and bound function and predicate variables, and quantification over them. These variables are related to function symbols and predicate symbols the same way that object variables are related to constant symbols. They play the same role in the formation of terms and formulas of second-order logic, and quantification over them is handled in a similar way. The central logical notions of validity, entailment, and satisfiability are defined the same way for second-order logic as they are for first-order logic, except that the underlying satisfaction relation is now that for second-order formulas. If Gamma is not satisfiable it is called unsatisfiable. End definition. End section.

Section. Expressive Power. Quantification over second-order variables is responsible for an immense increase in the expressive power of the language over that of first-order logic. Second-order existential quantification lets us say that functions or relations with certain properties exist. In first-order logic, the only way to do that is to specify a non-logical symbol (that is, a function symbol or predicate symbol) for this purpose. Second-order universal quantification lets us say that all subsets of, relations on, or functions from the domain to the domain have a property. In first-order logic, we can only say that the subsets, relations, or functions assigned to one of the non-logical symbols of the language have a property. And when we say that subsets, relations, functions exist that have a property, or that all of them have it, we can use second-order quantification in specifying this property as well. Chapter. Metatheory of Second-order Logic.

Section. Introduction. First-order logic has a number of nice properties. We know it is not decidable, but at least it is axiomatizable. That is, there are proof systems for first-order logic which are sound and complete, that is, they give rise to a derivability relation the derivability relation with the property that for any set of sentences Gamma and sentence A , Gamma logically entails A if and only if A is derivable from Gamma . This means in particular that the validities of first-order logic are computably enumerable. There is a computable function f from the natural numbers to the sentences of language L such that the values of f are all and only the valid sentences of the language L . This is so because derivations can be enumerated, and those that derive a single sentence are then mapped to that sentence. Second-order logic is more expressive than first-order logic, and so it is in general more complicated to capture its validities. In fact, we'll show that second-order logic is not only undecidable, but its validities are not even computably enumerable. This means there can be no sound and complete proof system for second-order logic (although sound, but incomplete proof systems are available and in fact are important objects of research). First-order logic also has two more properties: it is compact (if every finite subset of a set Gamma of sentences is satisfiable, Gamma itself is satisfiable) and the Loewenheim—Skolem Theorem holds for it (if Gamma has an infinite model it has a denumerable model). Both of these results fail for second-order logic. Again, the reason is that second-order logic can express facts about the size of domains that first-order logic cannot. End section.

Section. Second-order Logic is not Compact. Call a set of sentences Gamma finitely satisfiable if every one of its finite subsets is satisfiable. First-order logic has the property that if a set of sentences Gamma is finitely satisfiable, it is satisfiable. This property is called compactness. It has an equivalent version involving entailment: if Gamma logically entails A , then already Gamma subscript zero logically entails A for some finite subset Gamma subscript zero of Gamma . In this version it is an immediate corollary of the completeness theorem: for if Gamma logically entails A , by completeness A is derivable from Gamma . But a derivation can only make use of finitely many sentences of Gamma . Compactness is not true for second-order logic. There are sets of second-order sentences that are finitely satisfiable but not satisfiable, and that entail some A without a finite subset entailing A . Theorem. Second-order logic is not compact. Section. The Loewenheim—Skolem Theorem Fails for Second-order Logic. The (Downward) Loewenheim—Skolem Theorem states that every set of sentences with an infinite model has an enumerable model. Section. Introduction. Since second-order logic can quantify over subsets of the domain as well as functions, it is to be expected that some amount, at least, of set theory can be carried out in second-order logic. By “carry out,” we mean that it is possible to express set theoretic properties and statements in second-order logic, and is possible without any special, non-logical vocabulary for sets (for example, the membership predicate symbol of set theory). For instance, we can define unions and intersections of sets and the subset relationship, but also compare the sizes of sets, and state results such as Cantor's Theorem. End section.

Chapter. Introduction. Editorial note. This chapter consists of Jeremy's original concise notes on the lambda calculus. The sections need to be combined, and the material on lambda definability merged with the material in the separate, more detailed chapter on lambda definability. End editorial note.

Section. Overview. The lambda calculus was originally designed by Alonzo Church in the early nineteen thirties as a basis for constructive logic, and not as a model of the computable functions. But it was soon shown to be equivalent to other definitions of computability, such as the Turing computable functions and the partial recursive functions. The fact that this initially came as a small surprise makes the characterization all the more interesting. Lambda notation is a convenient way of referring to a function directly by a symbolic expression which defines it, instead of defining a name for it. Instead of saying “let f be the function defined by f of x equals x plus three ,” one can say, “let f be the function lambda x, with body x plus three .” In other words, lambda x, with body x plus three is just a name for the function that adds three to its argument. In this expression, x is a dummy variable, or a placeholder: the same function can just as well be denoted by lambda y, with body y plus three . The notation works even with other parameters around. For example, suppose g of x and y is a function of two variables, and k is a natural number. Then lambda x, with body g of x and k is the function which maps any x to g of x and k . This way of defining a function from a symbolic expression is known as lambda abstraction. The flip side of lambda abstraction is application: assuming one has a function f (say, defined on the natural numbers), one can apply it to any value, like two. In conventional notation, of course, we write f of two for the result. What happens when you combine lambda abstraction with application? Then the resulting expression can be simplified, by “plugging” the applicand in for the abstracted variable. For example, Displayed expression. the abstraction lambda x, with body x plus three, applied to two. End displayed expression. can be simplified to two plus three . Up to this point, we have done nothing but introduce new notations for conventional notions. The lambda calculus, however, represents a more radical departure from the set-theoretic viewpoint. In this framework: List. Next item. Everything denotes a function. Next item. Functions can be defined using lambda abstraction. Next item. Anything can be applied to anything else. End list. For example, if capital F is a term in the lambda calculus, capital F applied to itself is always assumed to be meaningful. This liberal framework is known as the untyped lambda calculus, where “untyped” means “no restriction on what can be applied to what.” Digression. There is also a typed lambda calculus, which is an important variation on the untyped version. Although in many ways the typed lambda calculus is similar to the untyped one, it is much easier to reconcile with a classical set-theoretic framework, and has some very different properties. Research on the lambda calculus has proved to be central in theoretical computer science, and in the design of programming languages. LISP, designed by John McCarthy in the nineteen fifties, is an early example of a language that was influenced by these ideas. End digression. End section.

Section. The Syntax of the Lambda Calculus. One starts with a sequence of variables x , y , z , and so on and some constant symbols a , b , c , and so on. The set of terms is defined inductively, as follows: List. Next item. Each variable is a term. Next item. Each constant is a term. Next item. If capital M and capital N are terms, so is capital M applied to capital N . Next item. If capital M is a term and x is a variable, then the abstraction lambda x, with body capital M is a term. End list. Terms of the form capital M applied to capital N are called applications and those of the form the abstraction lambda x, with body capital M abstractions. The system without any constants at all is called the pure lambda calculus. We'll mainly be working in the pure lambda -calculus, so all lowercase letters will stand for variables. We use uppercase letters ( capital M , capital N , etc.) to stand for terms of the lambda -calculus. We will follow a few notational conventions: Convention. List. Next item. When parentheses are left out, application takes place from left to right. For example, if capital M , capital N , capital P , and capital Q are terms, then capital M applied successively to capital N, capital P, and capital Q abbreviates the result of applying capital M to capital N, then to capital P, then to capital Q . From example, lambda x, with body capital M applied first to capital N and then to capital P is read lambda x, with body the result of applying capital M to capital N, applied to capital P . It will be convenient to think of these as being the “same” term; in other words, when we say that capital M and capital N are the same, we also mean “up to renamings of the bound variables.” Variables that are in the scope of a lambda are called “bound”, while others are called “free.” There are no free variables in the previous example; but in Displayed expression. the abstraction lambda z, with body y applied to z, applied to x. Section. Reduction of Lambda Terms. What can one do with lambda terms? Simplify them. If capital M and capital N are any lambda terms and x is any variable, we can use capital M with capital N substituted for free x, avoiding variable capture to denote the result of substituting capital N for x in capital M , after renaming any bound variables of capital M that would interfere with the free variables of capital N after the substitution. For example, Displayed expression. substituting the term y applied to y and then z for free x in lambda w with body x applied to x and then w, gives lambda w with body the term y applied to y and then z, applied to a second copy of that same term, then applied to w. Alternative notations for substitution are open square bracket, capital N slash x, close square bracket, followed by capital M , open square bracket, x slash capital N, close square bracket, followed by capital M , and also capital M followed by open square bracket, x slash capital N, close square bracket . Section. The Church—Rosser Property. Theorem. Let capital M , capital N subscript one , and capital N subscript two be terms, such that capital M beta reduces to capital N subscript one and capital M beta reduces to capital N subscript two . Then there is a term capital P such that capital N subscript one beta reduces to capital P and capital N subscript two beta reduces to capital P . End theorem. Corollary. Suppose capital M can be reduced to normal form. Then this normal form is unique. End corollary. Proof. If capital M beta reduces to capital N subscript one and capital M beta reduces to capital N subscript two , by the previous theorem there is a term capital P such that capital N subscript one and capital N subscript two both reduce to capital P . If capital N subscript one and capital N subscript two are both in normal form, this can only happen if capital N subscript one, capital P, and capital N subscript two are the same term, under the chapter's bound variable renaming convention . End proof. Finally, we will say that two terms capital M and capital N are beta -equivalent, or just equivalent, if they reduce to a common term; in other words, if there is some capital P such that capital M beta reduces to capital P and capital N beta reduces to capital P . This is written capital M is beta equivalent to capital N . Using the Church Rosser theorem , you can check that beta equivalence is an equivalence relation, with the additional property that for every capital M and capital N , if capital M beta reduces to capital N or capital N beta reduces to capital M , then capital M is beta equivalent to capital N . (In fact, one can show that beta equivalence is the smallest equivalence relation having this property.) End section.

Section. Currying. A lambda -abstract lambda x, with body capital M represents a function of one argument, which is quite a limitation when we want to define function accepting multiple arguments. One way to do this would be by extending the lambda -calculus to allow the formation of pairs, triples, etc., in which case, say, a three-place function lambda x, with body capital M would expect its argument to be a triple. However, it is more convenient to do this by Currying. Let's consider an example. We'll pretend for a moment that we have a plus operation in the lambda -calculus. The addition function is two place , that is, it takes two arguments. But a lambda -abstract only gives us functions of one argument: the syntax does not allow expressions like the proposed abstraction lambda, binding the pair x comma y, with body x plus y . However, we can consider the one-place function f subscript x applied to y given by lambda y, with body x plus y , which adds x to its single argument y . Actually, this is not a single function, but a family of different functions “add x ,” one for each number x . Now we can define another one-place function g as lambda x, with body f subscript x . Applied to argument x , g of x returns the function f subscript x —so its values are other functions. Now if we apply g to x , and then the result to y we get: g of x applied to y equals f subscript x of y, which equals x plus y . In this way, the one-place function g can do the same job as the two-place addition function. “Currying” simply refers to this trick for turning two-place functions into one place functions (whose values are one-place functions). Here is an example properly in the syntax of the lambda -calculus. How do we represent the function f of x and y equals x ? If we want to define a function that accepts two arguments and returns the first, we can write lambda x, then lambda y, with innermost body x , which literally is a function that accepts an argument x and returns the function lambda y, with body x . The function lambda y, with body x accepts another argument y , but drops it, and always returns x . Section. Lambda-definable Arithmetical Functions. How can the lambda calculus serve as a model of computation? At first, it is not even clear how to make sense of this statement. To talk about computability on the natural numbers, we need to find a suitable representation for such numbers. Here is one that works surprisingly well. Definition. For each natural number n , define the Church numeral n with an overbar to be the lambda term lambda x, then lambda y, with body x applied repeatedly to y, nested to the right, with the number of applications specified as n , where there are n x apostrophe s in all. Section. Lambda-definable Functions are Computable. Theorem. If a partial function f is lambda-defined by a lambda term, it is computable. End theorem. Proof. Suppose a function f is lambda-defined by a lambda term capital X . Let us describe an informal procedure to compute f . On input m subscript zero , and so on, m subscript n minus one , write down the term capital X applied successively to the Church numerals for m subscript zero through m subscript n minus one . Build a tree, first writing down all the one-step reductions of the original term; below that, write all the one-step reductions of those (that is, the two-step reductions of the original term); and keep going. If you ever reach a numeral, return that as the answer; otherwise, the function is undefined. An appeal to Church's thesis tells us that this function is computable. A better way to prove the theorem would be to give a recursive description of this search procedure. For example, one could define a sequence primitive recursive functions and relations, “ Is A Subterm ,” “ Substitute ,” “ Reduces To In One Step ,” “ Reduction Sequence ,” “ Numeral ,” etc. The partial recursive procedure for computing f of m subscript zero through m subscript n minus one is then to search for a sequence of one-step reductions starting with capital X applied successively to the Church numerals for m subscript zero through m subscript n minus one and ending with a numeral, and return the number corresponding to that numeral. Section. Terms. The terms of the lambda calculus are built up inductively from an infinite supply of variables v subscript zero , v subscript one , and so on, the symbol “ lambda ”, and parentheses. The set of terms of the lambda calculus is defined inductively by: List. Next item. If x is a variable, then x is a term. Next item. If both capital M and capital N are terms, then the application of capital M to capital N, end application is a term. End list. End definition. If a term lambda x, with body capital M, end abstraction is formed according to the abstraction formation clause we say it is the result of an abstraction, and the x in the lambda binder on x is called a parameter. Section. Unique Readability. We may wonder if for each term there is a unique way of forming it, and there is. For each lambda term there is only one way to construct and interpret it. In the following discussion, a formation is the procedure of constructing a term using the formation rules (one or several times) of the definition of lambda terms . Lemma. A term starts with either a variable or a parenthesis. End lemma. Proof. Something counts as a term only if it is constructed according to the definition of lambda terms . If it is the result of the variable formation clause , it must be a variable. If it is the result of the abstraction formation clause or the application formation clause , it starts with a parenthesis. End proof. Lemma. The result of an application starts with either two parentheses or a parenthesis and a variable. End lemma. Proof. If capital M is the result of an application, it is of the form the application of capital P to capital Q, end application , so it begins with a parenthesis. Since capital P is a term, by the lemma on the first symbol of a term , it begins either with a parenthesis or a variable. End proof. Lemma. No proper initial part of a term is itself a term. End lemma. Exercise. Prove the lemma that no proper initial part is a term by induction on the length of terms. End exercise. This exercise remains unsolved. Proposition. Unique Readability. There is a unique formation for each term. In other words, if a term capital M is formed by a formation, then it is the only formation that can form this term. End proposition. Proof. We prove this by induction on the formation of terms. List. Next item. capital M is of the form x , where x is some variable. Since the results of abstractions and applications always start with parentheses, they cannot have been used to construct capital M ; Thus, the formation of capital M must be a single step of the definition of lambda terms the variable formation clause . Next item. capital M is of the form lambda x, with body capital N, end abstraction , where x is some variable and capital N is a term. It could not have been constructed according to the definition of lambda terms the variable formation clause , because it is not a single variable. It is not the result of an application, by the lemma on the first symbols of an application . Thus capital M can only be the result of an abstraction on capital N . By inductive hypothesis we know that formation of capital N is itself unique. Next item. capital M is of the form the application of capital P to capital Q, end application , where capital P and capital Q are terms. Since it starts with a parentheses, it cannot also be constructed by the definition of lambda terms the variable formation clause . By the lemma on the first symbol of a term , capital P cannot begin with lambda , so the application of capital P to capital Q, end application cannot be the result of an abstraction. Now suppose there were another way of constructing capital M by application, for example, it is also of the form the application of capital P prime to capital Q prime, end application . Then capital P is a proper initial segment of capital P prime (or vice versa), and this is impossible by the lemma that no proper initial part is a term . So capital P and capital Q are uniquely determined, and by inductive hypothesis we know that formations of capital P and capital Q is unique. End list. End proof. A more readable paraphrase of the above proposition is as follows: Proposition. A term capital M can only be one of the following forms: List. Next item. x , where x is a variable uniquely determined by capital M . Next item. lambda x, with body capital N, end abstraction , where x is a variable and capital N is another term, both of which is uniquely determined by capital M . Next item. the application of capital P to capital Q, end application , where capital P and capital Q are two terms uniquely determined by capital M . End list. End proposition. End section.

Section. Free Variables. Lambda calculus is about functions, and lambda abstraction is how functions arise. Intuitively, lambda x, with body capital M, end abstraction is the function with values given by capital M when the argument to the function is assigned to x . A free variable is like a reference to the outside world (the environment ), and a term containing free variables can be seen as a partially specified term, since its behaviour depends on how we set up the environment. For example, in the term lambda x, with body the application of f to x, end application, end abstraction , which accepts an argument x and returns f of that argument, the variable f is free. This term is no longer dependent on the environment variable f , because it now designates a function that accepts two arguments and returns the result of applying the first to the second. Changing f in the environment won't have any effect on the behavior of this term, as the term will only use whatever is passed as an argument, and not the value of f in the environment. Definition. Chapter. The Church—Rosser Property.

Section. Definition and Properties. In this chapter we introduce the concept of Church—Rosser property and some common properties of this property. Definition. Church—Rosser property, CR. A relation the X arrow relation on terms is said to satisfy the Church—Rosser property if and only if, whenever M is X related to P and M is X related to Q , then there exists some N such that P is X related to N and Q is X related to N . End definition. We can view the lambda calculus as a model of computation in which terms in normal form are “values” and a reducibility relation on terms are the “calculation rules.” The Church—Rosser property states is that when there is more than one way to proceed with a calculation, there is still only a single value of the expression. To take an example from elementary algebra, there's more than one way to calculate four times the quantity one plus two, then plus three . It can either be reduced to four times three, then plus three (if we first reduce one plus two to three ) or to four times one, plus four times two, plus three (if we first reduce four times the quantity one plus two using distributivity). Both of these, however, can be further reduced to twelve plus three . If we take the X arrow relation to be beta -reduction, we easily see that a consequence of the Church—Rosser property is that if a term has a normal form, then it is unique. For suppose M can be reduced to P and Q , both of which are normal forms. By the Church—Rosser property, there exists some N such that both P and Q reduce to it. Since by assumption P and Q are normal forms, the reduction of P and Q to N can only be the trivial reduction, that is, P , Q , and N are identical. This justifies our speaking of the normal form of a term. In viewing the lambda calculus as a model of computation, then, the normal form of a term can be thought of as the “final result” of the computation starting with that term. The above corollary means there's only one, if any, final result of a computation, just like there is only one result of computing four times the quantity one plus two, then plus three , namely fifteen . If a relation the X arrow relation satisfies the Church—Rosser property, and the transitive X reduction relation is the smallest transitive relation containing the X arrow relation , then the transitive X reduction relation satisfies the Church—Rosser property too. Section. Introduction. At first glance, the lambda calculus is just a very abstract calculus of expressions that represent functions and applications of them to others. Nothing in the syntax of the lambda calculus suggests that these are functions of particular kinds of objects, in particular, the syntax includes no mention of natural numbers. Its basic operations—application and lambda abstractions—are operations that apply to any function, not just functions on natural numbers. Nevertheless, with some ingenuity, it is possible to define arithmetical functions, that is, functions on the natural numbers, in the lambda calculus. To do this, we define, for each natural number n is a natural number , a special lambda -term the Church numeral for n , the Church numeral for n . (Church numerals are named for Alonzo Church.) Definition. If n is a natural number , the corresponding Church numeral the Church numeral for n represents n : Displayed expression. the Church numeral for n is syntactically identical to lambda f then x, with body the result of iterating f n times on x, end iteration, end abstraction. End displayed expression. Here, the result of iterating f n times on x, end iteration stands for the result of applying f to x n times. For example, the Church numeral for zero is lambda f then x, with body x, end abstraction , and the Church numeral for three is lambda f then x, with body the application of f to the application of f to the application of f to x, end application, end application, end application, end abstraction . End definition. The Church numeral the Church numeral for n is encoded as a lambda term which represents a function accepting two arguments f and x , and returns the result of iterating f n times on x, end iteration . Church numerals are evidently in normal form. A representation of natural numbers in the lambda calculus is only useful, of course, if we can compute with them. Computing with Church numerals in the lambda calculus means applying a lambda -term capital F to such a Church numeral, and reducing the combined term the application of capital F to the Church numeral for n, end application to a normal form. If it always reduces to a normal form, and the normal form is always a Church numeral the Church numeral for m , we can think of the output of the computation as being the number m . We can then think of capital F as defining a function f from the natural numbers to the natural numbers , namely the function such that f of n equals m if and only if the application of capital F to the Church numeral for n, end application reduces to the Church numeral for m . Because of the Church—Rosser property, normal forms are unique if they exist. So if the application of capital F to the Church numeral for n, end application reduces to the Church numeral for m , there can be no other term in normal form, in particular no other Church numeral, that the application of capital F to the Church numeral for n, end application reduces to. Conversely, given a function f from the natural numbers to the natural numbers , we can ask if there is a term capital F that defines f in this way. In that case we say that capital F lambda-defines f , and that f is lambda-definable. We can generalize this to many-place and partial functions. Definition. Suppose f from k tuples of natural numbers to the natural numbers . We say that a lambda term capital F lambda-defines f if for all n subscript zero , and so on, n subscript k minus one , Displayed expression. capital F successively applied to the Church numerals for n subscript zero through n subscript k minus one, in that order reduces to the Church numeral for f of n subscript zero through n subscript k minus one. End displayed expression. if f of n subscript zero through n subscript k minus one is defined, and capital F successively applied to the Church numerals for n subscript zero through n subscript k minus one, in that order has no normal form otherwise. End definition. A very simple example are the constant functions. The term capital C subscript k is syntactically identical to lambda x, with body the Church numeral for k, end abstraction lambda-defines the function c subscript k from the natural numbers to the natural numbers such that c of n equals k . For the application of capital C subscript k to the Church numeral for n, end application is syntactically identical to the application of lambda x, with body the Church numeral for k, end abstraction to the Church numeral for n, end application, which reduces in one step to the Church numeral for k for any n . The identity function is lambda-defined by lambda x, with body x, end abstraction . More complex functions are of course harder to define, and often require a lot of ingenuity. So it is perhaps surprising that every computable function is lambda-definable. The converse is also true: if a function is lambda-definable, it is computable. Source anomaly note. Source caveat. Chapter. Syntax and Semantics.

Section. Introduction. In classical logic, we deal with formulas that are built from propositional variables using the propositional connectives negation , conjunction , disjunction , conditional , and biconditional . When we define a semantics for classical logic, we do so using the two truth values true and false . We interpret propositional variables in a valuation v , which assigns these truth values true , false to the propositional variables. Any valuation then determines a truth value of A under v for any formula A , and A formula is satisfied in a valuation v , valuation v satisfies A , if and only if the value of A under v equals true . Many-valued logics are generalizations of classical two-valued logic by allowing more truth values than just true and false . So in many-valued logic, a valuation v is a function assigning to every propositional variable p one of a range of possible truth values. We'll generally call the set of allowed truth values V . Classical logic is a many-valued logic where V equals the set containing true and false , and the truth value of A under v is computed using the familiar characteristic truth tables for the connectives. Once we add additional truth values, we have more than one natural option for how to compute the value of A under v for the connectives we read as “and,” “or,” “not,” and “if—then.” So a many-valued logic is determined not just by the set of truth values, but also by the truth functions we decide to use for each connective. Once these are selected for a many-valued logic L , however, the truth value of A under v in logic L is uniquely determined by the valuation, just like in classical logic. Many-valued logics, like classical logic, are truth functional. With this semantic building blocks in hand, we can go on to define the analogs of the semantic concepts of tautology, entailment, and satisfiability. In classical logic, a formula is a tautology if its truth value of A under v equals true for any v . In many-valued logic, we have to generalize this a bit as well. First of all, there is no requirement that the set of truth values V contains true . For instance, some many-valued logics use numbers, such as all rational numbers between zero and one as their set of truth values. In such a case, one usually plays the rule of true . In other logics, not just one but several truth values do. So, we require that every many-valued logic have a set V plus of designated values. We can then say that a formula is satisfied in a valuation v , valuation v satisfies A in logic L , if and only if the value of A under v in logic L belongs to the set of designated values V plus . A formula A is a tautology of the logic, A is a tautology of logic L , if and only if the value of A under v belongs to the set of designated values V plus for any v . And, finally, we say that A is entailed by a set of formulas, Gamma entails A in logic L , if every valuation that satisfies all the formulas in Gamma also satisfies A . End section.

Section. Languages and Connectives. Classical propositional logic, and many other logics, use a set supply of propositional constants and connectives. For instance, we use the following as primitives: List. Next item. The propositional constant for falsity the falsity constant . Next item. The logical connectives: negation (negation), conjunction (conjunction), disjunction (disjunction), conditional (conditional) End list. In addition to the primitive connectives above, we also use symbols defined as abbreviations, such as biconditional (biconditional), the truth constant (truth) The same connectives are used in many-valued logics as well. However, it is often useful to include different versions of, say, conjunction, in the same logic, and that would require different symbols to keep the versions separate. Some many-valued logics also include connectives that have no equivalent in classical logic. So, we'll be a bit more general than usual. Definition. A propositional language consists of a set L of connectives. Each connective star has an arity; a connective of arity n is said to be n place . Connectives of arity zero are also called constants; connectives of arity one are called unary, and connectives of arity two , binary. End definition. Example. For instance, in product logic, the conjunction symbol is often the circled dot conjunction symbol instead of conjunction . Sometimes it is convenient to add a new operator, for example, the determinateness operator triangle ( one place ). End example. End section.

Section. Valuations and Satisfaction. Definition. Valuations. Let V be a set of truth values. Next item. the value of p subscript n under the evaluation function determined by v equals the value assigned to p subscript n by v ; Next item. Section. Semantic Notions. Suppose a many-valued logic L is given by a matrix. Then we can define the usual semantic notions for L . Definition. List. Next item. If Gamma is a set of formulas, Gamma is satisfiable if there is a valuation v for which valuation v satisfies every formula in Gamma , and Gamma is unsatisfiable otherwise. End list. End definition. We have some of the same facts for these notions as we do for the case of classical logic: Proposition. List. Next item. Monotonicity: if Gamma is a subset of Delta and Gamma entails A then also Delta entails A ; Next item. Transitivity: if Gamma entails A and Delta together with A entails B then the union of Gamma and Delta entails B ; End list. End proposition. Proof. Exercise. End proof. Exercise. For instance, we have the validity of modus ponens: If Gamma entails A and Gamma entails the conditional if A then B then Gamma entails B . Another important relationship between semantic entailment and conditional in classical logic is the semantic deduction theorem: Gamma entails the conditional if A then B if and only if Gamma together with A entails B . These results do not always hold in many-valued logics. Whether they do depends on the truth function for the conditional . End section.

Section. Many-valued logics as sublogics of classical logic . The usual many-valued logics are all defined using matrices in which the value of a truth-function for arguments in the set containing true and false agrees with the classical truth functions. Specifically, in these logics, if x belongs to the set containing true and false , then the negation truth function of logic L at x equals the classical negation truth function at x , and for star any one of conjunction , disjunction , conditional , if x and y both belong to the set containing true and false , then the truth function for star in logic L at x and y equals the classical truth function for star at x and y . In other words, the truth functions for negation , conjunction , disjunction , conditional restricted to the set containing true and false are exactly the classical truth functions. Proposition. Suppose that a many-valued logic L contains the connectives negation , conjunction , disjunction , conditional in its language, true and false both belong to V , and its truth functions satisfy: List. Next item. the negation truth function of logic L at x equals the classical negation truth function at x if x equals true or x equals false ; Next item. the conjunction truth function of logic L at x and y equals the classical conjunction truth function at x and y , Next item. the disjunction truth function of logic L at x and y equals the classical disjunction truth function at x and y , Next item. the conditional truth function of logic L at x and y equals the classical conditional truth function at x and y , if x and y both belong to the set containing true and false . End list. Then, for any valuation v into V such that the value assigned to p by v belongs to the set containing true and false , the value of A under v in logic L equals its value under v in classical logic . End proposition. Source anomaly note. Source scope note. The displayed hypothesis restricts the value assigned to one variable p to true or false, but the conclusion concerns an arbitrary formula A. If A, namely p, is atomic, we have the value of A under v in logic L equals the value assigned to p by v, which equals the value of A under v in classical logic . Next item. The value of A under v in logic L equals the L negation truth function applied to the L value of B, by the evaluation definition. This equals that same truth function applied to the classical value of B, by the inductive hypothesis. This equals the classical negation truth function applied to the classical value of B, by the assumption that negation agrees on true and false, since the classical value of B is either true or false. Finally this equals the classical value of A under v, by the evaluation definition. End of equality chain. End displayed expression. End list. Chapter. Three-valued Logics.

Section. Introduction. If we just add one more value U to true and false , we get a three-valued logic. Even though there is only one more truth value, the possibilities for defining the truth-functions for negation , conjunction , disjunction , and the conditional are quite numerous. Then a logic might use any combination of these truth functions, and you also have a choice of making only true designated, or both true and U . We present here a selection of the most well-known three-valued logics, their motivations, and some of their properties. End section.

Section. Łukasiewicz logic. One of the first published, worked out proposals for a many-valued logic is due to the Polish philosopher Jan Łukasiewicz in one thousand nine hundred twenty one. Łukasiewicz was motivated by Aristotle's sea battle problem: It seems that, today, the sentence “There will be a sea battle tomorrow” is neither true nor false: its truth value is not yet settled. Łukasiewicz proposed to introduce a third truth value, to such “future contingent” sentences. Quotation. I can assume without contradiction that my presence in Warsaw at a certain moment of next year, for example, at noon on twenty one December, is at the present time determined neither positively nor negatively. Hence it is possible, but not necessary, that I shall be present in Warsaw at the given time. On this assumption the proposition “I shall be in Warsaw at noon on twenty one December of next year,” can at the present time be neither true nor false. For if it were true now, my future presence in Warsaw would have to be necessary, which is contradictory to the assumption. If it were false now, on the other hand, my future presence in Warsaw would have to be impossible, which is also contradictory to the assumption. Therefore the proposition considered is at the moment neither true nor false and must possess a third value, different from “zero” or falsity and “one” or truth. This value we can designate by “ one half .” It represents “the possible,” and joins “the true” and “the false” as a third value. End quotation. We will use U for Łukasiewicz's third truth value. Footnote. Łukasiewicz here uses “possible” in a way that is uncommon today, namely to mean possible but not necessary. End footnote. The truth functions for the connectives negation , conjunction , and disjunction are easy to determine on this interpretation: the negation of a future contingent sentence is also a future contingent sentence, so negation of U has value U . If one conjunct of a conjunction is undetermined and the other is true, the conjunction is also undetermined—after all, depending on how the future contingent conjunct turns out, the conjunction might turn out to be true, and it might turn out to be false. So Displayed expression. conjunction of true and U, and conjunction of U and true, both have value U. End displayed expression. If the other conjunct is false, however, it cannot turn out true, so Displayed expression. conjunction of false and U equals conjunction of false and U, and both equal false. End displayed expression. The other values (if the arguments are settled truth values, true or false , are like in classical logic. Source anomaly note. Source notation note. Suppose q is a future contingent statement. If p is false, then the conditional from p to q will be true, regardless of how q turns out, so we should set the conditional with false antecedent and U consequent to true . And if p is true, then the conditional from q to p will be true, regardless of what q turns out to be, so the conditional with U antecedent and true consequent has value true . If p is true, then the conditional from p to q might turn out to be true or false, so the conditional with true antecedent and U consequent has value U . Similarly, if p is false, then the conditional from q to p might turn out to be true or false, so the conditional with U antecedent and false consequent has value U . Section. Kleene logics. Stephen Kleene introduced two three-valued logics motivated by a logic in which truth values are thought of the outcomes of computational procedures: a procedure may yield true or false , but it may also fail to terminate. In that case the corresponding truth value is undefined, represented by the truth value U . To compute the negation of a proposition A , you would first compute the value of A , and then return the opposite of the result. If the computation of A does not terminate, then the entire procedure does not either: so the negation of U is U . To compute a conjunction A and B , there are two options: one can first compute A , then B , and then the result would be true if the outcome of both is true , and false otherwise. If either computation fails to halt, the entire procedure does as well. So in this case, the if one conjunct is undefined, the conjunction is as well. The same goes for disjunction. However, if we can evaluate A and B in parallel, we can do better. Then, if one of the two procedures halts and returns false , we can stop, as the answer must be false. So in that case a conjunction with one false conjunct is false, even if the other conjunct is undefined. Similarly, when computing a disjunction in parallel, we can stop once the procedure for one of the two disjuncts has returned true: then the disjunction must be true. So in this case we can know what the outcome of a compound claim is, even if one of the components is undefined. On this interpretation, we might read U as “unknown” rather than “undefined.” The two interpretations give rise to Kleene's strong and weak logic. Section. Introduction. The sequent calculus for classical logic is an efficient and simple derivation system. If a many-valued logic is defined by a matrix with finitely many truth values, that is, the set V of truth values is finite, it is possible to provide a sequent calculus for it. The idea for how to do this comes from considering the meanings of sequents and the form of inference rules in the classical case. Now recall that a sequent Displayed expression. In other words, A valuation v satisfies a sequent with antecedent Gamma and succedent Delta if and only if either the value of formula A under valuation v is false for some A in Gamma or the value of formula A under valuation v is true for some A in Delta . The label of the next inference is right conditional rule . If we apply the above semantic interpretation of a sequent, we can read the left conditional rule as saying that if the value of formula A under valuation v is true and the value of formula B under valuation v is false , then the value of the conditional from A to B under valuation v is false . Similarly, the right conditional rule says that if either the value of formula A under valuation v is false or the value of formula B under valuation v is true , then the value of the conditional from A to B under valuation v is true . Chapter. Syntax and Semantics.

Section. Introduction. Modal logic deals with modal propositions and the entailment relations among them. Examples of modal propositions are the following: List. Next item. It is necessary that two plus two equals four . Next item. It is necessarily possible that it will rain tomorrow. Next item. If it is necessarily possible that formula A then it is possible that formula A . End list. Possibility and necessity are not the only modalities: other unary connectives are also classified as modalities, for instance, “it ought to be the case that formula A ,” “It will be the case that formula A ,” “Dana knows that formula A ,” or “Dana believes that formula A .” Modal logic makes its first appearance in Aristotle's De Interpretatione: he was the first to notice that necessity implies possibility, but not vice versa; that possibility and necessity are inter-definable; that If A and B is possibly true then formula A is possibly true and formula B is possibly true, but not conversely; and that if A implies B is necessary, then if formula A is necessary, so is formula B . The first modern approach to modal logic was the work of C. I. Lewis, culminating with Lewis and Langford, Symbolic Logic (one thousand nine hundred thirty two). Lewis and Langford were unhappy with the representation of implication by means of the material conditional: if A, then B is a poor substitute for “ formula A implies formula B .” Instead, they proposed to characterize implication as “Necessarily, if formula A then formula B ,” symbolized as necessarily, if A then B . In trying to sort out the different properties, Lewis identified five different modal systems, Sone, and so on, Sfour, Sfive, the last two of which are still in use. The approach of Lewis and Langford was purely syntactical: they identified reasonable axioms and rules and investigated what was provable with those means. A semantic approach remained elusive for a long time, until a first attempt was made by Rudolf Carnap in Meaning and Necessity (one thousand nine hundred forty seven) using the notion of a state description, that is, a collection of atomic sentences (those that are “true” in that state description). After lifting the truth definition to arbitrary sentences formula A , Carnap defines formula A to be necessarily true if it is true in all state descriptions. Carnap's approach could not handle iterated modalities, in that sentences of the form “Possibly necessarily and so on possibly formula A ” always reduce to the innermost modality. The major breakthrough in modal semantics came with Saul Kripke's article “A Completeness Theorem in Modal Logic” (JSL one thousand nine hundred fifty nine). Kripke based his work on Leibniz's idea that a statement is necessarily true if it is true “at all possible worlds.” This idea, though, suffers from the same drawbacks as Carnap's, in that the truth of statement at a world w (or a state description s ) does not depend on w at all. So Kripke assumed that worlds are related by an accessibility relation R , and that a statement of the form “Necessarily formula A ” is true at a world w if and only if formula A is true at all worlds w prime accessible from w . Semantics that provide some version of this approach are called Kripke semantics and made possible the tumultuous development of modal logics (in the plural). When interpreted by the Kripke semantics, modal logic shows us what relational structures look like “from the inside.” A relational structure is just a set equipped with a binary relation (for instance, the set of students in the class ordered by their social security number is a relational structure). But in fact relational structures come in all sorts of domains: besides relative possibility of states of the world, we can have epistemic states of some agent related by epistemic possibility, or states of a dynamical system with their state transitions, etc. Modal logic can be used to model all of these: the first gives us ordinary, alethic, modal logic; the others give us epistemic logic, dynamic logic, etc. We focus on one particular angle, known to modal logicians as “correspondence theory.” One of the most significant early discoveries of Kripke's is that many properties of the accessibility relation R (whether it is transitive, symmetric, etc.) can be characterized in the modal language itself by means of appropriate “modal schemas.” Modal logicians say, for instance, that the reflexivity of R “corresponds” to the schema “If necessarily formula A , then formula A ”. We explore mainly the correspondence theory of a number of classical systems of modal logic (for example, Sfour and Sfive) obtained by a combination of the schemas axiom D, axiom T, axiom B, axiom four, and axiom five. End section.

Section. Relational Models. The basic concept of semantics for normal modal logics is that of a relational model. It consists of a set of worlds, which are related by a binary “accessibility relation,” together with an assignment which determines which propositional variables count as “true” at which worlds. R is a binary accessibility relation on W , and Next item. V is a function assigning to each propositional variable p a set V of p of possible worlds. End list. When world w prime is accessible from world w holds, we say that w prime is accessible from w . When w belongs to V of p we say p is true at w . End definition. Section. Truth at a World. Every modal model determines which modal formulas count as true at which worlds in it. The relation “model model M makes formula A true at world w ” is the basic notion of relational semantics. The relation is defined inductively and coincides with the usual characterization using truth tables for the non-modal operators. Definition. Truth of a formula A at w in a model M , in symbols: model M satisfies A at world w , is defined inductively as follows: List. Next item. Case: A is the falsity constant. Never model M satisfies falsity at world w . Next item. model M satisfies p at world w if and only if w belongs to V of p . Next item. Case: A is the negation of B. model M satisfies the formula in the current induction case at world w if and only if model M does not satisfy B at world w . Next item. Case: A is the conjunction of B and C. model M satisfies the formula in the current induction case at world w if and only if model M satisfies B at world w and model M satisfies C at world w . Next item. Case: A is the disjunction of B and C. model M satisfies the formula in the current induction case at world w if and only if model M satisfies B at world w or model M satisfies C at world w (or both). Next item. Case: A is the conditional from B to C. model M satisfies the formula in the current induction case at world w if and only if model M does not satisfy B at world w or model M satisfies C at world w . Next item. Case: A is necessarily B. model M satisfies the formula in the current induction case at world w if and only if model M satisfies B at world w prime for all w prime belongs to W with world w prime is accessible from world w . Section. Validity. Formulas that are true in all models, that is, true at every world in every model, are particularly interesting. They represent those modal propositions which are true regardless of how necessity and possibility are interpreted, as long as the interpretation is “normal” in the sense that it is generated by some accessibility relation on possible worlds. We call such formulas valid. For instance, if the conjunction of p and q is necessary, then p is necessary is valid. Some formulas one might expect to be valid on the basis of the alethic interpretation of necessity , such as if necessarily p, then p , are not valid, however. Part of the interest of relational models is that different interpretations of necessity and possibility can be captured by different kinds of accessibility relations. This suggests that we should define validity not just relative to all models, but relative to all models of a certain kind. It will turn out, for example, that if necessarily p, then p is true in all models where every world is accessible from itself, that is, R is reflexive. Defining validity relative to classes of models enables us to formulate this succinctly: if necessarily p, then p is valid in the class of reflexive models. Definition. A formula A is valid in a class the class C of models of models if it is true in every model in the class C of models (that is, true at every world in every model in the class C of models ). If formula A is valid in the class C of models , we write A is valid in the class C of models , and we write A is valid in all models if formula A is valid in the class of all models. End definition. Proposition. If formula A is valid in the class C of models it is also valid in each class the class C prime is a subclass of the class C . End proposition. Proposition. If formula A is valid, then so is necessity of A . End proposition. Proof. Assume A is valid in all models . To show necessarily A is valid in all models let model M is the ordered triple W, R, V be a model and w belongs to W . If world w prime is accessible from world w then model M satisfies A at world w prime , since formula A is valid, and so also model M satisfies necessity of A at world w . Since model M and w were arbitrary, necessarily A is valid in all models . End proof. Exercise. Show that the following are valid: List. Section. Tautological Instances. A modal-free formula is a tautology if it is true under every truth-value assignment. Clearly, every tautology is true at every world in every model. But for formulas involving necessity and possibility , the notion of tautology is not defined. Is it the case, for example, that either necessarily p or not necessarily p —an instance of the principle of excluded middle—is valid? The notion of a tautological instance helps: a formula that is a substitution instance of a (non-modal) tautology. It is not surprising, but still requires proof, that every tautological instance is valid. Definition. A modal formula B is a tautological instance if and only if there is a modal-free tautology formula A with propositional variables p subscript one , and so on, p subscript n and formulas D subscript one , and so on, formula D subscript n such that B is syntactically identical to the result of simultaneously substituting D subscript one through D subscript n for p subscript one through p subscript n in A . Section. Entailment. With the definition of truth at a world, we can define an entailment relation between formulas. A formula B entails formula A if and only if, whenever formula B is true, formula A is true as well. Here, “whenever” means both “whichever model we consider” as well as “whichever world in that model we consider.” Definition. If Gamma is a set of formulas and formula A a formula, then Gamma entails formula A , in symbols: Gamma entails A , if and only if for every model model M is the ordered triple W, R, V and world w belongs to W , if model M satisfies B at world w for every B belongs to Gamma , then model M satisfies A at world w . If Gamma contains a single formula B , then we write B entails A . End definition. Example. To show that a formula entails another, we have to reason about all models, using the definition of satisfaction in model M at world w . For instance, to show if p then possibly p entails if necessarily not p then not p , we might argue as follows: Consider a model model M is the ordered triple W, R, V and w belongs to W , and suppose model M satisfies the conditional from p to possibly p at world w . We have to show that model M satisfies the conditional from necessarily not p to not p at world w . Suppose not. Then model M satisfies necessarily not p at world w and model M does not satisfy not p at world w . Since model M does not satisfy not p at world w , model M satisfies p at world w . By assumption, model M satisfies the conditional from p to possibly p at world w , hence model M satisfies possibility of p at world w . By definition of model M satisfies possibility of p at world w , there is some w prime with world w prime is accessible from world w such that model M satisfies p at world w prime . Since also model M satisfies necessarily not p at world w , model M satisfies not p at world w prime , a contradiction. To show that a formula B does not entail another formula A , we have to give a counterexample, that is, a model model M is the ordered triple W, R, V where we show that at some world w belongs to W , model M satisfies B at world w but model M does not satisfy A at world w . Chapter. Frame Definability.

Section. Introduction. One question that interests modal logicians is the relationship between the accessibility relation and the truth of certain formulas in models with that accessibility relation. For instance, suppose the accessibility relation is reflexive, that is, for every w belongs to W , R relates w to itself . In other words, every world is accessible from itself. That means that when necessarily A is true at a world w , w itself is among the accessible worlds at which A must therefore be true. So, if the accessibility relation R of M is reflexive, then whatever world w and formula A we take, if necessarily A, then A will be true there (in other words, the schema if necessarily p, then p and all its substitution instances are true in M ). The converse, however, is false. It's not the case, for example, that if if necessarily p, then p is true in M , then R is reflexive. For we can easily find a non-reflexive model M where if necessarily p, then p is true at all worlds: take the model with a single world w , not accessible from itself, but with w belongs to V of p . By picking the truth value of p suitably, we can make if necessarily A, then A true in a model that is not reflexive. The solution is to remove the variable assignment V from the equation. If we require that if necessarily p, then p is true at all worlds in M , regardless of which worlds are in V of p , then it is necessary that R is reflexive. For in any non-reflexive model, there will be at least one world w such that not R relates w to itself . If we set V of p equals W with w removed , then p will be true at all worlds other than w , and so at all worlds accessible from w (since w is guaranteed not to be accessible from w , and w is the only world where p is false). On the other hand, p is false at w , so if necessarily p, then p is false at w . This suggests that we should introduce a notation for model structures without a valuation: we call these frames. A frame F is simply a pair the ordered pair W, R consisting of a set of worlds with an accessibility relation. Every model the ordered triple W, R, V is then, as we say, based on the frame the ordered pair W, R . Conversely, a frame determines the class of models based on it; and a class of frames determines the class of models which are based on any frame in the class. And we can define A is valid in frame F , the notion of a formula being valid in a frame as: A is true in modal model M for all M based on F . With this notation, we can establish correspondence relations between formulas and classes of frames: for example, the conditional from necessarily p to p is valid in frame F if, and only if, F is reflexive. End section.

Section. Properties of Accessibility Relations. Many modal formulas turn out to be characteristic of simple, and even familiar, properties of the accessibility relation. In one direction, that means that any model that has a given property makes a corresponding formula (and all its substitution instances) true. We begin with five classical examples of kinds of accessibility relations and the formulas the truth of which they guarantee. Theorem. Let modal model M equals the ordered triple W, R, V be a model. If R has the property on the left side of the table of five classical correspondence facts , every instance of the formula on the right side is true in M . End theorem. Table. t. Although we will focus on the five classical formulas axiom D, axiom T, axiom B, axiom four, and axiom five, we record in the table of five additional correspondence facts a few more properties of accessibility relations. The accessibility relation R is partially functional, if from every world at most one world is accessible. If it is the case that from every world exactly one world is accessible, we call it functional. (Thus the functional relations are precisely those that are both serial and partially functional). They are called “functional” because the accessibility relation operates like a (partial) function. A relation is weakly dense if whenever R relates u to v , there is a w “between” u and v . So weakly dense relations are in a sense the opposite of transitive relations: in a transitive relation, whenever you can reach v from u by a detour via w , you can reach v from u directly; in a weakly dense relation, whenever you can reach v from u directly, you can also reach it by a detour via some w . A relation is weakly directed if whenever you can reach worlds u and v from some world w , you can reach a single world t from both u and v —this is sometimes called the “diamond property” or “confluence.” Table. t.
