Section. Frames. Definition. A frame is a pair frame F equals the ordered pair W, R where W is a non-empty set of worlds and R a binary relation on W . A model M is based on a frame frame F equals the ordered pair W, R if and only if modal model M equals the ordered triple W, R, V for some valuation V . End definition. Definition. If F is a frame, we say that A is valid in F , A is valid in frame F , if A is true in modal model M for every model M based on F . If F is a class of frames, we say A is valid in F , A is valid in the class of frames F , if and only if A is valid in frame F for every frame frame F belongs to the class of frames F . End definition. The reason frames are interesting is that correspondence between schemas and properties of the accessibility relation R is at the level of frames, not of models. For instance, although axiom T is true in all reflexive models, not every model in which axiom T is true is reflexive. However, it is true that not only is axiom T valid on all reflexive frames, also every frame in which axiom T is valid is reflexive. Remark. Validity in a class of frames is a special case of the notion of validity in a class of models: A is valid in the class of frames F if and only if A is valid in the class of models C where C is the class of all models based on a frame in F . Obviously, if a formula or a schema is valid, that is, valid with respect to the class of all models, it is also valid with respect to any class F of frames. End remark. Disclosed reader correction. Section. First-order Definability. We've seen that a number of properties of accessibility relations of frames can be defined by modal formulas. For instance, symmetry of frames can be defined by the formula axiom B, if p, then necessarily possibly p . The conditions we've encountered so far can all be expressed by first-order formulas in a language involving a single two-place predicate symbol. For instance, symmetry is defined by for every x and every y, if Q relates x to y, then Q relates y to x in the sense that a first-order structure M with the domain of structure M equals W and the interpretation of Q in structure M equals R satisfies the preceding formula if and only if R is symmetric. This suggests the following definition: Definition. A class F of frames is first-order definable if there is a sentence A in the first-order language with a single two-place predicate symbol Q such that frame F, equal to the ordered pair W, R, belongs to the class of frames F if and only if structure M satisfies A in the first-order structure M with the domain of structure M equals W and the interpretation of Q in structure M equals R . End definition. It turns out that the properties and modal formulas that define them considered so far are exceptional. Not every formula defines a first-order definable class of frames, and not every first-order definable class of frames is definable by a modal formula. End displayed expression. axiom W defines the class of transitive and converse well-founded frames. For instance, the relation the less than relation on the natural numbers is well-founded, whereas the relation the less than relation on the integers is not. So converse well-founded relations are those where there is no infinite sequence w subscript one , w subscript two , and so on such that R relates w subscript one to w subscript two , R relates w subscript two to w subscript three , and so on. Every finite subset of Gamma is satisfiable: Let k be largest such that A subscript k is in the subset, the domain of structure M subscript k equals the set of integers from one through k , the interpretation of a subscript i in structure M subscript k equals i , and the interpretation of Q in structure M subscript k equals the less than relation . Since the less than relation on the set of integers from one through k is transitive and converse well-founded, structure M subscript k satisfies F . structure M subscript k satisfies A subscript i by construction, for all i is less than or equal to k . By the Compactness Theorem for first-order logic, Gamma is satisfiable in some structure M . By hypothesis, since structure M satisfies F , the relation the interpretation of Q in structure M is converse well-founded. But clearly, the interpretation of a subscript one in structure M , the interpretation of a subscript two in structure M , and so on would form an infinite sequence of the kind ruled out by converse well-foundedness. A counterexample to the second claim is given by the property of universality: for every u and v , R relates u to v . Universal frames are first-order definable by the formula for every x and every y, Q relates x to y . However, no modal formula is valid in all and only the universal frames. This is a consequence of a result that is independently interesting: the formulas valid in universal frames are exactly the same as those valid in reflexive, symmetric, and transitive frames. There are reflexive, symmetric, and transitive frames that are not universal, hence every formula valid in all universal frames is also valid in some non-universal frames. End section.

Section. Equivalence Relations and Sfive. The modal logic Sfive is characterized as the set of formulas valid on all universal frames, that is, every world is accessible from every world, including itself. In such a scenario, the necessity operator corresponds to necessity and the possibility operator to possibility: necessarily A is true if A is true at every world, and possibly A is true if A is true at some world. It turns out that Sfive can also be characterized as the formulas valid on all reflexive, symmetric, and transitive frames, that is, on all equivalence relations. Definition. A binary relation R on W is an equivalence relation if and only if it is reflexive, symmetric and transitive. A relation R on W is universal if and only if R relates u to v for all u and v belong to W . End definition. Since axiom T, axiom B, and axiom four characterize the reflexive, symmetric, and transitive frames, the frames where the accessibility relation is an equivalence relation are exactly those in which all three formulas are valid. It turns out that the equivalence relations can also be characterized by other combinations of formulas, since the conditions with which we've defined equivalence relations are equivalent to combinations of other familiar conditions on R . Section. Second-order Definability. Not every frame property definable by modal formulas is first-order definable. However, if we allow quantification over one-place predicates (that is, monadic second-order quantification), we define all modally definable frame properties. The trick is to exploit a systematic way in which the conditions under which a modal formula is true at a world are related to first-order formulas. This is the so-called standard translation of modal formulas into first-order formulas in a language containing not just a two-place predicate symbol Q for the accessibility relation, but also a one-place predicate symbol P subscript i for the propositional variables p subscript i occurring in A . Definition. The standard translation the standard translation at x of A is inductively defined as follows: List. Next item. Case: A is the falsity constant. the standard translation at x of the current formula equals falsity . Next item. Case: A is the propositional variable p subscript i. the standard translation at x of the current formula equals P subscript i of x . Next item. Case: A is the negation of B. the standard translation at x of the current formula equals the negation of the standard translation at x of B . Next item. Case: A is the conjunction of B and C. the standard translation at x of the current formula equals the conjunction of the standard translation at x of B and the standard translation at x of C . Next item. Case: A is the disjunction of B and C. the standard translation at x of the current formula equals the disjunction of the standard translation at x of B and the standard translation at x of C . Next item. Case: A is the conditional from B to C. the standard translation at x of the current formula equals the conditional from the standard translation at x of B to the standard translation at x of C . Next item. Case: A is necessarily B. the standard translation at x of the current formula equals: for every y, if Q relates x to y, then the standard translation at y of B . Next item. Case: A is possibly B. the standard translation at x of the current formula equals: there exists a y such that Q relates x to y and the standard translation at y of B . End list. End definition. For instance, the standard translation at x of the conditional from necessarily p to p is if, for every y, Q relates x to y only if P holds of y, then P holds of x . In other words, the components of such a structure are exactly those of a model for A : the domain is the set of worlds, the two-place relation assigned to Q is the accessibility relation, and the subsets assigned to P subscript i are just the assignments V of p subscript i . Chapter. Axiomatic Derivations.

Section. Introduction. We have a semantics for the basic modal language in terms of modal models, and a notion of a formula being valid—true at all worlds in all models—or valid with respect to some class of models or frames—true at all worlds in all models in the class, or based on the frame. Logic usually connects such semantic characterizations of validity with a proof-theoretic notion of derivability. The aim is to define a notion of derivability in some system such that a formula is derivable if and only if it is valid. The simplest and historically oldest derivation systems are so-called Hilbert-type or axiomatic derivation systems. Hilbert-type derivation systems for many modal logics are relatively easy to construct: they are simple as objects of metatheoretical study (for example, to prove soundness and completeness). However, they are much harder to use to prove formulas in than, say, natural deduction systems. In Hilbert-type derivation systems, a derivation of a formula is a sequence of formulas leading from certain axioms, via a handful of inference rules, to the formula in question. Since we want the derivation system to match the semantics, we have to guarantee that the set of derivable formulas are true in all models (or true in all models in which all axioms are true). We'll first isolate some properties of modal logics that are necessary for this to work: the “normal” modal logics. For normal modal logics, there are only two inference rules that need to be assumed: modus ponens and necessitation. As axioms we take all (substitution instances) of tautologies, and, depending on the modal logic we deal with, a number of modal axioms. Even if we are just interested in the class of all models, we must also count all substitution instances of axiom K and axiom dual as axioms. This alone generates the minimal normal modal logic modal system K . Definition. The rule of modus ponens is the inference schema Source premise node one: formula A . Section. Derivations and Modal Systems. We first define what a derivation is for normal modal logics. Roughly, a derivation is a sequence of formulas in which every element is either (a substitution instance of) one of a number of axioms, or follows from previous elements by one of a few inference rules. For normal modal logics, all instances of tautologies, axiom K, and Dual count as axioms. This results in the modal system modal system K , the smallest normal modal logic. We may wish to add additional axioms to obtain other systems, however. The rules are always modus ponens modus ponens and necessitation necessitation. Definition. Chapter. Completeness and Canonical Models.

Section. Introduction. If Sigma is a modal system, then the soundness theorem establishes that if Sigma derives formula A , then formula A is valid in any class class C of models in which all instances of all formulas in Sigma are valid. In particular that means that if logic K derives formula A then formula A is true in all models; if logic K T derives formula A then formula A is true in all reflexive models; if logic K D derives formula A then formula A is true in all serial models, etc. Completeness is the converse of soundness: that K is complete means that if a formula A is valid, formula A is derivable , for instance. Proving completeness is a lot harder to do than proving soundness. It is useful, first, to consider the contrapositive: K is complete if and only if whenever formula A is not derivable , there is a countermodel, that is, a model model M such that formula A is not true throughout model M . Equivalently (negating formula A ), we could prove that whenever not formula A is not derivable , there is a model of formula A . In the construction of such a model, we can use information contained in formula A . When we find models for specific formulas we often do the same: for example, if we want to find a countermodel to p implies necessarily q , we know that it has to contain a world where p is true and necessarily q is false. And a world where necessarily q is false means there has to be a world accessible from it where q is false. And that's all we need to know: which worlds make the propositional variables true, and which worlds are accessible from which worlds. In the case of proving completeness, however, we don't have a specific formula A for which we are constructing a model. We want to establish that a model exists for every formula A such that not formula A is not derivable in system Sigma . This is a minimal requirement, since if not formula A is derivable in system Sigma , by soundness, there is no model for formula A (in which Sigma is true). Now note that not formula A is not derivable in system Sigma if and only if formula A is Sigma -consistent. (Recall that Sigma does not derive not formula A in system Sigma and formula A does not derive falsity in system Sigma are equivalent.) So our task is to construct a model for every Sigma -consistent formula. The trick we'll use is to find a Sigma -consistent set of formulas that contains formula A , but also other formulas which tell us what the world that makes formula A true has to look like. Such sets are complete Sigma -consistent sets. It's not enough to construct a model with a single world to make formula A true, it will have to contain multiple worlds and an accessibility relation. The complete Sigma -consistent set containing formula A will also contain other formulas of the form necessarily formula B and possibly formula C . In all accessible worlds, formula B has to be true; in at least one, formula C has to be true. In order to accomplish this, we'll simply take all possible complete Sigma -consistent sets as the basis for the set of worlds. A tricky part will be to figure out when a complete Sigma -consistent set should count as being accessible from another in our model. We'll show that in the model so defined, formula A is true at a world—which is also a complete Sigma -consistent set—if and only if formula A is an element of that set. If formula A is Sigma -consistent, it will be an element of at least one complete Sigma -consistent set (a fact we'll prove), and so there will be a world where formula A is true. So we will have a single model where every Sigma -consistent formula A is true at some world. This single model is the canonical model for Sigma . End section.

Section. Complete Sigma -Consistent Sets. Suppose Sigma is a set of modal formulas—think of them as the axioms or defining principles of a normal modal logic. A set Gamma is Sigma -consistent if and only if Gamma does not derive falsity in system Sigma , that is, if there is no derivation of the nested conditional from A sub one, through A sub n, to falsity from Sigma , where each formula A sub i belongs to Gamma . We will construct a “canonical” model in which each world is taken to be a special kind of Sigma -consistent set: one which is not just Sigma -consistent, but maximally so, in the sense that it settles the truth value of every modal formula: for every formula A , either formula A belongs to Gamma or not formula A belongs to Gamma : Definition. A set Gamma is complete Sigma -consistent if and only if it is Sigma -consistent and for every formula A , either formula A belongs to Gamma or not formula A belongs to Gamma . End definition. Complete Sigma -consistent sets Gamma have a number of useful properties. For one, they are deductively closed, that is, if Gamma derives formula A in system Sigma then formula A belongs to Gamma . This means in particular that every instance of a formula A belongs to Sigma is also belongs to Gamma . Moreover, membership in Gamma mirrors the truth conditions for the propositional connectives. Section. Lindenbaum's Lemma. Lindenbaum's Lemma establishes that every Sigma -consistent set of formulas is contained in at least one complete Sigma -consistent set. Chapter. Filtrations and Decidability.

Section. Introduction. One important question about a logic is always whether it is decidable, that is, if there is an effective procedure which will answer the question “is this formula valid.” Propositional logic is decidable: we can effectively test if a formula is a tautology by constructing a truth table, and for a given formula, the truth table is finite. But we can't obviously test if a modal formula is true in all models, for there are infinitely many of them. We can list all the finite models relevant to a given formula, since only the assignment of subsets of worlds to propositional variables which actually occur in the formula are relevant. If the accessibility relation is fixed, the possible different assignments valuation V applied to p are just all the subsets of world set W , and if the cardinality of world set W equals n there are two raised to the power n of those. If our formula A contains m propositional variables there are then two raised to the power n times m different models with n worlds. Section. Preliminaries. Filtrations allow us to establish the decidability of our systems of modal logic by showing that they have the finite model property, that is, that any formula that is true (false) in a model is also true (false) in a finite model. Filtrations are defined relative to sets of formulas which are closed under subformulas. Definition. A set Gamma of formulas is closed under subformulas if it contains every subformula of a formula in Gamma . Further, Gamma is modally closed if it is closed under subformulas and moreover formula A belongs to Gamma implies necessarily A and possibly A both belong to Gamma . End definition. Section. Filtrations are Finite. We've defined filtrations for any set Gamma that is closed under sub-formulas. Nothing in the definition itself guarantees that filtrations are finite. Section. K and Sfive have the Finite Model Property. Definition. A system Sigma of modal logic is said to have the finite model property if whenever a formula A is true at a world in a model of Sigma then formula A is true at a world in a finite model of Sigma . End definition. Proposition. K has the finite model property. End proposition. Proof. K is the set of valid formulas, that is, any model is a model of K. By the Filtration Theorem preserving truth of formulas in Gamma , if formula A is true at world w in model M , then formula A is true at world w in model M star for any filtration of model M through the set Gamma of sub-formulas of formula A . Any formula only has finitely many sub-formulas, so Gamma is finite. By the proposition bounding the size of a filtration , the cardinality of world set W star is at most two to the power n , where n is the number of formulas in Gamma . And since K imposes no restriction on models, model M star is a K-model. End proof. Source anomaly note. Source world-label caveat. Section. Sfive is Decidable. The finite model property gives us an easy way to show that systems of modal logic given by schemas are decidable (that is, that there is a computable procedure to determine whether a formula is derivable in the system or not). Theorem. Sfive is decidable. End theorem. Proof. Let formula A be given, and suppose the propositional variables occurring in formula A are among p sub one , and so on, p sub k . Since for each n there are only finitely many models with n worlds assigning a value to p sub one , and so on, p sub k , we can enumerate, in parallel, all the theorems of Sfive by generating proofs in some systematic way; and all the models containing one , two , and so on worlds and checking whether formula A fails at a world in some such model. Eventually one of the two parallel processes will give an answer, as by the general canonical-model determination theorem and the finite model property corollary for S five , either formula A is derivable or it fails in a finite universal model. End proof. Source anomaly note. Source proof caveat. The proposed countermodel lane says to enumerate all finite models, although the final justification requires failure in a finite universal model. Section. Introduction. Tableaux are certain (downward-branching) trees of signed formulas, that is, pairs consisting of a truth value sign ( true sign or false sign ) and a sentence Displayed expression. true A or false A. End displayed expression. A tableau begins with a number of assumptions. Each further signed formula is generated by applying one of the inference rules. Some inference rules add one or more signed formulas to a tip of the tree; others add two new tips, resulting in two branches. Rules result in signed formulas where the formula is less complex than that of the signed formula to which it was applied. When a branch contains both true formula A and false formula A , we say the branch is closed. If every branch in a tableau is closed, the entire tableau is closed. A closed tableau constitutes a derivation that shows that the set of signed formulas which were used to begin the tableau are unsatisfiable. This can be used to define a the derivability symbol relation: Gamma derives formula A if and only if there is some finite set Gamma sub zero is the set of formulas B sub one through B sub n, and is a subset of Gamma such that there is a closed tableau for the assumptions Displayed expression. the set containing false A and true B sub one through true B sub n. End displayed expression. For modal logics, we have to both extend the notion of signed formula and add rules that cover the necessity operator and the possibility operator In addition to a sign( true sign or false sign ), formulas in modal tableaux also have prefixes prefix sigma . The prefixes are non-empty sequences of positive integers, that is, prefix sigma belongs to the set of nonempty finite sequences of positive integers . When we write such prefixes without the surrounding the empty sequence , and separate the individual elements by source period apostrophe s instead of source comma apostrophe s . If prefix sigma is a prefix, then prefix sigma dot n is prefix sigma concatenated with the one-element sequence n ; for example, if prefix sigma equals prefix one point two point one , then prefix sigma dot three is prefix one point two point one point three . So for instance, Displayed expression. true the conditional from necessarily formula A to formula A at prefix one point two. End displayed expression. is a prefixed signed formula (or just a prefixed formula for short). Intuitively, the prefix names a world in a model that might satisfy the formulas on a branch of a tableau, and if prefix sigma names some world, then prefix sigma dot n names a world accessible from (the world named by) prefix sigma . End section.

Section. Rules for axiom K. The rules for the regular propositional connectives are the same as for regular propositional signed tableaux, just with prefixes added. In each case, the rule applied to a signed formula with sign S formula A at prefix sigma produces new formulas that are also prefixed by prefix sigma . This should be intuitively clear: for example, if the conjunction of formula A and formula B is true at (a world named by) prefix sigma , then formula A and formula B are true at prefix sigma (and not at any other world). Section. Simple Tableaux for Sfive. Sfive is sound and complete with respect to the class of universal models, that is, models where every world is accessible from every world. In universal models the accessibility relation doesn't matter: “there is a world world w where formula A is true at world w in model M ” is true if and only if there is such a world w that's accessible from world u . So in Sfive, we can define models as simply a set of worlds and a valuation V . This suggests that we should be able to simplify the tableau rules as well. In the general case, we take as prefixes sequences of positive integers, so that we can keep track of which such prefixes name worlds which are accessible from others: prefix sigma dot n names a world accessible from prefix sigma . Section. Completeness for K. To show that the method of tableaux is complete, we have to show that whenever there is no closed tableau to show Gamma derives formula A , then Gamma does not semantically entail formula A , that is, there is a countermodel. But “there is no closed tableau” means that every way we could try to construct one has to fail to close. The trick is to see that if every such way fails to close, then a specific, systematic and exhaustive way also fails to close. And this systematic and exhaustive way would close if a closed tableau exists. The single tableau will contain, among its open branches, all the information required to define a countermodel. The countermodel given by an open branch in this tableau will contain the all the prefixes used on that branch as the worlds, and a propositional variable p is true at prefix sigma if and only if true p at prefix sigma occurs on the branch. Section. Countermodels from Tableaux. The proof of the completeness theorem doesn't just show that if formula A is semantically valid then formula A is derivable , it also gives us a method for constructing countermodels to formula A if the source expression A, without a formula marker, is not semantically valid . In the case of logic K , this method constitutes a decision procedure. For suppose formula A is not semantically valid . Then the proof of the proposition that every finite Gamma has a complete tableau gives a method for constructing a complete tableau. The method in fact always terminates. The propositional rules for logic K only add prefixed formulas of lower complexity, that is, each propositional rule need only be applied once on a branch for any signed formula with sign S formula A at prefix sigma . New prefixes are only generated by the false necessity rule and true possibility rules, and also only have to be applied once (and produce a single new prefix). true necessity rule and false possibility rule have to be applied potentially multiple times, but only once per prefix, and only finitely many new prefixes are generated. So the construction either results in a closed branch or a complete branch after finitely many stages. Source anomaly note. Source caveat. Chapter. Temporal Logics. Editorial note. This chapter covers temporal logics. End editorial note.

Section. Introduction. Temporal logics deal with claims about things that will or have been the case. Arthur Prior is credited as the originator of temporal logic, which he called tense logic. Our treatment of temporal logic here will largely follow Prior's original modal treatment of introducing temporal operators into the basic framework of propositional logic, which treats claims as generally lacking in tense. For example, in propositional logic, I might talk about a dog, Beezie, who sometimes sits and sometimes doesn't sit, as dogs are wont to do. It would be contradictory in classical logic to claim that Beezie is sitting and also that Beezie is not sitting. But obviously both can be true, just not at the same time; adding temporal operators to the language can allow us to express that claim relatively easily. The addition of temporal operators also allows us to account for the validity of inferences like the one from “Beezie will get a treat or a ball" to “Beezie will get a treat or Beezie will get a ball." However, a lot of philosophical issues arise with temporal logic that might lead us to adopt one framework of temporal logic over another. For example, a future contingent is a statement about the future that is neither necessary nor impossible. If we say “Richard will go to the grocery store tomorrow," we are expressing a claim about something that has not yet happened, and whose truth value is contestable. In fact, it is contestable whether that claim can even be assigned a truth value in the first place. If we are strict determinists, then perhaps we can be comfortable with the idea that this sentence is in fact true or false, even before the event in question is supposed to take place—it just may be that we do not know its truth value yet. In contrast, we might believe in a genuinely open future, in which the truth values of future contingents are undetermined. As it turns out, a lot of these commitments about the structure and nature of time are built in to our choices of models and frameworks of temporal logics. For example, we might ask ourselves whether we should construct models in which time is linear, branching or even circular. We might have to make decisions about whether our temporal models will have beginning and end points, and whether time is to be represented using discrete instants or as a continuum. End section.

Chapter. Epistemic Logics. Editorial note. This chapter covers the metatheory of epistemic logics. It is structured in a similar way to Aldo Antonelli's notes on classical basic modal logic, but has been rewritten by Audrey Yap in order to add material on bisimulation and dynamic epistemic logics. End editorial note.

Section. Introduction. Just as modal logic deals with modal propositions and the entailment relations among them, epistemic logic deals with epistemic propositions and the entailment relations among them. Rather than interpreting the modal operators as representing possibility and necessity, the unary connectives are interpreted in epistemic or doxastic ways, to model knowledge and belief. For example, we might want to express claims like the following: List. Next item. Richard knows that Calgary is in Alberta. Next item. Audrey thinks it is possible that a dog is on the couch. Next item. Richard knows that Audrey knows that her class is on Tuesdays. Next item. Everyone knows that a year has twelve months. End list. Contemporary epistemic logic is often traced to Jaako Hintikka's Knowledge and Belief, from one thousand nine hundred sixty two, and it was written at a time when possible worlds semantics were becoming increasingly more used in logic. In fact, epistemic logics use most of the same semantic tools as other modal logics, but will interpret them differently. The main change is in what we take the accessibility relation to represent. In epistemic logics, they represent some form of epistemic possibility. We'll see that the epistemic notion that we're modelling will affect the constraints that we want to place on the accessibility relation. And we'll also see what happens to correspondence theory when it is given an epistemic interpretation. You'll notice that the examples above mention two agents: Richard and Audrey, and the relationship between the things that each one knows. The epistemic logics we'll consider will be multi-agent logics, in which such things can be expressed. In contrast, a single-agent epistemic logic would only talk about what one individual knows or believes. End section.

Section. Relational Models. The basic semantic concept for epistemic logics is the same as that of ordinary modal logics. Relational models still consist of a set of worlds, and an assignment that determines which propositional variables count as “true” at which worlds. And if we are only dealing with a single agent, we have a single accessibility relation as usual. However, if we have a multi-agent epistemic logic, then our single accessibility relation becomes a set of accessibility relations, one for each agent a in our set of agent symbols agent set G . A relational model consists of a set of worlds, which are related by binary accessibility relations—one for each agent—together with an assignment which determines which propositional variables are true at which worlds. Section. Accessibility Relations and Epistemic Principles. Given what we already know about frame correspondence in normal modal logics, we might want to see what the characteristic formulas look like given epistemic interpretations. We have already said that epistemic logics are typically interpreted in Sfive. So let's take a look at how various epistemic principles are represented, and consider how they correspond to various frame conditions. Recall from normal modal logic, that different modal formulas characterized different properties of accessibility relations. This table picks out a few that correspond to particular epistemic principles. Table. t. Epistemic correspondence table. Column headers: if accessibility relation R has the stated property; then the displayed principle is true in model M . Row two, reflexive: for every world w, w is accessible from itself under relation R ; Veridicality: if p is known, then p is true . Row three, transitive: for every u, v, and w, if v is accessible from u and w is accessible from v, then w is accessible from u ; Positive Introspection: if p is known, then it is known that p is known . End table. Caption. Four epistemic principles. End caption. End table. Veridicality, corresponding to the axiom T axiom, is often treated as the most uncontroversial of these principles, as it represents that claim that if a formula is known, then it must be true. Closure, as well as Positive and Negative Introspection are much more contested. Closure, corresponding to the axiom K axiom, represents the idea that an agent's knowledge is closed under implication. This might seem plausible to us in some cases. For instance, I might know that if I am in Victoria, then I am on Vancouver Island. Barring odd skeptical scenarios, I do know that I am in Victoria, and this should also suggest that I know I am on Vancouver Island. So in this case, the logical closure of my knowledge might seem relatively intuitive. On the other hand, we do not always think through the consequences of our knowledge, and so this might lead to less intuitive results in other cases. Positive Introspection, sometimes known as the KK-principle, is sometimes articulated as the statement that if I know something, then I know that I know. It is the epistemic counterpart of the four axiom. Correspondingly, negative introspection is articulated as the statement that if I don't know something, then I know that I don't know it, which is the counterpart of the five axiom. Both of these seem to admit of relatively ordinary counterexamples, in which I am unsure whether or not I know something that I do in fact know. End section.

We have seen from our frame correspondence results that when certain formulas are valid in a frame, they will also ensure that those frames satisfy certain properties. But does our modal language, for example, allow us to distinguish between a world at which there is a reflexive arrow, and an infinite chain of worlds, each of which leads to the next? That is, is there any formula A that might hold at only one of these two worlds? Bisimulation is a relationship that we can define between relational models to say that they have effectively the same structure. Chapter. Introduction.

Section. Constructive Reasoning. In contrast to extensions of classical logic by modal operators or second-order quantifiers, intuitionistic logic is “non-classical” in that it restricts classical logic. Classical logic is non-constructive in various ways. Intuitionistic logic is intended to capture a more “constructive” kind of reasoning characteristic of a kind of constructive mathematics. The following examples may serve to illustrate some of the underlying motivations. Suppose someone claimed that they had determined a natural number n with the property that if n is even, the Riemann hypothesis is true, and if n is odd, the Riemann hypothesis is false. Great news! Whether the Riemann hypothesis is true or not is one of the big open questions of mathematics, and they seem to have reduced the problem to one of calculation, that is, to the determination of whether a specific number is even or not. What is the magic value of n ? They describe it as follows: n is the natural number that is equal to two if the Riemann hypothesis is true, and three otherwise. Angrily, you demand your money back. From a classical point of view, the description above does in fact determine a unique value of n ; but what you really want is a value of n that is given explicitly. To take another, perhaps less contrived example, consider the following question. We know that it is possible to raise an irrational number to a rational power, and get a rational result. For example, the square of the square root of two equals two . What is less clear is whether or not it is possible to raise an irrational number to an irrational power, and get a rational result. The following theorem answers this in the affirmative: Theorem. There are irrational numbers a and b such that a raised to the power b is rational. End theorem. Proof. Consider the square root of two raised to the square root of two . If this is rational, we are done: we can let a and b both equal the square root of two . Otherwise, it is irrational. Then we have Displayed expression. the square root of two raised to the square root of two, all raised to the square root of two, equals the square root of two raised to the product of two square roots of two, equals the square of the square root of two, equals two. End displayed expression. which is rational. So, in this case, let a be the square root of two raised to the square root of two , and let b be the square root of two . End proof. Does this constitute a valid proof? Most mathematicians feel that it does. But again, there is something a little bit unsatisfying here: we have proved the existence of a pair of real numbers with a certain property, without being able to say which pair of numbers it is. It is possible to prove the same result, but in such a way that the pair a , b is given in the proof: take a equals the square root of three and b equals the logarithm base three of four . Then Displayed expression. a raised to b equals the square root of three raised to the logarithm base three of four, equals three raised to one half times that logarithm, equals three raised to that logarithm and then to the one-half power, equals four to the one-half power, equals two. End displayed expression. since three raised to the logarithm base three of x equals x . Intuitionistic logic is designed to capture a kind of reasoning where moves like the one in the first proof are disallowed. Proving the existence of an x satisfying A of x means that you have to give a specific x , and a proof that it satisfies A , like in the second proof. Proving that A or B holds requires that you can prove one or the other. Formally speaking, intuitionistic logic is what you get if you restrict a derivation system for classical logic in a certain way. From the mathematical point of view, these are just formal deductive systems, but, as already noted, they are intended to capture a kind of mathematical reasoning. One can take this to be the kind of reasoning that is justified on a certain philosophical view of mathematics (such as Brouwer's intuitionism); one can take it to be a kind of mathematical reasoning which is more “concrete” and satisfying (along the lines of Bishop's constructivism); and one can argue about whether or not the formal description captures the informal motivation. But whatever philosophical positions we may hold, we can study intuitionistic logic as a formally presented logic; and for whatever reasons, many mathematical logicians find it interesting to do so. End section.

Section. Syntax of Intuitionistic Logic. The syntax of intuitionistic logic is the same as that for propositional logic. In classical propositional logic it is possible to define connectives by others, for example, one can define if A, then B by not A or B , or A or B by not both not A and not B . Thus, presentations of classical logic often introduce some connectives as abbreviations for these definitions. This is not so in intuitionistic logic, with two exceptions: not A can be—and often is—defined as an abbreviation for if A, then falsity . Then, of course, falsity must not itself be defined! Also, A if and only if B can be defined, as in classical logic, as the conditional from A to B and the conditional from B to A . Chapter. Semantics. Editorial note. This chapter collects definitions for semantics for intuitionistic logic. So far only Kripke and topological semantics are covered. There are no examples yet, either of how models make formulas true or of proofs that formulas are valid. End editorial note.

Section. Introduction. No logic is satisfactorily described without a semantics, and intuitionistic logic is no exception. Whereas for classical logic, the semantics based on valuations is canonical, there are several competing semantics for intuitionistic logic. None of them are completely satisfactory in the sense that they give an intuitionistically acceptable account of the meanings of the connectives. The semantics based on relational models, similar to the semantics for modal logics, is perhaps the most popular one. In this semantics, propositional variables are assigned to worlds, and these worlds are related by an accessibility relation. That relation is always a partial order, that is, it is reflexive, antisymmetric, and transitive. Intuitively, you might think of these worlds as states of knowledge or “evidentiary situations.” A state w prime is accessible from w if and only if, for all we know, w prime is a possible (future) state of knowledge, that is, one that is compatible with what's known at w . Once a proposition is known, it can't become un-known, that is, whenever A is known at w and world w prime is accessible from world w , A is known at w prime as well. So “knowledge” is monotonic with respect to the accessibility relation. If we define “ A is known” as in epistemic logic as “true in all epistemic alternatives,” then A and B is known at w if in all epistemic alternatives, both A and B are known. But since knowledge is monotonic and R is reflexive, that means that A and B is known at w if and only if A and B are known at w . For the same reason, A or B is known at w if and only if at least one of them is known. So for conjunction and disjunction , the truth conditions of the connectives coincide with those in classical logic. The truth conditions for the conditional, however, differ from classical logic. if A, then B is known at w if and only if at no w prime with world w prime is accessible from world w , A is known without B also being known. This is not the same as the condition that A is unknown or B is known at w . For if we know neither A nor B at w , there might be a future epistemic state w prime with world w prime is accessible from world w such that at w prime , A is known without also coming to know B . We know not A only if there is no possible future epistemic state in which we know A . Here the idea is that if A were knowable, then in some possible future epistemic state A becomes known. Since we can't know falsity , in that future epistemic state, we would know A but not know falsity . On this interpretation the principle of excluded middle fails. For there are some A which we don't yet know, but which we might come to know. For such a formula A , both A and not A are unknown, so A or not A is not known. But we do know, for example, that not both A and not A . For no future state in which we know both A and not A is possible, and we know this independently of whether or not we know A or not A . Relational models are not the only available semantics for intuitionistic logic. The topological semantics is another: here propositions are interpreted as open sets in a topological space, and the connectives are interpreted as operations on these sets (for example, conjunction corresponds to intersection). End section.

Section. Introduction. Tableaux are certain (downward-branching) trees of signed formulas, that is, pairs consisting of a truth value sign ( true or false ) and a sentence Displayed expression. signed true A, or signed false A. End displayed expression. A tableau begins with a number of assumptions. Each further signed formula is generated by applying one of the inference rules. Some inference rules add one or more signed formulas to a tip of the tree; others add two new tips, resulting in two branches. Rules result in signed formulas where the formula is less complex than that of the signed formula to which it was applied. When a branch contains both signed true A and signed false A , we say the branch is closed. If every branch in a tableau is closed, the entire tableau is closed. A closed tableau constitutes a derivation that shows that the set of signed formulas which were used to begin the tableau are unsatisfiable. This can be used to define a proves relation: Gamma proves A if and only if there is some finite set Gamma sub zero equals the finite set containing B sub one through B sub n, and is a subset of Gamma such that there is a closed tableau for the assumptions Displayed expression. the set containing signed false A and signed true B sub one through signed true B sub n. The prefixes are non-empty sequences of positive integers, that is, sigma is a nonempty finite sequence of positive integers . Chapter. Introduction.

Section. The Material Conditional. In its simplest form in English, a conditional is a sentence of the form “If and so on then and so on,” where the and so on are themselves sentences, such as “If the butler did it, then the gardener is innocent.” In introductory logic courses, we earn to symbolize conditionals using the the material conditional connective connective: symbolize the parts indicated by and so on, for example, by formulas A and B , and the entire conditional is symbolized by if A then B . The connective the material conditional connective is truth-functional, that is, the truth value— true or false —of if A then B is determined by the truth values of A and B : if A then B is true if and only if A is false or B is true, and false otherwise. Relative to a truth value assignment the truth-value assignment v , we define v satisfies if A then B if and only if v does not satisfy A or v satisfies B . The connective the material conditional connective with this semantics is called the material conditional. This definition results in a number of elementary logical facts. First of all, the deduction theorem holds for the material conditional: Displayed expression. if Gamma together with A entails B, then Gamma entails if A then B. End displayed expression. It is truth-functional: if A then B and not A or B are equivalent: Displayed expression. Material-conditional entailments. If A then B is equivalent, in both directions, to not A or B. B entails if A then B, and not A entails if A then B. Not if A then B is equivalent, in both directions, to A and not B. Modus ponens: A together with if A then B entails B. Agglomeration: if A then B together with if A then C entails if A then both B and C. Antecedent strengthening: if A then B entails if both A and C then B. Transitivity: if A then B together with if B then C entails if A then C. Contraposition holds in both directions between if A then B and if not B then not A. End of entailments. End displayed expression. These are all useful and unproblematic inferences in mathematical reasoning. However, the philosophical and linguistic literature is replete with purported counterexamples to the equivalent inferences in non-mathematical contexts. These suggest that the material conditional the material conditional connective is not—or at least not always—the appropriate connective to use when symbolizing English “if and so on then and so on ” statements. End section.

Section. Paradoxes of the Material Conditional. One of the first to criticize the use of if A then B as a way to symbolize “if and so on then and so on ” statements of English was C. I. Lewis. Lewis was criticizing the use of the material condition in Whitehead and Russell's Principia Mathematica, who pronounced the material conditional connective as “implies.” Lewis rightly complained that if the material conditional connective meant “implies,” then any false proposition p implies that p implies q , since if p, then if p then q is true if p is false, and that any true proposition q implies that p implies q , since if q, then if p then q is true if q is true. Logicians of course know that implication, that is, logical entailment, is not a connective but a relation between formulas or statements. So we should just not read the material conditional connective as “implies” to avoid confusion. Footnote. Reading “ the material conditional connective ” as “implies” is still widely practised by mathematicians and computer scientists, although philosophers try to avoid the confusions Lewis highlighted by pronouncing it as “only if.”. End footnote. As long as we don't, the particular worry that Lewis had simply does not arise: p does not “imply” q even if we think of p as standing for a false English sentence. To determine if p entails q we must consider all valuations, and p does not entail q even when we use p to symbolize a sentence which happens to be false. But there is still something odd about “if and so on then and so on ” statements such as Lewis's Quotation. If the moon is made of green cheese, then two plus two equals four . End quotation. and about the inferences Quotation. The moon is not made of green cheese. Therefore, if the moon is made of green cheese, then two plus two equals four . two plus two equals four . Therefore, if the moon is made of green cheese, then two plus two equals four . End quotation. Yet, if “if and so on then and so on ” were just the material conditional connective , the sentence would be unproblematically true, and the inferences unproblematically valid. Another example of concerns the tautology either if A then B, or if B then A . This would suggest that if you take two indicative sentences S and T from the newspaper at random, the sentence “If S then T , or if T then S ” should be true. End section.

Section. The Strict Conditional. Lewis introduced the strict conditional the strict conditional connective and argued that it, not the material conditional, corresponds to implication. In alethic modal logic, A strictly implies B can be defined as necessarily, if A then B . A strict conditional is thus true (at a world) if and only if the corresponding material conditional is necessary. How does the strict conditional fare vis-a-vis the paradoxes of the material conditional? A strict conditional with a false antecedent and one with a true consequent, may be true, or it may be false. Moreover, either A strictly implies B, or B strictly implies A is not valid. The strict conditional A strictly implies B is also not equivalent to not A or B , so it is not truth functional. However, the strict conditional still has its own “paradoxes.” Just as a material conditional with a false antecedent or a true consequent is true, a strict conditional with a necessarily false antecedent or a necessarily true consequent is true. Moreover, any true strict conditional is necessarily true, and any false strict conditional is necessarily false. In other words, we have Displayed expression. But they do raise issues if you want to use the strict conditional connective as a logical connective that is supposed to capture “if and so on then and so on,” especially the last two. Section. Counterfactuals. A very common and important form of “if and so on then and so on ” constructions in English are built using the past subjunctive form of to be: “if it were the case that and so on then it would be the case that and so on ” Because usually the antecedent of such a conditional is false, that is, counter to fact, they are called counterfactual conditionals (and because they use the subjunctive form of to be, also subjunctive conditionals. They are distinguished from indicative conditionals which take the form of “if it is the case that and so on then it is the case that and so on ” Counterfactual and indicative conditionals differ in truth conditions. Consider Adams's famous example: Quotation. If Oswald didn't kill Kennedy, someone else did. If Oswald hadn't killed Kennedy, someone else would have. End quotation. The first is indicative, the second counterfactual. The first is clearly true: we know President John F. Kennedy was killed by someone, and if that someone wasn't (contrary to the Warren Report) Lee Harvey Oswald, then someone else killed Kennedy. The second one says something different. It claims that if Oswald hadn't killed Kennedy, that is, if the Dallas shooting had been avoided or had been unsuccessful, history would have subsequently unfolded in such a way that another assassination would have been successful. In order for it to be true, it would have to be the case that powerful forces had conspired to ensure JFK's death (as many JFK conspiracy theorists believe). It is a live debate whether the indicative conditional is correctly captured by the material conditional, in particular, whether the paradoxes of the material conditional can be “explained” in a way that is compatible with it giving the truth conditions for English indicative conditionals. By contrast, it is uncontroversial that counterfactual conditionals cannot be symbolized correctly by the material conditionals. That is clear because, even though generally the antecedents of counterfactuals are false, not all counterfactuals with false antecedents are true—for instance, if you believe the Warren Report, and there was no conspiracy to assassinate JFK, then Adams's counterfactual conditional is an example. Counterfactual conditionals play an important role in causal reasoning: a prime example of the use of counterfactuals is to express causal relationships. for example, striking a match causes it to light, and you can express this by saying “if this match were struck, it would light.” Material, and generally indicative conditionals, cannot be used to express this: “the match is struck the material conditional connective the match lights” is true if the match is never struck, regardless of what would happen if it were. Even worse, “the match is struck the material conditional connective the match turns into a bouquet of flowers” is also true if it is never struck, but the match would certainly not turn into a bouquet of flowers if it were struck. It is still debated What exactly the correct logic of counterfactuals is. An influential analysis of counterfactuals was given by Stalnaker and Lewis. According to them, a counterfactual “if it were the case that S then it would be the case that T ” is true if and only if T is true in the counterfactual situation (“possible world”) that is closest to the way the actual world is and where S is true. This is called an “ontic” analysis, since it makes reference to an ontology of possible worlds. Other analyses make use of conditional probabilities or theories of belief revision. There is a proliferation of different proposed logics of counterfactuals. There isn't even a single Lewis—Stalnaker logic of counterfactuals: even though Stalnaker and Lewis proposed accounts along similar lines with reference to closest possible worlds, the assumptions they made result in different valid inferences. End section. End chapter.

Chapter. Minimal Change Semantics.

Section. Introduction. Stalnaker and Lewis proposed accounts of counterfactual conditionals such as “If the match were struck, it would light.” Their accounts were proposals for how to properly understand the truth conditions for such sentences. The idea behind both proposals is this: to evaluate whether a counterfactual conditional is true, we have to consider those possible worlds which are minimally different from the way the world actually is to make the antecedent true. If the consequent is true in these possible worlds, then the counterfactual is true. For instance, suppose I hold a match and a matchbook in my hand. In the actual world I only look at them and ponder what would happen if I were to strike the match. The minimal change from the actual world where I strike the match is that where I decide to act and strike the match. It is minimal in that nothing else changes: I don't also jump in the air, striking the match doesn't also light my hair on fire, I don't suddenly lose all strength in my fingers, I am not simultaneously doused with water in a SuperSoaker ambush, etc. In that alternative possibility, the match lights. Hence, it's true that if I were to strike the match, it would light. This intuitive account can be paired with formal semantics for logics of counterfactuals. Lewis introduced the symbol “ Lewis's box-right counterfactual symbol ” for the counterfactual while Stalnaker used the symbol “ Stalnaker's greater-than counterfactual symbol ”. We'll use the counterfactual conditional connective , and add it as a binary connective to propositional logic. So, we have, in addition to formulas of the form if A then B also formulas of the form if it were A then it would be B . The formal semantics, like the relational semantics for modal logic, is based on models in which formulas are evaluated at worlds, and the satisfaction condition defining in model capital M at world w, the counterfactual if it were A then it would be B is satisfied is given in terms of in model capital M at world w prime, A is satisfied and in model capital M at world w prime, B is satisfied for some (other) worlds w prime . Which w prime ? Intuitively, the one(s) closest to w for which it holds that in model capital M at world w prime, A is satisfied . This requires that a relation of “closeness” has to be included in the model as well. Lewis introduced an instructive way of representing counterfactual situations graphically. Section. Antecedent Strengthening. “Strengthening the antecedent” refers to the inference if A then C entails if both A and B then C . It is valid for the material conditional, but invalid for counterfactuals. Suppose it is true that if I were to strike this match, it would light. (That means, there is nothing wrong with the match or the matchbook surface, I will not break the match, etc.) But it is not true that if I were to light this match in outer space, it would light. So the following inference is invalid: Quotation. If the match were struck, it would light. Therefore, if the match were struck in outer space, it would light. End quotation. The Lewis—Stalnaker account of conditionals explains this: the closest world where I light the match and I do so in outer space is much further removed from the actual world than the closest world where I light the match is. So although it's true that the match lights in the latter, it is not in the former. And that is as it should be. Example. Section. Transitivity. For the material conditional, the chain rule holds: if A then B together with if B then C entails if A then C . In other words, the material conditional is transitive. Is the same true for counterfactuals? Consider the following example due to Stalnaker. Quotation. If J. Edgar Hoover had been born a Russian, he would have been a Communist. If J. Edgar Hoover were a Communist, he would have been be a traitor. Therefore, If J. Edgar Hoover had been born a Russian, he would have been be a traitor. End quotation. If Hoover had been born (at the same time he actually did), not in the United States, but in Russia, he would have grown up in the Soviet Union and become a Communist (let's assume). So the first premise is true. Likewise, the second premise, considered in isolation is true. The conclusion, however, is false: in all likelihood, Hoover would have been a fervent Communist if he had been born in the USSR, and not been a traitor (to his country). The intuitive assignment of truth values is borne out by the Stalnaker—Lewis account. The closest possible world to ours with the only change being Hoover's place of birth is the one where Hoover grows up to be a good citizen of the USSR. This is the closest possible world where the antecedent of the first premise and of the conclusion is true, and in that world Hoover is a loyal member of the Communist party, and so not a traitor. To evaluate the second premise, we have to look at a different world, however: the closest world where Hoover is a Communist, which is one where he was born in the United States, turned, and thus became a traitor. Footnote. Of course, to appreciate the force of the example we have to take on board some metaphysical and political assumptions, for example, that it is possible that Hoover could have been born to Russian parents, or that Communists in the US of the nineteen fifties were traitors to their country. End footnote. Exercise. Find a convincing, intuitive example for the failure of transitivity of counterfactuals. End exercise. This exercise remains unsolved. Example. Section. Contraposition. Material and strict conditionals are equivalent to their contrapositives. Counterfactuals are not. Here is an example due to Kratzer: Quotation. If Goethe hadn't died in one thousand eight hundred thirty two, he would (still) be dead now. If Goethe weren't dead now, he would have died in one thousand eight hundred thirty two. End quotation. The first sentence is true: humans don't live hundreds of years. The second is clearly false: if Goethe weren't dead now, he would be still alive, and so couldn't have died in one thousand eight hundred thirty two. Example. So w is the actual world where Goethe died in one thousand eight hundred thirty two and is still dead; w sub one is the (close) world where Goethe died in, say, one thousand eight hundred thirty three, and is still dead; and w sub two is a (remote) world where Goethe is still alive.
