If is less than well-orders capital A , then every non-empty subset of capital A has a unique is less than -least member, and is less than is irreflexive, asymmetric and transitive. End proposition. Proof. If capital X is a non-empty subset of capital A , it has a is less than -minimal element m , that is, for every z in capital X, z is not less than m . Since is less than is connected, for every z in capital X, m is less than or equal to z . So m is the is less than -least element of capital X . For irreflexivity, fix a belongs to capital A ; the is less than -least element of the set containing a is a , so a is not less than a . For transitivity, if a is less than b is less than c , then since the set containing a, then b, then c has a is less than -least element, a is less than c . Asymmetry follows from irreflexivity and transitivity End proof. Proposition. If is less than well-orders capital A , then for any formula phi of x : Displayed expression. if phi holds of each a in capital A whenever it holds of every b less than a, then phi holds of every a in capital A. End displayed expression. End proposition. Proof. We will prove the contrapositive. Suppose not for every a in capital A, phi of a , that is, that capital X is the nonempty set of x in capital A for which phi does not hold . Then capital X has an is less than -minimal element, a . So for every b less than a, phi of b but not phi of a . End proof. This last property should remind you of the principle of strong induction on the naturals, that is: if for every n in omega, if phi holds for every m less than n, then phi holds for n , then for every n in omega, phi of n . And this property makes well-ordering into a very robust notion. Footnote. A reminder: all formulas can have parameters (unless explicitly stated otherwise). End footnote. End section.

Section. Order-Isomorphisms. To explain how robust well-ordering is, we will start by introducing a method for comparing well-orderings. Definition. A well-ordering is a pair the ordered pair consisting of capital A and the less-than relation , such that is less than well-orders capital A . The well-orderings the ordered pair consisting of capital A and the less-than relation and the ordered pair consisting of capital B and the less-dot relation are order-isomorphic if and only if there is a bijection f maps capital A to capital B such that: x is less than y if and only if f of x is strictly smaller than f of y . In this case, we write capital A under less-than is order-isomorphic to capital B under less-dot , and say that f is an order-isomorphism. End definition. In what follows, for brevity, we will speak of “isomorphisms” rather than “order-isomorphisms”. Intuitively, isomorphisms are structure-preserving bijections. Here are some simple facts about isomorphisms. Lemma. Compositions of isomorphisms are isomorphisms, that is: if f maps capital A to capital B and g maps capital B to capital C are isomorphisms, then g composed with f maps capital A to capital C is an isomorphism. End lemma. Exercise. Prove lemma one in chapter Ordinals . End exercise. This exercise remains unsolved. Proof. Left as an exercise. End proof. Corollary. capital X is order-isomorphic to capital Y is an equivalence relation. End corollary. Proposition. If the ordered pair consisting of capital A and the less-than relation and the ordered pair consisting of capital B and the less-dot relation are isomorphic well-orderings, then the isomorphism between them is unique. End proposition. Proof. Let f and g be isomorphisms functions from capital A to capital B . We will prove the result by induction, that is using proposition two in chapter Ordinals . Fix a belongs to capital A , and suppose (for induction) that for every b less than a, f of b equals g of b . Fix x belongs to capital B . If x is strictly smaller than f of a , then the inverse of f at x is less than a , so g of the inverse of f at x is less-dot below g of a , invoking the fact that f and g are isomorphisms. But since the inverse of f at x is less than a , by our supposition x equals f of the inverse of f at x, which equals g of the inverse of f at x . So x is strictly smaller than g of a . Similarly, if x is strictly smaller than g of a then x is strictly smaller than f of a . Generalising, for every x in capital B, x is less-dot below f of a if and only if x is less-dot below g of a . It follows that f of a equals g of a by the proposition on extensionality strictlinearorders . So for every a in capital A, f of a equals g of a by proposition two in chapter Ordinals . End proof. This gives some sense that well-orderings are robust. But to continue explaining this, it will help to introduce some more notation. Definition. When the ordered pair consisting of capital A and the less-than relation is a well-ordering with a belongs to capital A , let capital A subscript a equals the set of x in capital A that are less than a . We say that capital A subscript a is a proper initial segment of capital A (and allow that capital A itself is an improper initial segment of capital A ). Let the less-than relation restricted below a be the restriction of is less than to the initial segment, that is, the restriction of the less-than relation to capital A subscript a squared . End definition. Using this notation, we can state and prove that no well-ordering is isomorphic to any of its proper initial segments. Lemma. If the ordered pair consisting of capital A and the less-than relation is a well-ordering with a belongs to capital A , then capital A under less-than is not order-isomorphic to its initial segment capital A subscript a under the restricted relation End lemma. Proof. For reductio, suppose f maps capital A to capital A subscript a is an isomorphism. Since f is a bijection and capital A subscript a is a proper subset of capital A , using proposition one in chapter Ordinals let b belongs to capital A be the is less than -least element of capital A such that b is not equal to f of b . We'll show that for every x in capital A, x is less than b if and only if x is less than f of b , from which it will follow by the proposition on extensionality strictlinearorders that b equals f of b , completing the reductio. Suppose x is less than b . So x equals f of x , by the choice of b . And f of x is less than f of b , as f is an isomorphism. So x is less than f of b . Suppose x is less than f of b . So the inverse of f at x is less than b , since f is an isomorphism, and so the inverse of f at x equals x by the choice of b . So x is less than b . End proof. Our next result shows, roughly put, that an “initial segment” of an isomorphism is an isomorphism: Lemma. Let the ordered pair consisting of capital A and the less-than relation and the ordered pair consisting of capital B and the less-dot relation be well-orderings. If f maps capital A to capital B is an isomorphism and a belongs to capital A , then the restriction of f to capital A subscript a maps capital A subscript a to capital B subscript f of a is an isomorphism. End lemma. Proof. Since f is an isomorphism: Displayed expression. Source-ordered equality chain. The image of capital A subscript a under f equals the image under f of all x in capital A below a. This equals the image under f of all inverse images of y that lie below a. It equals the set of y in capital B that are less-dot below f of a, and therefore equals capital B subscript f of a. End equality chain. End displayed expression. And the restriction of f to capital A subscript a preserves order because f does. End proof. Our next two results establish that well-orderings are always comparable: Lemma. Let the ordered pair consisting of capital A and the less-than relation and the ordered pair consisting of capital B and the less-dot relation be well-orderings. If the initial segment capital A subscript a subscript one under restricted less-than is order-isomorphic to the initial segment capital B subscript b subscript one under restricted less-dot and the initial segment capital A subscript a subscript two under restricted less-than is order-isomorphic to the initial segment capital B subscript b subscript two under restricted less-dot , then a subscript one is less than a subscript two if and only if b subscript one is strictly smaller than b subscript two End lemma. Proof. We will prove left to right; the other direction is similar. Suppose both the initial segment capital A subscript a subscript one under restricted less-than is order-isomorphic to the initial segment capital B subscript b subscript one under restricted less-dot and the initial segment capital A subscript a subscript two under restricted less-than is order-isomorphic to the initial segment capital B subscript b subscript two under restricted less-dot , with f maps capital A subscript a subscript two to capital B subscript b subscript two our isomorphism. Let a subscript one is less than a subscript two ; then the initial segment capital A subscript a subscript one under restricted less-than is order-isomorphic to the initial segment capital B subscript f of a subscript one under restricted less-dot by lemma three in chapter Ordinals . So the initial segment capital B subscript b subscript one is order-isomorphic to the initial segment capital B subscript f of a subscript one, using their restricted less-dot relations , and so b subscript one equals f of a subscript one by lemma two in chapter Ordinals . Now b subscript one is strictly smaller than b subscript two as f apostrophe s domain is capital B subscript b subscript two . End proof. Theorem. Given any two well-orderings, one is isomorphic to an initial segment (not necessarily proper) of the other. End theorem. Proof. Let the ordered pair consisting of capital A and the less-than relation and the ordered pair consisting of capital B and the less-dot relation be well-orderings. Using Separation, let Displayed expression. f equals the set of ordered pairs a and b in the Cartesian product of capital A and capital B such that the initial segment of capital A below a is order-isomorphic to the initial segment of capital B below b. End displayed expression. By lemma four in chapter Ordinals , a subscript one is less than a subscript two if and only if b subscript one is strictly smaller than b subscript two for all the ordered pairs a subscript one with b subscript one, and a subscript two with b subscript two, belong to f . So f maps its domain to its range is an isomorphism. If a subscript two belongs to the domain of f and a subscript one is less than a subscript two , then a subscript one belongs to the domain of f by lemma three in chapter Ordinals ; so the domain of f is an initial segment of capital A . Similarly, the range of f is an initial segment of capital B . For reductio, suppose both are proper initial segments. Then let a be the is less than -least element of capital A set minus the domain of f , so that the domain of f equals capital A subscript a , and let b be the is strictly smaller than -least element of capital B set minus the range of f , so that the range of f equals capital B subscript b . So f maps capital A subscript a to capital B subscript b is an isomorphism, and hence the ordered pair a, then b belongs to f , a contradiction. End proof. End section.

Section. Von Neumann's Construction of the Ordinals. the theorem on woalwayscomparable gives rise to a thought. We could introduce certain objects, called order types, to go proxy for the well-orderings. Writing the order type of capital A under the less-than relation for the order type of the well-ordering the ordered pair consisting of capital A and the less-than relation , we would hope to secure the following two principles: Displayed expression. Two proposed order-type principles. First, the order type of capital A under less-than equals the order type of capital B under less-dot if and only if those two well-orderings are order-isomorphic. Second, the first order type is less than the second if and only if the first well-ordering is order-isomorphic to the initial segment of capital B below some b. End principles. End displayed expression. Moreover, we might hope to introduce order-types as certain sets, just as we can introduce the natural numbers as certain sets. The most common way to do this—and the approach we will follow—is to define these order-types via certain canonical well-ordered sets. These canonical sets were first introduced by von Neumann: Definition. The set capital A is transitive if and only if for every x in capital A, x is a subset of capital A . Then capital A is an ordinal if and only if capital A is transitive and well-ordered by the membership relation . End definition. In what follows, we will use Greek letters for ordinals. It follows immediately from the definition that, if alpha is an ordinal, then the ordered pair consisting of alpha and membership restricted to alpha is a well-ordering, where membership restricted to alpha equals the set of ordered pairs x and y in alpha squared such that x belongs to y . So, abusing notation a little, we can just say that alpha itself is a well-ordering. Here are our first few ordinals: Displayed expression. the empty set; then the singleton containing the empty set; then the set containing the empty set and that singleton; then the set containing the empty set, that singleton, and the preceding two-element set; and so on. End displayed expression. You will note that these are the first few ordinals that we encountered in our Axiom of Infinity, that is, in von Neumann's definition of omega (see section Infinity in chapter Steps towards set theory Z ). This is no coincidence. Von Neumann's definition of the ordinals treats natural numbers as ordinals, but allows for transfinite ordinals too. As always, we can now ask: are these the ordinals? Or has von Neumann simply given us some sets that we can treat as the ordinals? The kinds of discussions one might have about this question are similar to the discussions we had in section Philosophical Reflections in chapter Relations , section Some Philosophical Reflections in chapter Arithmetization , section Dedekind's “Proof” of the Existence of an Infinite Set in chapter Infinite Sets , and section Selecting our Natural Numbers in chapter Steps towards set theory Z , so we will not belabour the point. Instead, in what follows, we will simply use “the ordinals” to speak of “the von Neumann ordinals”. End section.

Section. Basic Properties of the Ordinals. We observed that the first few ordinals are the natural numbers. The main reason for developing a theory of ordinals is to extend the principle of induction which holds on the natural numbers. We will build up to this via a sequence of elementary results. Lemma. Every element of an ordinal is an ordinal. End lemma. Proof. Let alpha be an ordinal with b belongs to alpha . Since alpha is transitive, b is a subset of alpha . So the membership relation well-orders b as the membership relation well-orders alpha . To see that b is transitive, suppose x belongs to c, and c belongs to b . So c belongs to alpha as b is a subset of alpha . Again, as alpha is transitive, c is a subset of alpha , so that x belongs to alpha . So x, c, and b belong to alpha . But the membership relation well-orders alpha , so that the membership relation is a transitive relation on alpha by proposition one in chapter Ordinals . So since x belongs to c, and c belongs to b , we have x belongs to b . Generalising, c is a subset of b End proof. Corollary. alpha equals the set of ordinals beta that belong to alpha , for any ordinal alpha End corollary. Proof. Immediate from lemma five in chapter Ordinals . End proof. The rough gist of the next two main results, theorem Transfinite Induction in chapter Ordinals and theorem Trichotomy in chapter Ordinals , is that the ordinals themselves are well-ordered by membership: Theorem. Transfinite Induction. For any formula phi of x : Displayed expression. if some alpha satisfies phi, then there is an alpha satisfying phi such that no beta belonging to alpha satisfies phi. End displayed expression. where the displayed quantifiers are implicitly restricted to ordinals. End theorem. Proof. Suppose phi of alpha , for some ordinal alpha . If for every beta in alpha, not phi of beta , then we are done. Otherwise, as alpha is an ordinal, it has some the membership relation -least element which is phi , and this is an ordinal by lemma five in chapter Ordinals . End proof. Note that we can equally express theorem Transfinite Induction in chapter Ordinals as the scheme: Displayed expression. if phi holds of every alpha whenever it holds of every beta belonging to alpha, then phi holds of every alpha. End displayed expression. just by taking not phi of alpha in theorem Transfinite Induction in chapter Ordinals , and then performing elementary logical manipulations. Theorem. Trichotomy. alpha belongs to beta or alpha equals beta or beta belongs to alpha , for any ordinals alpha and beta . End theorem. Proof. The proof is by double induction, that is, using theorem Transfinite Induction in chapter Ordinals twice. Say that x is comparable with y if and only if x belongs to y or x equals y or y belongs to x . For induction, suppose that every ordinal in alpha is comparable with every ordinal. For further induction, suppose that alpha is comparable with every ordinal in beta . We will show that alpha is comparable with beta . By induction on beta , it will follow that alpha is comparable with every ordinal; and so by induction on alpha , every ordinal is comparable with every ordinal, as required. It suffices to assume that alpha does not belong to beta and beta does not belong to alpha , and show that alpha equals beta . To show that alpha is a subset of beta , fix gamma belongs to alpha ; this is an ordinal by lemma five in chapter Ordinals . So by the first induction hypothesis, gamma is comparable with beta . But if either gamma equals beta or beta belongs to gamma then beta belongs to alpha (invoking the fact that alpha is transitive if necessary), contrary to our assumption; so gamma belongs to beta . Generalising, alpha is a subset of beta . Exactly similar reasoning, using the second induction hypothesis, shows that beta is a subset of alpha . So alpha equals beta . End proof. As such, we will sometimes write alpha is less than beta rather than alpha belongs to beta , since the membership relation is behaving as an ordering relation. There are no deep reasons for this, beyond familiarity, and because it is easier to write alpha is less than or equal to beta than alpha belongs to beta or alpha equals beta . Footnote. We could write alpha bears the underlined membership relation to beta ; but that would be wholly non-standard. End footnote. Here are two quick consequences of our last results, the first of which puts our new notation into action: Corollary. If there exists alpha, phi of alpha , then there exists an alpha satisfying phi such that every beta satisfying phi is greater than or equal to alpha . Moreover, for any ordinals alpha, then beta, then gamma , both alpha does not belong to alpha and if alpha belongs to beta and beta belongs to gamma, then alpha belongs to gamma . End corollary. Proof. Just like proposition one in chapter Ordinals . End proof. Exercise. Complete the “exactly similar reasoning” in the proof of theorem Trichotomy in chapter Ordinals . End exercise. This exercise remains unsolved. Corollary. capital A is an ordinal if and only if capital A is a transitive set of ordinals. End corollary. Proof. Left-to-right. By lemma five in chapter Ordinals . Right-to-left. If capital A is a transitive set of ordinals, then the membership relation well-orders capital A by theorem Transfinite Induction in chapter Ordinals and theorem Trichotomy in chapter Ordinals . End proof. Now, we glossed theorem Transfinite Induction in chapter Ordinals and theorem Trichotomy in chapter Ordinals as telling us that the membership relation well-orders the ordinals. However, we have to be very cautious about this sort of claim, thanks to the following result: Theorem. Burali-Forti Paradox. There is no set of all the ordinals End theorem. Proof. For reductio, suppose capital O is the set of all ordinals. If alpha belongs to beta, and beta belongs to capital O , then alpha is an ordinal, by lemma five in chapter Ordinals , so alpha belongs to capital O . So capital O is transitive, and hence capital O is an ordinal by corollary four in chapter Ordinals . Hence capital O belongs to capital O , contradicting corollary three in chapter Ordinals . End proof. This result is named after Cesare Burali-Forti . But, it was Cantor in one thousand eight hundred ninety nine—in a letter to Dedekind—who first saw clearly the contradiction in supposing that there is a set of all the ordinals. As van Heijenoort explains: Quotation. Burali-Forti himself considered the contradiction as establishing, by reductio ad absurdum, the result that the natural ordering of the ordinals is just a partial ordering. (Jean van Heijenoort, one thousand nine hundred sixty seven, page one hundred five) End quotation. Setting Burali-Forti's mistake to one side, we can summarize the foregoing as follows. Ordinals are sets which are individually well-ordered by membership, and collectively well-ordered by membership (without collectively constituting a set). Rounding this off, here are some more basic properties about the ordinals which follow from theorem Transfinite Induction in chapter Ordinals and theorem Trichotomy in chapter Ordinals . Proposition. Any strictly descending sequence of ordinals is finite. End proposition. Proof. Any infinite strictly descending sequence of ordinals alpha subscript zero is greater than alpha subscript one, which is greater than alpha subscript two, and the descending sequence continues has no is less than -minimal member, contradicting theorem Transfinite Induction in chapter Ordinals . End proof. Proposition. alpha is a subset of beta or beta is a subset of alpha , for any ordinals alpha, then beta . End proposition. Proof. If alpha belongs to beta , then alpha is a subset of beta as beta is transitive. Similarly, if beta belongs to alpha , then beta is a subset of alpha . And if alpha equals beta , then alpha is a subset of beta and beta is a subset of alpha . So by theorem Trichotomy in chapter Ordinals we are done. End proof. Proposition. alpha equals beta if and only if alpha is order-isomorphic to beta , for any ordinals alpha, then beta . End proposition. Proof. The ordinals are well-orders; so this is immediate from Trichotomy ( theorem Trichotomy in chapter Ordinals ) and lemma two in chapter Ordinals . End proof. Exercise. Prove that, if every member of capital X is an ordinal, then the union of capital X is an ordinal. End exercise. This exercise remains unsolved. End section.

Section. Replacement. In section Von Neumann's Construction of the Ordinals in chapter Ordinals , we motivated the introduction of ordinals by suggesting that we could treat them as order-types, that is, canonical proxies for well-orderings. In order for that to work, we would need to prove that every well-ordering is isomorphic to some ordinal. This would allow us to define the order type of capital A under the less-than relation as the ordinal alpha such that capital A under less-than is isomorphic to alpha . Unfortunately, we cannot prove the desired result only the Axioms we provided introduced so far. (We will see why in section The Strength of Replacement in chapter Replacement , but for now the point is: we can't.) We need a new thought, and here it is: Axiom. Scheme of Replacement. For any formula phi of x and y , the following is an axiom: Quotation. for any capital A , if for every x in capital A, there exists exactly one y, phi of x and y , then the set of y such that there exists x in capital A, phi of x and y exists. End quotation. End axiom. As with Separation, this is a scheme: it yields infinitely many axioms, for each of the infinitely many different phi apostrophe s . And it can equally well be (and normally is) written down thus: For any formula phi of x and y which does not contain “ capital B ”, the following is an axiom: Displayed expression. for every capital A, if every x in capital A has exactly one y such that phi holds of x and y, then there exists a capital B such that, for every y, y belongs to capital B if and only if phi holds of x and y for some x in capital A. End displayed expression. On first encounter, however, this is quite a tangled formula. The following quick consequence of Replacement probably gives a clearer expression to the intuitive idea we are working with: Footnote. A term is an expression which picks out exactly one object (on any completion of its free variables). For example, “ the empty set ” is a term which picks out the empty set; “ the set containing x ” is a term which picks out x apostrophe s singleton (whatever x might be); “ x union y ” is a term which picks out the union of x and y (whatever they might be). End footnote. Corollary. For any term tau of x , and any set capital A , this set exists: Displayed expression. the set of tau of x such that x belongs to capital A, equals the set of y such that there exists x in capital A, y equals tau of x. End displayed expression. End corollary. Proof. Since tau is a term, for every x, there exists exactly one y, tau of x equals y . A fortiori, for every x in capital A, there exists exactly one y, tau of x equals y . So the set of y such that there exists x in capital A, tau of x equals y exists by Replacement. End proof. This suggests that “Replacement” is a good name for the Axiom: given a set capital A , you can form a new set, the set of tau of x such that x belongs to capital A , by replacing every member of capital A with its image under tau . Indeed, following the notation for the image of a set under a function, we might write the image of capital A under tau for the set of tau of x such that x belongs to capital A . Crucially, however, tau is a term. It need not be (a name for) a function, in the sense of section Functions as Relations in chapter Functions , that is, a certain set of ordered pairs. After all, if f is a function (in that sense), then the set the image of capital A under f equals the set of f of x such that x belongs to capital A is just a particular subset of the range of f , and that is already guaranteed to exist, just using the axioms of set theory Z minus . Footnote. Just consider the set of y in the double union of f such that y equals f of x for some x in capital A . End footnote. Replacement, by contrast, is a powerful addition to our axioms, as we will see in chapter Replacement . End section.

Section. set theory Z F minus : a milestone. The question of how to justify Replacement (if at all) is not straightforward. As such, we will reserve that for chapter Replacement . However, with the addition of Replacement, we have reached another important milestone. We now have all the axioms required for the theory set theory Z F minus . In detail: Definition. The theory set theory Z F minus has these axioms: Extensionality, Union, Pairs, Powersets, Infinity, and all instances of the Separation and Replacement schemes. Otherwise put, set theory Z F minus adds Replacement to set theory Z minus . End definition. This stands for Zermelo—Fraenkel set theory ( minus something which we will come to later). Fraenkel gets the honour, since he is credited with the formulation of Replacement in one thousand nine hundred twenty two , although the first precise formulation was due to Thoralf Skolem (one thousand nine hundred twenty two) . End section.

Section. Ordinals as Order-Types. Armed with Replacement, and so now working in set theory Z F minus , we can finally prove the result we have been aiming for: Theorem. Every well-ordering is isomorphic to a unique ordinal. End theorem. Proof. Let the ordered pair consisting of capital A and the less-than relation be a well-order. By proposition six in chapter Ordinals , it is isomorphic to at most one ordinal. So, for reductio, suppose the ordered pair consisting of capital A and the less-than relation is not isomorphic to any ordinal. We will first “make the ordered pair consisting of capital A and the less-than relation as small as possible”. In detail: if some proper initial segment the ordered pair consisting of capital A subscript a and its restricted less-than relation is not isomorphic to any ordinal, there is a least a belongs to capital A with that property; then let capital B equals capital A subscript a and the less-dot relation equals the less-than relation restricted below a . Otherwise, let capital B equals capital A and the less-dot relation equals the less-than relation . By definition, every proper initial segment of capital B is isomorphic to some ordinal, which is unique as above. So by Replacement, the following set exists, and is a function: Displayed expression. f equals the set of ordered pairs beta and b such that b belongs to capital B and beta is order-isomorphic to the initial segment capital B subscript b under restricted less-dot. End displayed expression. To complete the reductio, we'll show that f is an isomorphism functions from alpha to capital B , for some ordinal alpha . It is obvious that the range of f equals capital B . And by lemma four in chapter Ordinals , f preserves ordering, that is, gamma belongs to beta if and only if f of gamma is strictly smaller than f of beta . To show that the domain of f is an ordinal, by corollary four in chapter Ordinals it suffices to show that the domain of f is transitive. So fix beta belongs to the domain of f , that is, beta is order-isomorphic to the initial segment capital B subscript b under restricted less-dot for some b . If gamma belongs to beta , then gamma belongs to the domain of f by lemma three in chapter Ordinals ; generalising, beta is a subset of the domain of f . End proof. This result licenses the following definition, which we have wanted to offer since section Von Neumann's Construction of the Ordinals in chapter Ordinals : Definition. If the ordered pair consisting of capital A and the less-than relation is a well-ordering, then its order type, the order type of capital A under the less-than relation , is the unique ordinal alpha such that capital A under less-than is order-isomorphic to alpha . End definition. Moreover, this definition licenses two nice principles: Corollary. Where the ordered pair consisting of capital A and the less-than relation and the ordered pair consisting of capital B and the less-dot relation are well-orderings: Displayed expression. Two order-type principles. First, the order types are equal if and only if capital A under less-than is order-isomorphic to capital B under less-dot. Second, the first order type belongs to the second if and only if capital A under less-than is order-isomorphic to the initial segment of capital B below some b. End principles. End displayed expression. End corollary. Proof. The identity holds by proposition six in chapter Ordinals . To prove the second claim, let the order type of capital A under less-than equals alpha and the order type of capital B under less-dot equals beta , and let f maps beta isomorphically to capital B under the less-dot relation be our isomorphism. Then: Displayed expression. Three equivalent conditions. Alpha belongs to beta if and only if the restriction of f to alpha is an isomorphism from alpha to the initial segment of capital B below f of alpha. This holds if and only if capital A under less-than is order-isomorphic to that initial segment, and if and only if it is order-isomorphic to the initial segment of capital B below some b. End equivalences. End displayed expression. by proposition three in chapter Ordinals , lemma three in chapter Ordinals , and corollary two in chapter Ordinals . End proof. End section.

Section. Successor and Limit Ordinals. In the next few chapters, we will use ordinals a great deal. So it will help if we introduce some simple notions. Definition. For any ordinal alpha , its successor is the ordinal successor of alpha equals alpha union the set containing alpha . We say that alpha is a successor ordinal if the ordinal successor of beta equals alpha for some ordinal beta . We say that alpha is a limit ordinal if and only if alpha is neither empty nor a successor ordinal. End definition. The following result shows that this is the right notion of successor: Proposition. For any ordinal alpha : List. Next item. alpha belongs to the ordinal successor of alpha ; Next item. the ordinal successor of alpha is an ordinal; Next item. there is no ordinal beta such that alpha belongs to beta, and beta belongs to the ordinal successor of alpha . End list. End proposition. Proof. Trivially, alpha belongs to alpha union the set containing alpha equals the ordinal successor of alpha . Equally, the ordinal successor of alpha is a transitive set of ordinals, and hence an ordinal by corollary four in chapter Ordinals . And it is impossible that alpha belongs to beta, and beta belongs to the ordinal successor of alpha , since then either beta belongs to alpha or beta equals alpha , contradicting corollary three in chapter Ordinals . End proof. This also licenses a variant of proof by transfinite induction: Theorem. Simple Transfinite Induction. Let phi of x be a formula such that: List. Next item. phi of the empty set ; and Next item. for any ordinal alpha , if phi of alpha then phi of the ordinal successor of alpha ; and Next item. if alpha is a limit ordinal and for every beta in alpha, phi of beta , then phi of alpha . End list. Then for every alpha, phi of alpha . End theorem. Proof. We prove the contrapositive. So, suppose there is some ordinal which is not phi ; let gamma be the least such ordinal. Then either gamma equals the empty set , or gamma equals the ordinal successor of alpha for some alpha such that phi of alpha ; or gamma is a limit ordinal and for every beta in gamma, phi of beta . End proof. A final bit of notation will prove helpful later on: Definition. If capital X is a set of ordinals, then the strict supremum of capital X equals the union, over alpha in capital X, of the ordinal successors of alpha . End definition. Here, “lsub” stands for “least strict upper bound”. Footnote. Some books use “ the supremum of capital X ” for this. But other books use “ the supremum of capital X ” for the least non-strict upper bound, that is, simply the union of capital X . If capital X has a greatest element, alpha , these notions come apart: the least strict upper bound is the ordinal successor of alpha , whereas the least non-strict upper bound is just alpha . End footnote. The following result explains this: Proposition. If capital X is a set of ordinals, the strict supremum of capital X is the least ordinal greater than every ordinal in capital X . End proposition. Proof. Let capital Y equals the set of ordinal successors of alpha as alpha ranges over capital X , so that the strict supremum of capital X equals the union of capital Y . Since ordinals are transitive and every member of an ordinal is an ordinal, the strict supremum of capital X is a transitive set of ordinals, and so is an ordinal by corollary four in chapter Ordinals . If alpha belongs to capital X , then the ordinal successor of alpha belongs to capital Y , so the ordinal successor of alpha is a subset of the union of capital Y equals the strict supremum of capital X , and hence alpha belongs to the strict supremum of capital X . So the strict supremum of capital X is strictly greater than every ordinal in capital X . Conversely, if alpha belongs to the strict supremum of capital X , then alpha belongs to the ordinal successor of beta, and that successor belongs to capital Y for some beta belongs to capital X , so that alpha is less than or equal to beta, and beta belongs to capital X . So the strict supremum of capital X is the least strict upper bound on capital X . End proof. End section. End chapter.
Chapter. Stages and Ranks.

Section. Defining the Stages as the capital V subscript alpha s. In chapter Ordinals , we defined well-orderings and the (von Neumann) ordinals. In this chapter, we will use these to characterise the hierarchy of sets itself. To do this, recall that in section Successor and Limit Ordinals in chapter Ordinals , we defined the idea of successor and limit ordinals. We use these ideas in following definition: Definition. Displayed expression. Source-ordered display. capital V subscript the empty set is defined as the empty set. Then, capital V subscript the ordinal successor of alpha is defined as the power set of capital V subscript alpha for any ordinal, alpha. Then, capital V subscript alpha is defined as the union over gamma is less than alpha of capital V subscript gamma, when, alpha, is a limit ordinal. End display. End displayed expression. End definition. This will be a definition by transfinite recursion on the ordinals. In this regard, we should compare this with recursive definitions of functions on the natural numbers. Footnote. Cf. the definitions of addition, multiplication, and exponentiation in section Dedekind Algebras in chapter Infinite Sets . End footnote. As when dealing with natural numbers, one defines a base case and successor cases; but when dealing with ordinals, we also need to describe the behaviour of limit cases. This definition of the capital V subscript alpha s will be an important milestone. We have informally motivated our hierarchy of sets as forming sets by stages. The capital V subscript alpha s are, in effect, just those stages. Importantly, though, this is an internal characterisation of the stages. Rather than suggesting a possible model of the theory, we will have defined the stages within our set theory. End section.

Section. Foundation. Section. set theory Z and set theory Z F : A Milestone. With Foundation, we reach another important milestone. We have considered theories set theory Z minus and set theory Z F minus , which we said were certain theories “minus” a certain something. That certain something is Foundation. So: Definition. The theory set theory Z adds Foundation to set theory Z minus . So its axioms are Extensionality, Union, Pairs, Powersets, Infinity, Foundation, and all instances of the Separation scheme. The theory set theory Z F adds Foundation to set theory Z F minus . Otherwise put, set theory Z F adds all instances of Replacement to set theory Z . End definition. Still, one question might have occurred to you. If Regularity is equivalent over set theory Z F minus to Foundation, and Regularity's justification is clear, why bother to go around the houses, and take Foundation as our basic axiom, rather than Regularity? Setting aside historical reasons (to do with who formulated what and when), the basic reason is that Foundation can be presented without employing the definition of the capital V subscript alpha s. That definition relied upon all of the work of section The Transfinite Recursion Theorem(s) in chapter Stages and Ranks : we needed to prove Transfinite Recursion, to show that it was justified. But our proof of Transfinite Recursion employed Replacement. So, whilst Foundation and Regularity are equivalent modulo set theory Z F minus , they are not equivalent modulo set theory Z minus . Indeed, the matter is more drastic than this simple remark suggests. Though it goes well beyond this book's remit, it turns out that both set theory Z minus and set theory Z are too weak to define the capital V subscript alpha s. So, if you are working only in set theory Z , then Regularity (as we have formulated it) does not even make sense. This is why our official axiom is Foundation, rather than Regularity. From now on, we will work in set theory Z F (unless otherwise stated), without any further comment. End section.

Chapter. Replacement.

Section. Introduction. Replacement is the axiom scheme which makes the difference between set theory Z F and set theory Z . We helped ourselves to it throughout chapters Ordinals through Stages and Ranks . In this chapter, we will finally consider the question: is Replacement justified? To make the question sharp, it is worth observing that Replacement is really rather strong. We will get a sense of just how strong it is, during this chapter (and again in section aleph-Fixed Points in chapter Cardinal Arithmetic ). But this will suggest that justification really is required. We will discuss two kinds of justification. Roughly: an extrinsic justification is an attempt to justify an axiom by its fruits; an intrinsic justification is an attempt to justify an axiom by suggesting that it is vindicated by the mathematical concepts in question. We will get a greater sense of what this means during this chapter, but it is just the tip of an iceberg. For more, see in particular Penelope Maddy ( one thousand nine hundred eighty eight and one thousand nine hundred eighty eight ). End section.

Section. The Strength of Replacement. We begin with a simple observation about the strength of Replacement: unless we go beyond set theory Z , we cannot prove the existence of any von Neumann ordinal greater than or equal to omega plus omega . Here is a sketch of why. Working in set theory Z F , consider the set capital V subscript omega plus omega . This set acts as the domain for a model for set theory Z . To see this, we introduce some notation for the relativization of a formula: Definition. For any set capital M , and any formula phi , let phi superscript capital M be the formula which results by restricting all of phi apostrophe s quantifiers to capital M . That is, replace “ there exists x ” with “ open scope, there exists x belongs to capital M, close scope ”, and replace “ for every x ” with “ open scope, for every x belongs to capital M, close scope ”. End definition. It can be shown that, for every axiom phi of set theory Z , we have that set theory Z F derives phi superscript capital V subscript omega plus omega . But omega plus omega is not in capital V subscript omega plus omega , by corollary two in chapter Stages and Ranks . So set theory Z is consistent with the non-existence of omega plus omega . This is why we said, in section Replacement in chapter Ordinals , that theorem five in chapter Ordinals cannot be proved without Replacement. For it is easy, within set theory Z , to define an explicit well-ordering which intuitively should have order-type omega plus omega . Indeed, we gave an informal example of this in section The General Idea of an Ordinal in chapter Ordinals , when we presented the ordering on the natural numbers given by: Displayed expression. Source-ordered display. n is strictly smaller than m if and only if either, n is less than m and m minus n, is even,. Then, or n is even and m is odd.. End display. End displayed expression. But if omega plus omega does not exist, this well-ordering is not isomorphic to any ordinal. So set theory Z does not prove theorem five in chapter Ordinals . Flipping things around: Replacement allows us to prove the existence of omega plus omega , and hence must allow us to prove the existence of capital V subscript omega plus omega . And not just that. For any well-ordering we can define, theorem five in chapter Ordinals tells us that there is some alpha isomorphic with that well-ordering, and hence that capital V subscript alpha exists. In a straightforward way, then, Replacement guarantees that the hierarchy of sets must be very tall. Over the next few sections, and then again in section aleph-Fixed Points in chapter Cardinal Arithmetic , we'll get a better sense of better just how tall Replacement forces the hierarchy to be. The simple point, for now, is that Replacement really does stand in need of justification! End section.

Section. Extrinsic Considerations about Replacement. We start by considering an extrinsic attempt to justify Replacement. Boolos suggests one, as follows. Quotation. Open bracket. Ellipsis. Close bracket. the reason for adopting the axioms of replacement is quite simple: they have many desirable consequences and (apparently) no undesirable ones. In addition to theorems about the iterative conception, the consequences include a satisfactory if not ideal theory of infinite numbers, and a highly desirable result that justifies inductive definitions on well-founded relations. (George Boolos, one thousand nine hundred seventy one, two hundred twenty nine) End quotation. The gist of Boolos's idea is that we should justify Replacement by its fruits. And the specific fruits he mentions are the things we have discussed in the past few chapters. Replacement allowed us to prove that the von Neumann ordinals were excellent surrogates for the idea of a well-ordering type (this is our “satisfactory if not ideal theory of infinite numbers”). Replacement also allowed us to define the capital V subscript alpha s, establish the notion of rank, and prove the membership relation -Induction (this amounts to our “theorems about the iterative conception”). Finally, Replacement allows us to prove the Transfinite Recursion Theorem (this is the “inductive definitions on well-founded relations”). These are, indeed, desirable consequences. But do these desirable consequences suffice to justify Replacement? No. Or at least, not straightforwardly. Here is a simple problem. Whilst we have stated some desirable consequences of Replacement, we could have obtained many of them via other means. This is not as well known as it ought to be, though, so we should pause to explain the situation. There is a simple theory of sets, Level Theory, or the language of set theory for short. Footnote. The first versions of the language of set theory are offered by Richard Montague (one thousand nine hundred sixty five) and Dana Scott (one thousand nine hundred seventy four) ; this was simplified, and given a book-length treatment, by Michael Potter (two thousand four) ; and Tim Button (two thousand twenty one) has recently simplified the language of set theory further. End footnote. the language of set theory apostrophe s axioms are just Extensionality, Separation, and the claim that every set is a subset of some level, where “level” is cunningly defined so that the levels behave like our friends, the capital V subscript alpha s. So set theory Z F proves the language of set theory ; but the language of set theory is much weaker than set theory Z F . In fact, the language of set theory does not give you Pairs, Powersets, Infinity, or Replacement. Let the set theory Z sub r be the result of adding Infinity and Powersets to the language of set theory ; this delivers Pairs too, so, the set theory Z sub r is at least as strong as set theory Z . But, in fact, the set theory Z sub r is strictly stronger than set theory Z , since it adds the claim that every set has a rank (hence my suggestion that we call it the set theory Z sub r ). Indeed, the set theory Z sub r delivers: a perfectly satisfactory theory of ordinals; results which stratify the hierarchy into well-ordered stages; a proof of the membership relation -Induction; and a version of Transfinite Recursion. In short: although Boolos didn't know this, all of the desirable consequences which he mentions could have been arrived at without Replacement; he simply needed to use the set theory Z sub r rather than set theory Z . (Given all of this, why did we follow the conventional route, of teaching you set theory Z F , rather than the language of set theory and the set theory Z sub r ? There are two reasons. First: for purely historical reasons, starting with the language of set theory is rather nonstandard; we wanted to equip you to be able to read more standard discussions of set theory. Second: when you are ready to appreciate the language of set theory and the set theory Z sub r , you can simply read Michael Potter two thousand four and Tim Button two thousand twenty one .) Of course, since the set theory Z sub r is strictly weaker than set theory Z F , there are results which set theory Z F proves which the set theory Z sub r leaves open. So one could try to justify Replacement on extrinsic grounds by pointing to one of these results. But, once you know how to use the set theory Z sub r , it is quite hard to find many examples of things that are (a) settled by Replacement but not otherwise, and (b) are intuitively true. (For more on this, see Michael Potter two thousand four, section thirteen point two .) The bottom line is this. To provide a compelling extrinsic justification for Replacement, one would need to find a result which cannot be achieved without Replacement. And that's not an easy enterprise. Let's consider a further problem which arises for any attempt to offer a purely extrinsic justification for Replacement. (This problem is perhaps more fundamental than the first.) Boolos does not just point out that Replacement has many desirable consequences. He also states that Replacement has “(apparently) no undesirable” consequences. But this parenthetical caveat, “apparently,” is surely absolutely crucial. Recall how we ended up here: Naïve Comprehension ran into inconsistency, and we responded to this inconsistency by embracing the cumulative-iterative conception of set. This conception comes equipped with a story which, we hope, assures us of its consistency. But if we cannot justify Replacement from within that story, then we have (as yet) no reason to believe that set theory Z F is consistent. Or rather: we have no reason to believe that set theory Z F is consistent, apart from the (perhaps merely contingent) fact that no one has discovered a contradiction yet. In exactly that sense, Boolos's comment seems to come down to this: “(apparently) set theory Z F is consistent”. We should demand greater reassurance of consistency than this. This issue will affect any purely extrinsic attempt to justify Replacement, that is, any justification which is couched solely in terms of the (known) consequences of set theory Z F . As such, we will want to look for an intrinsic justification of Replacement, that is, a justification which suggests that the story which we told about sets somehow “already” commits us to Replacement. End section.

Section. Limitation-of-size. Perhaps the most common attempt to offer an “intrinsic” justification of Replacement comes via the following notion: List. Next item.. Limitation of size. Any things form a set, provided that there are not too many of them. End list. This principle will immediately vindicate Replacement. After all, any set formed by Replacement cannot be any larger than any set from which it was formed. Stated precisely: suppose you form a set the image of capital A under tau equals the set of tau of x such that x belongs to capital A using Replacement; then the image of capital A under tau has cardinality at most that of capital A ; so if the elements of capital A were not too numerous to form a set, their images are not too numerous to form the image of capital A under tau . The obvious difficulty with invoking Limitation of size to justify Replacement is that we have not yet laid down any principle like Limitation of size. Moreover, when we told our story about the cumulative-iterative conception of set in chapters The Iterative Conception through Steps towards set theory Z , nothing ever hinted in the direction of Limitation of size. This, indeed, is precisely why Boolos at one point wrote: “Perhaps one may conclude that there are at least two thoughts `behind' set theory” (one thousand nine hundred eighty nine, page nineteen) . On the one hand, the ideas surrounding the cumulative-iterative conception of set are meant to vindicate set theory Z . On the other hand, Limitation of size is meant to vindicate Replacement. But the issue it is not just that we have thus far been silent about Limitation of size. Rather, the issue is that Limitation of size (as just formulated) seems to sit quite badly with the cumulative-iterative notion of set. After all, it mentions nothing about the idea of sets as formed in stages. This is really not much of a surprise, given the history of these “two thoughts” (that is, the cumulative-iterative conception of set, and Limitation of size ). These “two thoughts” ultimately amount to two rather different projects for blocking the set-theoretic paradoxes. The cumulative-iterative notion of set blocks Russell's paradox by saying, roughly: we should never have expected a Russell set to exist, because it would not be “formed” at any stage. By contrast, Limitation of size is meant to rule out the Russell set, by saying, roughly: we should never have expected a Russell set to exist, because it would have been too big. Put like this, then, let's be blunt: considered as a reply to the paradoxes, Limitation of size stands in need of much more justification. Consider, for example, this version of Russell's Paradox: no pug sniffs exactly the pugs which don't sniff themselves (see section Russell's Paradox (again) in chapter The Iterative Conception ). If you ask “why is there no such pug?”, it is not a good answer to be told that such a pug would have to sniff too many pugs. So why would it be a good intuitive explanation, of the non-existence of a Russell set, that it would have to be “too big” to exist? In short, it's forgivable if you are a bit mystified concerning the “intuitive” motivation for Limitation of size. End section.

Section. Replacement and “Absolute Infinity”. We will now put Limitation of size behind us, and explore a different family of (intrinsic) attempts to justify Replacement, which do take seriously the idea of the sets as formed in stages. When we first outlined the iterative process, we offered some principles which explained what happens at each stage. These were Stages are key, Stages are ordered, and Stages accumulate. Later, we added some principles which told us something about the number of stages: Stages keep going told us that the process of set-formation never ends, and Stages hit infinity told us that the process goes through an infinite-th stage. It is reasonable to suggest that these two latter principles fall out of some a broader principle, like: List. Next item.. Stages are inexhaustible. There are absolutely infinitely many stages; the hierarchy is as tall as it could possibly be. End list. Obviously this is an informal principle. But even if it is not immediately entailed by the cumulative-iterative conception of set, it certainly seems consonant with it. At the very least, and unlike Limitation of size, it retains the idea that sets are formed stage-by-stage. The hope, now, is to leverage Stages are inexhaustible into a justification of Replacement. So let us see how this might be done. In section The General Idea of an Ordinal in chapter Ordinals , we saw that it is easy to construct a well-ordering which (morally) should be isomorphic to omega plus omega . Otherwise put, we can easily imagine a stage-by-stage iterative process, whose order-type (morally) is omega plus omega . As such, if we have accepted Stages are inexhaustible, then we should surely accept that there is at least an omega plus omega indexed stage of the hierarchy, that is, capital V subscript omega plus omega , for the hierarchy surely could continue thus far. This thought generalizes as follows: for any well-ordering, the process of building the iterative hierarchy should run at least as far as that well-ordering. And we could guarantee this, just by treating theorem five in chapter Ordinals as an axiom. This would tell us that any well-ordering is isomorphic to a von Neumann ordinal. Since each von Neumann ordinal will be equal to its own rank, theorem five in chapter Ordinals will then tell us that, whenever we can describe a well-ordering in our set theory, the iterative process of set building must outrun that well-ordering. This idea certainly seems like a corollary of Stages are inexhaustible. Unfortunately, if our aim is to extract Replacement from this idea, then we face a simple, technical, barrier: Replacement is strictly stronger than theorem five in chapter Ordinals . (This observation is made by Michael Potter (two thousand four), section thirteen point two ; we will prove it in section Appendix: Finite axiomatizability in chapter Replacement .) The upshot is that, if we are going to understand Stages are inexhaustible in such a way as to yield Replacement, then it cannot merely say that the hierarchy outruns any well-ordering. It must make a stronger claim than that. To this end, Joseph R. Shoenfield (one thousand nine hundred seventy seven) proposed a very natural strengthening of the idea, as follows: the hierarchy is not cofinal with any set. Footnote. Gödel seems to have proposed a similar thought; see Michael Potter (two thousand four), page two hundred twenty three . For discussion of Gödel and Joseph R. Shoenfield , see Luca Incurvati (two thousand twenty), ninety through ninety five . End footnote. In slightly more detail: if tau is a mapping which sends sets to stages of the hierarchy, the image of any set capital A under tau does not exhaust the hierarchy. Otherwise put (schematically): List. Next item.. Stages are super cofinal. If capital A is a set and tau of x is a stage for every x belongs to capital A , then there is a stage which comes after each tau of x for x belongs to capital A . End list. It is obvious that set theory Z F proves a suitably formalised version of Stages are super cofinal. Conversely, we can informally argue that Stages are super cofinal justifies Replacement. Footnote. It would be harder to prove Replacement using some formalisation of Stages are super cofinal, since set theory Z on its own is not strong enough to define the stages, so it is not clear how one would formalise Stages are super cofinal. One option, though, is to work in some extension of the language of set theory , as discussed in section Extrinsic Considerations about Replacement in chapter Replacement . End footnote. For suppose for every x in capital A, there exists exactly one y, phi of x and y . Then for each x belongs to capital A , let sigma of x be the y such that phi of x and y , and let tau of x be the stage at which sigma of x is first formed. By Stages are super cofinal, there is a stage capital V such that for every x in capital A, tau of x belongs to capital V . Now since each tau of x belongs to capital V and sigma of x is a subset of tau of x , by Separation we can obtain the set of y belongs to capital V such that there exists x in capital A, sigma of x equals y, equals the set of y such that there exists x in capital A, phi of x and y . Exercise. Formalize Stages are super cofinal within set theory Z F . End exercise. This exercise remains unsolved. So Stages are super cofinal vindicates Replacement. And it is at least plausible that Stages are inexhaustible vindicates Stages are super cofinal. For suppose Stages are super cofinal fails. So the hierarchy is cofinal with some set capital A , that is, we have a map tau such that for any stage capital S there is some x belongs to capital A such that capital S belongs to tau of x . In that case, we do have a way to get a handle on the supposed “absolute infinity” of the hierarchy: it is exhausted by the range of tau applied to capital A . And that compromises the thought that the hierarchy is “absolutely infinite”. Contraposing: Stages are inexhaustible entails Stages are super cofinal, which in turn justifies Replacement. This represents a genuinely promising attempt to provide an intrinsic justification for Replacement. But whether it ultimately works, or not, we will have to leave to you to decide. End section.

Given this equivalence, one might hope to justify Reflection and Replacement via Stages are inexhaustible as follows: given Stages are inexhaustible, the hierarchy should be very, very tall; so tall, in fact, that nothing we can say about it is sufficient to bound its height. Chapter. Ordinal Arithmetic.

Section. Introduction. In chapter Ordinals , we developed a theory of ordinal numbers. We saw in chapter Stages and Ranks that we can think of the ordinals as a spine around which the remainder of the hierarchy is constructed. But that is not the only role for the ordinals. There is also the task of performing ordinal arithmetic. We already gestured at this, back in section The General Idea of an Ordinal in chapter Ordinals , when we spoke of omega , omega plus one and omega plus omega . At the time, we spoke informally; the time has come to spell it out properly. However, we should mention that there is not much philosophy in this chapter; just technical developments, coupled with a (mildly) interesting observation that we can do the same thing in two different ways. End section.

Section. Ordinal Addition. Suppose we want to add alpha and beta . We can simply put a copy of beta immediately after a copy of alpha . (We need to take copies, since we know from proposition five in chapter Ordinals that either alpha is a subset of beta or beta is a subset of alpha .) The intuitive effect of this is to run through an alpha -sequence of steps, and then to run through a beta -sequence. The resulting sequence will be well-ordered; so by theorem five in chapter Ordinals it is isomorphic to a (unique) ordinal. That ordinal can be regarded as the sum of alpha and beta . That is the intuitive idea behind ordinal addition. To define it rigorously, we start with the idea of taking copies of sets. The idea here is to use arbitrary tags, zero and one , to keep track of which object came from where: Definition. Section. Ordinal Multiplication. We now turn to ordinal multiplication, and we approach this much like ordinal addition. So, suppose we want to multiply alpha by beta . Chapter. Cardinals.

Section. Cantor's Principle. Cast your mind back to section Von Neumann's Construction of the Ordinals in chapter Ordinals . We were discussing well-ordered sets, and suggested that it would be nice to have objects which go proxy for well-orders. With this is mind, we introduced ordinals, and then showed in corollary six in chapter Ordinals that these behave as we would want them to, that is: Displayed expression. the order type of capital A is less than equals the order type of capital B is strictly smaller than if and only if the ordered pair capital A, then is less than is isomorphic to the ordered pair capital B, then is strictly smaller than. End displayed expression. Cast your mind back even further, to section Equinumerosity in chapter The Size of Sets . There, working naïvely, we introduced the notion of the “size” of a set. Specifically, we said that two sets are equinumerous, capital A is equinumerous with capital B , just in case there is a bijection f colon capital A maps to capital B . This is an intrinsically simpler notion than that of a well-ordering: we are only interested in bijections, and not (as with order-isomorphisms) whether the bijections “preserve any structure”. This all gives rise to an obvious thought. Just as we introduced certain objects, ordinals, to calibrate well-orders, we can introduce certain objects, cardinals, to calibrate size. That is the aim of this chapter. Before we say what these cardinals will be, we should lay down a principle which they ought to satisfy. Writing the cardinality of capital X for the cardinality of the set capital X , we would want them to obey: Displayed expression. the cardinality of capital A equals the cardinality of capital B if and only if capital A is equinumerous with capital B. End displayed expression. We'll call this Cantor's Principle, since Cantor was probably the first to have it very clearly in mind. (We'll say more about its relationship to Hume's Principle in section Appendix: Hume's Principle in chapter Cardinals .) So our aim is to define the cardinality of capital X , for each capital X , in such a way that it delivers Cantor's Principle. End section.

Section. Cardinals as Ordinals. In fact, our theory of cardinals will just make (shameless) use of our theory of ordinals. That is: we will just define cardinals as certain specific ordinals. In particular, we will offer the following: Definition. If capital A can be well-ordered, then the cardinality of capital A is the least ordinal gamma such that capital A is equinumerous with gamma . For any ordinal gamma , we say that gamma is a cardinal if and only if gamma equals the cardinality of gamma . End definition. We just used the phrase “ capital A can be well-ordered”. As is almost always the case in mathematics, the modal locution here is just a hand-waving gloss on an existential claim: to say “ capital A can be well-ordered” is just to say “there is a relation which well-orders capital A ”. But there is a snag with definition one in chapter Cardinals . We would like it to be the case that every set has a size, that is, that the cardinality of capital A exists for every capital A . The definition we just gave, though, begins with a conditional: “ If capital A can be well-ordered and so on ”. If there is some set capital A which cannot be well-ordered, then our definition will simply fail to define an object the cardinality of capital A . So, to use definition one in chapter Cardinals , we need a guarantee that every set can be well-ordered. Sadly, though, this guarantee is unavailable in set theory Z F . So, if we want to use definition one in chapter Cardinals , there is no alternative but to add a new axiom, such as: Axiom. Well-Ordering. Every set can be well-ordered. End axiom. We will discuss whether the Well-Ordering Axiom is acceptable in chapter Choice . From now on, though, we will simply help ourselves to it. And, using it, it is quite straightforward to prove that cardinals (as defined in definition one in chapter Cardinals ) exist and behave nicely: Lemma. For every set capital A : List. Next item. the cardinality of capital A exists and is unique; Next item. the cardinality of capital A is equinumerous with capital A ; Next item. the cardinality of capital A is a cardinal, that is, the cardinality of capital A equals the cardinality of the cardinality of capital A ; End list. End lemma. Proof. Fix capital A . By Well-Ordering, there is a well-ordering the ordered pair capital A, then capital R . By theorem five in chapter Ordinals , the ordered pair capital A, then capital R is isomorphic to a unique ordinal, beta . So capital A is equinumerous with beta . By Transfinite Induction, there is a uniquely least ordinal, gamma , such that capital A is equinumerous with gamma . So the cardinality of capital A equals gamma , establishing item 1 of lemma one in chapter Cardinals and item 2 of lemma one in chapter Cardinals . To establish item 3 of lemma one in chapter Cardinals , note that if delta belongs to gamma then delta has smaller cardinality than capital A , by our choice of gamma , so that also delta has smaller cardinality than gamma since equinumerosity is an equivalence relation ( proposition Equinumerosity as an equivalence relation in chapter The Size of Sets ). So gamma equals the cardinality of gamma . End proof. The next result guarantees Cantor's Principle, and more besides. (Note that cardinals inherit their ordering from the ordinals, that is, the cardinal a is less than the cardinal b if and only if the cardinal a belongs to the cardinal b . In formulating this, we will use Fraktur letters for objects we know to be cardinals. This is fairly standard. A common alternative is to use Greek letters, since cardinals are ordinals, but to choose them from the middle of the alphabet, for example: kappa, then lambda .): Lemma. For any sets capital A and capital B : Displayed expression. Source-ordered display. capital A is equinumerous with capital B if and only if the cardinality of capital A equals the cardinality of capital B. Then, capital A has cardinality at most that of capital B if and only if the cardinality of capital A is less than or equal to the cardinality of capital B. Then, capital A has smaller cardinality than capital B if and only if the cardinality of capital A is less than the cardinality of capital B. End display. End displayed expression. End lemma. Proof. We will prove the left-to-right direction of the second claim (the other cases are similar, and left as an exercise). So, consider the following diagram: Commutative comparison diagram. On the top row, capital A maps by an injection to capital B . Vertical bijections connect those two sets, respectively, with the cardinality of capital A and the cardinality of capital B . A dashed bottom arrow is the resulting injection between the two cardinalities. End of diagram. The double-headed arrows indicate bijections, whose existence is guaranteed by the lemma on Cardinals Exist . In assuming that capital A has cardinality at most that of capital B , there is an injection capital A maps to capital B . Now, chasing the arrows around from the cardinality of capital A to capital A to capital B to the cardinality of capital B , we obtain an injection the cardinality of capital A maps to the cardinality of capital B (the dashed arrow). End proof. We can also use the lemma on Cardinals Behave Right to re-prove Schröder—Bernstein. This is the claim that if capital A has cardinality at most that of capital B and capital B has cardinality at most that of capital A then capital A is equinumerous with capital B . We stated this as the theorem on schroder bernstein , but first proved it—with some effort—in section Appendix: Proving Schröder-Bernstein in chapter Infinite Sets . Now consider: Proof. Re-proof of Schröder-Bernstein. If capital A has cardinality at most that of capital B and capital B has cardinality at most that of capital A , then the cardinality of capital A is less than or equal to the cardinality of capital B and the cardinality of capital B is less than or equal to the cardinality of capital A by the lemma on Cardinals Behave Right . So the cardinality of capital A equals the cardinality of capital B and capital A is equinumerous with capital B by Trichotomy and the lemma on Cardinals Behave Right . End proof. Whilst this is a very simple proof, it implicitly relies on both Replacement (to secure theorem five in chapter Ordinals ) and on Well-Ordering (to guarantee the lemma on Cardinals Behave Right ). By contrast, the proof of section Appendix: Proving Schröder-Bernstein in chapter Infinite Sets was much more self-standing (indeed, it can be carried out in set theory Z minus ). End section.

Section. set theory Z F C : A Milestone. With the addition of Well-Ordering, we have reached the final theoretical milestone. We now have all the axioms required for set theory Z F C . In detail: Definition. The theory set theory Z F C has these axioms: Extensionality, Union, Pairs, Powersets, Infinity, Foundation, Well-Ordering and all instances of the Separation and Replacement schemes. Otherwise put, set theory Z F C adds Well-Ordering to set theory Z F . End definition. set theory Z F C stands for Zermelo—Fraenkel set theory with Choice. Now this might seem slightly odd, since the axiom we added was called “Well-Ordering”, not “Choice”. But, when we later formulate Choice, it will turn out that Well-Ordering is equivalent (modulo set theory Z F ) to Choice (see theorem in set theory Z F in chapter Choice ). So which to take as our “basic” axiom is a matter of indifference. And the name “ set theory Z F C ” is entirely standard in the literature. End section.

Section. Finite, Enumerable, Non-enumerable. Now that we have been introduced to cardinals, it is worth spending a little time talking about different varieties of cardinals; specifically, finite, enumerable, and non-enumerable cardinals. Our first two results entail that the finite cardinals will be exactly the finite ordinals, which we defined as our natural numbers back in definition of the natural numbers and omega in chapter Steps towards set theory Z : Proposition. Let n, then m belongs to omega . Then n equals m if and only if n is equinumerous with m . End proposition. Proof. Left-to-right is trivial. To prove right-to-left, suppose n is equinumerous with m although n is not equal to m . By Trichotomy, either n belongs to m or m belongs to n ; suppose n belongs to m without loss of generality. Then n is a proper subset of m and there is a bijection f colon m maps to n , so that m is Dedekind infinite, contradicting proposition that natural numbers are not Dedekind infinite in chapter Steps towards set theory Z . End proof. Corollary. If n belongs to omega , then n is a cardinal. End corollary. Proof. Immediate. End proof. It also follows that several reasonable notions of what it might mean to describe a cardinal as “finite” or “infinite” coincide: Theorem. For any set capital A , the following are equivalent: List. Next item. the cardinality of capital A does not belong to omega , that is, capital A is not a natural number; Next item. omega is less than or equal to the cardinality of capital A ; Next item. capital A is Dedekind infinite. End list. End theorem. Proof. From lemma five in chapter Ordinal Arithmetic , the lemma on Cardinals Behave Right , and corollary one in chapter Cardinals . End proof. This licenses the following definition of some notions which we used rather informally in part Naïve Set Theory : Definition. We say that capital A is finite if and only if the cardinality of capital A is a natural number, that is, the cardinality of capital A belongs to omega . Otherwise, we say that capital A is infinite. End definition. But note that this definition is presented against the background of set theory Z F C . After all, we needed Well-Ordering to guarantee that every set has a cardinality. And indeed, without Well-Ordering, there can be a set which is neither finite nor Dedekind infinite. We will return to this sort of issue in chapter Choice . For now, we continue to rely upon Well-Ordering. Let us now turn from the finite cardinals to the infinite cardinals. Here are two elementary points: Corollary. omega is the least infinite cardinal. End corollary. Proof. omega is a cardinal, since omega is Dedekind infinite and if omega is equinumerous with n for any n belongs to omega then n would be Dedekind infinite, contradicting proposition that natural numbers are not Dedekind infinite in chapter Steps towards set theory Z . Now omega is the least infinite cardinal by definition. End proof. Corollary. Every infinite cardinal is a limit ordinal. End corollary. Proof. Let alpha be an infinite successor ordinal, so alpha equals beta ordinal plus one for some beta . By proposition one in chapter Cardinals , beta is also infinite, so beta is equinumerous with beta ordinal plus one by lemma five in chapter Ordinal Arithmetic . Now the cardinality of beta equals the cardinality of beta ordinal plus one by the lemma on Cardinals Behave Right , so that alpha is not equal to the cardinality of alpha . End proof. Now, as early as the definition on enumerable , we flagged we can distinguish between enumerable and non-enumerable infinite sets. That definition naturally leads to the following: Proposition. capital A is enumerable if and only if the cardinality of capital A is less than or equal to omega , and capital A is non-enumerable if and only if omega is less than the cardinality of capital A . End proposition. Proof. By Trichotomy, the two claims are equivalent, so it suffices to prove that capital A is enumerable if and only if the cardinality of capital A is less than or equal to omega . For right-to-left: if the cardinality of capital A is less than or equal to omega , then capital A has cardinality at most that of omega by the lemma on Cardinals Behave Right and corollary two in chapter Cardinals . For left-to-right: suppose capital A is enumerable; then by the definition on enumerable there are three possible cases: List. Next item. if capital A equals the empty set , then the cardinality of capital A equals zero belongs to omega , by corollary one in chapter Cardinals and the lemma on Cardinals Behave Right . End displayed expression. And, at this point, some commentary and comparison might help. There are two ways to take a principle like Hume's Principle or Basic Law V: predicatively or impredicatively (recall section Predicative and Impredicative in chapter The Iterative Conception ). On the impredicative reading of Basic Law V, for each capital F , the object the Frege extension of x capital F of x falls within the domain of quantification that we used in formulating Basic Law V itself. Similarly, on the impredicative reading of Hume's Principle, for each capital F , the object the Frege number of x capital F of x falls within the domain of quantification that we used in formulating Hume's Principle. By contrast, on the predicative understanding, the objects the Frege extension of x capital F of x and the Frege number of x capital F of x would be entities from some different domain. Now, if we read Basic Law V impredicatively, it leads to inconsistency, via Naïve Comprehension (for the details, see section Appendix: Frege's Basic Law V in chapter The Iterative Conception ). Much like Naïve Comprehension, it can be rendered consistent by reading it predicatively. But it probably will not do everything that we wanted it to. Hume's Principle, however, can consistently be read impredicatively. And, read thus, it is quite powerful. To illustrate: consider the predicate “ x is not equal to x ”, which obviously nothing satisfies. Hume's Principle now yields an object the number of x such that x is not equal to x . We might treat this as the number zero . Now, on the impredicative understanding—but only on the impredicative understanding—this entity zero falls within our original domain of quantification. So we can sensibly apply Hume's Principle with the predicate “ x equals zero ” to obtain an object the number of x such that x equals zero . We might treat this as the number one . Moreover, Hume's Principle entails that zero is not equal to one , since there cannot be a bijection from the non-self-identical objects to the objects identical with zero (there are none of the former, but one of the latter). Now, working impredicatively again, one falls within our original domain of quantification. So we can sensibly apply Hume's Principle with the predicate “ open scope, x equals zero or x equals one, close scope ” to obtain an object the number of x such that x equals zero or x equals one . We might treat this as the number two , and we can show that zero is not equal to two and one is not equal to two and so on. In short, taken impredicatively, Hume's Principle entails that there are infinitely many objects. And this has encouraged neo-Fregean logicists to take Hume's Principle as the foundation for arithmetic. Frege himself, though, did not take Hume's Principle as his foundation for arithmetic. Instead, Frege proved Hume's Principle from an explicit definition: the Frege number of x capital F of x is defined as the extension of the concept capital F is equivalent to capital Phi . In modern terms, we might attempt to render this as the Frege number of x capital F of x equals the set of capital G such that capital F is equivalent to capital G ; but this will pull us back into the problems of Naïve Comprehension. End section. End chapter.
