Section. The Continuum Hypothesis. The previous result hints (correctly) that cardinal exponentiation would be quite easy, if infinite cardinals are guaranteed to “play straightforwardly” with powers of two , that is, (by the lemma on Size Powersettwo Exp ) with taking powersets. But we cannot assume that infinite cardinals do play straightforwardly powersets. To start unpacking this, we introduce some nice notation. Definition. Where the cardinal successor of the cardinal a is the least cardinal strictly greater than the cardinal a , we define two infinite sequences: Displayed expression. Source-ordered display. aleph over zero of is defined as omega applied to beth over zero. Then, aleph over alpha ordinal plus one of is defined as the cardinal successor of open scope, aleph over alpha, close scope beth over alpha plus one. Then, aleph over alpha of is defined as the union over beta is less than alpha of aleph over beta of beth over alpha. End display. End displayed expression. End definition. The definition of the cardinal successor of the cardinal a is in order, since the lemma on No Largest Cardinal tells us that, for each cardinal the cardinal a , there is some cardinal greater than the cardinal a , and Transfinite Induction guarantees that there is a least cardinal greater than the cardinal a . The rest of the definition of the cardinal a is provided by transfinite recursion. Cantor introduced this “ aleph ” notation; this is aleph, the first letter in the Hebrew alphabet and the first letter in the Hebrew word for “infinite”. Peirce introduced the “ beth ” notation; this is beth, which is the second letter in the Hebrew alphabet. Footnote. Peirce used this notation in a letter to Cantor of December one thousand nine hundred. Unfortunately, Peirce also gave a bad argument there that beth subscript alpha does not exist for alpha is greater than or equal to omega . End footnote. Now, these notations provide us with infinite cardinals. Proposition. aleph subscript alpha and beth subscript alpha are cardinals, for every ordinal alpha . End proposition. Proof. Both results hold by a simple transfinite induction. aleph subscript zero of equals beth subscript zero is a cardinal by corollary two in chapter Cardinals . Assuming aleph subscript alpha and beth subscript alpha are both cardinals, aleph over alpha plus one and beth over alpha plus one are explicitly defined as cardinals. And the union of a set of cardinals is a cardinal, by proposition three in chapter Cardinals . End proof. Moreover, every infinite cardinal is an aleph : Proposition. If the cardinal a is an infinite cardinal, then the cardinal a equals aleph subscript gamma for some unique gamma . End proposition. Proof. By transfinite induction on cardinals. For induction, suppose that if the cardinal b is less than the cardinal a then the cardinal b equals aleph over gamma subscript the cardinal b . If the cardinal a equals the cardinal successor of the cardinal b for some the cardinal b , then the cardinal a equals the cardinal successor of open scope, aleph over gamma subscript the cardinal b, close scope . If the cardinal a is not the successor of any cardinal, then since cardinals are ordinals the cardinal a equals the union over the cardinal b is less than the cardinal a of the cardinal b , so the cardinal a equals aleph subscript gamma where gamma equals the union over the cardinal b is less than the cardinal a of gamma subscript the cardinal b . End proof. Since every infinite cardinal is an aleph , this prompts us to ask: is every infinite cardinal a beth ? Certainly if that were the case, then the infinite cardinals would “play straightforwardly” with the operation of taking powersets. Indeed, we would have the following: Generalized Continuum Hypothesis (GCH). aleph subscript alpha of equals beth subscript alpha , for all alpha . Moreover, if GCH held, then we could make some considerable simplifications with cardinal exponentiation. In particular, we could show that when the cardinal b is less than the cardinal a , the value of cardinal exponentiation of the cardinal a to the power the cardinal b is trapped by the cardinal a is less than or equal to cardinal exponentiation of the cardinal a to the power the cardinal b . We could then go on to give precise conditions which determine which of the two possibilities obtains (that is, whether the cardinal a equals cardinal exponentiation of the cardinal a to the power the cardinal b or cardinal exponentiation of the cardinal a to the power the cardinal b equals the cardinal successor of the cardinal a ). Footnote. The condition is dictated by cofinality. End footnote. But GCH is a hypothesis, not a theorem. In fact, Kurt Gödel (one thousand nine hundred thirty eight) proved that if set theory Z F C is consistent, then so is set theory Z F C plus GCH . But it later turned out that we can equally add negation GCH to set theory Z F C . Indeed, consider the simplest non-trivial instance of GCH, namely: Continuum Hypothesis (CH). aleph subscript one of equals beth subscript one . Paul J. Cohen (one thousand nine hundred sixty three) proved that if set theory Z F C is consistent then so is set theory Z F C plus not CH . So the Continuum Hypothesis is independent from set theory Z F C . The Continuum Hypothesis is so-called, since “the continuum” is another name for the real line, the real numbers . theorem one in chapter Cardinal Arithmetic tells us that the cardinality of the real numbers equals beth subscript one . So the Continuum Hypothesis states that there is no cardinal between the cardinality of the natural numbers, aleph subscript zero of equals beth subscript zero , and the cardinality of the continuum, beth subscript one . Given the independence of (G)CH from set theory Z F C , what should say about their truth? Well, there is much to say. Indeed, and much fertile recent work in set theory has been directed at investigating these issues. But two very quick points are certainly worth emphasising. First: it does not immediately follow from these formal independence results that either GCH or CH is indeterminate in truth value. After all, maybe we just need to add more axioms, which strike us as natural, and which will settle the question one way or another. Gödel himself suggested that this was the right response. Second: the independence of CH from set theory Z F C is certainly striking, but it is certainly not incredible (in the literal sense). The point is simply that, for all set theory Z F C tells us, moving from cardinals to their successors may involve a less blunt tool than simply taking powersets. With those two observations made, if you want to know more, you will now have to turn to the various philosophers and mathematicians with horses in the race. Footnote. Though you might want to start by reading Michael Potter (two thousand four), section fifteen point six . End footnote. End section.

But is the existence of kappa so bad? It might help, here, to consider Russell's Tristram Shandy paradox. Tristram Shandy documents his life in his diary, but it takes him a year to record a single day. With every passing year, Tristram falls further and further behind: after one year, he has recorded only one day, and has lived three hundred sixty four days unrecorded days; after two years, he has only recorded two days, and has lived seven hundred twenty eight unrecorded days; after three years, he has only recorded three days, and lived one thousand ninety two unrecorded days and so on Footnote. Forgetting about leap years. End footnote. Still, if Tristram is immortal, Tristram will manage to record every day, for he will record the n indexed day on the n indexed year of his life. And so, “at the end of time”, Tristram will have a complete diary. Chapter. Choice.

Section. Introduction. In chapters Cardinals through Cardinal Arithmetic , we developed a theory of cardinals by treating cardinals as ordinals. That approach depends upon the Axiom of Well-Ordering. It turns out that Well-Ordering is equivalent to another principle—the Axiom of Choice—and there has been serious philosophical discussion of its acceptability. Our question for this chapter are: How is the Axiom used, and can it be justified? End section.

Section. The Tarski—Scott Trick. In definition one in chapter Cardinals , we defined cardinals as ordinals. To do this, we assumed the Axiom of Well-Ordering. We did this, for no other reason than that it is the “industry standard”. Before we discuss any of the philosophical issues surrounding Well-Ordering, then, it is important to be clear that we can depart from the industry standard, and develop a theory of cardinals without assuming Well-Ordering. We can still employ the definitions of capital A is equinumerous with capital B , capital A has cardinality at most that of capital B and capital A has smaller cardinality than capital B , as they appeared in chapter The Size of Sets . We will just need a new notion of cardinal. A naïve thought would be to attempt to define capital A apostrophe s cardinality thus: Displayed expression. the set of x such that capital A is equinumerous with x. End displayed expression. You might want to compare this with Frege's definition of the number determined by x applied to Fx , sketched at the very end of section Appendix: Hume's Principle in chapter Cardinals . And, for reasons we gestured at there, this definition fails. Any singleton set is equinumerous with the set containing the empty set . But new singleton sets are formed at every successor stage of the hierarchy (just consider the singleton of the previous stage). Section. The Well-Ordering Problem. Evidently rather a lot hangs on whether we accept Well-Ordering. But the discussion of this principle has tended to focus on an equivalent principle, the Axiom of Choice. So we will now turn our attention to that (and prove the equivalence). In one thousand eight hundred eighty three , Cantor expressed his support for the Axiom of Well-Ordering, calling it “a law of thought which appears to me to be fundamental, rich in its consequences, and particularly remarkable for its general validity” (cited in Michael Potter two thousand four, page two hundred forty three ). But Cantor ultimately became convinced that the “Axiom” was in need of proof. So did the mathematical community. The problem was “solved” by Zermelo in one thousand nine hundred four . To explain his solution, we need some definitions. Definition. A function f is a choice function if and only if f of x belongs to x for all x belongs to the domain of f . We say that f is a choice function for capital A if and only if f is a choice function with the domain of f equals capital A set minus the set containing the empty set . End definition. Intuitively, for every (non-empty) set x belongs to capital A , a choice function for capital A chooses a particular element, f of x , from x . The Axiom of Choice is then: Axiom. Choice. Every set has a choice function. End axiom. Zermelo showed that Choice entails well-ordering, and vice versa: Theorem. in set theory Z F . Well-Ordering and Choice are equivalent. End theorem. Proof. End displayed expression. The indication to “stop!” is just a shorthand for what would otherwise be a more long-winded definition. End proof. But matters get murkier as soon as we consider infinite sets. For example, consider this “minimal” extension to the above: Countable Choice. Every countable set has a choice function. This is a special case of Choice. And it transpires that this principle was invoked fairly frequently, without an obvious awareness of its use. Here are two nice examples. Footnote. Due to Michael Potter (two thousand four), section nine point four and Luca Incurvati. End footnote. Example. Cautious as we are, we proved this in theorem one in chapter Cardinals . But in that proof we were working in set theory Z F C , since we were assuming that any set capital A can be well-ordered, and hence that the cardinality of capital A is guaranteed to exist. That is: we explicitly assumed Choice. Did you spot the use of the Countable Choice? It is used to choose our sequence of functions f subscript zero , f subscript one , f subscript two , and so on Footnote. A similar use of Choice occurred in proposition four in chapter Cardinal Arithmetic , when we gave the instruction “For each beta belongs to the cardinal a , fix an injection f subscript beta ”. End footnote. And again, the result fails in the absence of any Choice principle. Specifically, Solomon Feferman and Azriel Levy (one thousand nine hundred sixty three) proved that it is consistent with set theory Z F that a countable union of countable sets has cardinality beth subscript one . But here is a much funnier statement of the point, from Russell: Quotation. This is illustrated by the millionaire who bought a pair of socks whenever he bought a pair of boots, and never at any other time, and who had such a passion for buying both that at last he had aleph subscript zero pairs of boots and aleph subscript zero pairs of socks and so on Among boots we can distinguish right and left, and therefore we can make a selection of one out of each pair, namely, we can choose all the right boots or all the left boots; but with socks no such principle of selection suggests itself, and we cannot be sure, unless we assume the multiplicative axiom Open bracket. That is, in effect Choice. Close bracket., that there is any class consisting of one sock out of each pair. (Bertrand Russell, one thousand nine hundred nineteen, page one hundred twenty six) End quotation. In short, some form of Choice is needed to prove the following: If you have countably many pairs of socks, then you have (only) countably many socks. And in fact, without Countable Choice (or something equivalent), a countable union of countable sets can fail to be countable. End example. The moral is that Countable Choice was used repeatedly, without much awareness of its users. The philosophical question is: How could we justify Countable Choice? An attempt at an intuitive justification might invoke an appeal to a supertask. Suppose we make the first choice in the fraction one over two a minute, our second choice in the fraction one over four a minute, and so on, our n indexed choice in the fraction one over two superscript n a minute, and so on Then within one minute, we will have made an omega -sequence of choices, and defined a choice function. But what, really, could such a thought-experiment tell us? For a start, it relies upon taking this idea of “choosing” rather literally. For another, it seems to bind up mathematics in metaphysical possibility. More important: it is not going to give us any justification for Choice tout court, rather than mere Countable Choice. For if we need every set to have a choice function, then we'll need to be able to perform a “supertask of arbitrary ordinal length.” Bluntly, that idea is laughable. End section.

Section. Intrinsic Considerations about Choice. The broader question, then, is whether Well-Ordering, or Choice, or indeed the comparability of all sets as regards their size—it doesn't matter which—can be justified. Here is an attempted intrinsic justification. Back in section The Story in More Detail in chapter Steps towards set theory Z , we introduced several principles about the hierarchy. One of these is worth restating: List. Next item.. Stages accumulate. For any stage capital S , and for any sets which were formed before stage capital S : a set is formed at stage capital S whose members are exactly those sets. Nothing else is formed at stage capital S . End list. In fact, many authors have suggested that the Axiom of Choice can be justified via (something like) this principle. We will briefly provide a gloss on that approach. We will start with a simple little result, which offers yet another equivalent for Choice: Theorem. in set theory Z F . Choice is equivalent to the following principle. If the elements of capital A are disjoint and non-empty, then there is some capital C such that capital C intersected with x is a singleton for every x belongs to capital A . (We call such a capital C a choice set for capital A .) End theorem. The proof of this result is straightforward, and we leave it as an exercise for the reader. Exercise. Prove theorem in set theory Z F in chapter Choice . If you struggle, you can find a proof in Michael Potter (two thousand four), pages two hundred forty two through two hundred forty three . End exercise. This exercise remains unsolved. The essential point is that a choice set for capital A is just the range of a choice function for capital A . So, to justify Choice, we can simply try to justify its equivalent formulation, in terms of the existence of choice sets. And we will now try to do exactly that. Let capital A apostrophe s elements be disjoint and non-empty. By Stages are key (see section The Story in More Detail in chapter Steps towards set theory Z ), capital A is formed at some stage capital S . Note that all the elements of the union of capital A are available before stage capital S . Now, by Stages accumulate, for any sets which were formed before capital S , a set is formed whose members are exactly those sets. Otherwise put: every possible collections of earlier-available sets will exist at capital S . But it is certainly possible to select objects which could be formed into a choice set for capital A ; that is just some very specific subset of the union of capital A . So: some such choice set exists, as required. Well, that's a very quick attempt to offer a justification of Choice on intrinsic grounds. But, to pursue this idea further, you should read Potter's ( two thousand four, section fourteen point eight ) neat development of it. End section.

Section. The Banach—Tarski Paradox. We might also attempt to justify Choice, as Boolos attempted to justify Replacement, by appealing to extrinsic considerations (see section Extrinsic Considerations about Replacement in chapter Replacement ). After all, adopting Choice has many desirable consequences: the ability to compare every cardinal; the ability to well-order every set; the ability to treat cardinals as a particular kind of ordinal; etc. Sometimes, however, it is claimed that Choice has undesirable consequences. Mostly, this is due to a result by Stefan Banach and Alfred Tarski (one thousand nine hundred twenty four) . Theorem. Banach—Tarski Paradox (in set theory Z F C ). Any ball can be decomposed into finitely many pieces, which can be reassembled (by rotation and transportation) to form two copies of that ball. End theorem. At first glance, this is a bit amazing. Clearly the two balls have twice the volume of the original ball. But rigid motions—rotation and transportation—do not change volume. So it looks as if Banach—Tarski allows us to magick new matter into existence. It gets worse. Footnote. See Grzegorz Tomkowicz and Stan Wagon (two thousand sixteen), Theorem three point one two . End footnote. Similar reasoning shows that a pea can be cut into finitely many pieces, which can then be reassembled (by rotation and transportation) to form an entity the shape and size of Big Ben. None of this, however, holds in set theory Z F on its own. Footnote. Though Banach—Tarski can be proved with principles which are strictly weaker than Choice; see Grzegorz Tomkowicz and Stan Wagon (two thousand sixteen), three hundred three . End footnote. So we face a decision: reject Choice, or learn to live with the “paradox”. We're going to suggest that we should learn to live with the “paradox”. Chapter. Proofs.

Section. Introduction. Based on your experiences in introductory logic, you might be comfortable with a derivation system—probably a natural deduction or Fitch style derivation system, or perhaps a proof-tree system. You probably remember doing proofs in these systems, either proving a formula or show that a given argument is valid. In order to do this, you applied the rules of the system until you got the desired end result. In reasoning about logic, we also prove things, but in most cases we are not using a derivation system. In fact, most of the proofs we consider are done in English (perhaps, with some symbolic language thrown in) rather than entirely in the language of first-order logic. When constructing such proofs, you might at first be at a loss—how do I prove something without a derivation system? How do I start? How do I know if my proof is correct? Before attempting a proof, it's important to know what a proof is and how to construct one. As implied by the name, a proof is meant to show that something is true. You might think of this in terms of a dialogue—someone asks you if something is true, say, if every prime other than two is an odd number. To answer “yes” is not enough; they might want to know why. In this case, you'd give them a proof. In everyday discourse, it might be enough to gesture at an answer, or give an incomplete answer. In logic and mathematics, however, we want rigorous proof—we want to show that something is true beyond any doubt. This means that every step in our proof must be justified, and the justification must be cogent (that is, the assumption you're using is actually assumed in the statement of the theorem you're proving, the definitions you apply must be correctly applied, the justifications appealed to must be correct inferences, etc.). Usually, we're proving some statement. We call the statements we're proving by various names: propositions, theorems, lemmas, or corollaries. A proposition is a basic proof-worthy statement: important enough to record, but perhaps not particularly deep nor applied often. A theorem is a significant, important proposition. Its proof often is broken into several steps, and sometimes it is named after the person who first proved it (for example, Cantor's Theorem, the Loewenheim—Skolem theorem) or after the fact it concerns (for example, the completeness theorem). A lemma is a proposition or theorem that is used in the proof of a more important result. Confusingly, sometimes lemmas are important results in themselves, and also named after the person who introduced them (for example, Zorn's Lemma). A corollary is a result that easily follows from another one. A statement to be proved often contains assumptions that clarify which kinds of things we're proving something about. It might begin with “Let formula A be a formula of the form formula B implies formula C ” or “Suppose Gamma proves formula A ” or something of the sort. These are hypotheses of the proposition, theorem, or lemma, and you may assume these to be true in your proof. They restrict what we're proving, and also introduce some names for the objects we're talking about. For instance, if your proposition begins with “Let formula A be a formula of the form formula B implies formula C ,” you're proving something about all formulas of a certain sort only (namely, conditionals), and it's understood that formula B implies formula C is an arbitrary conditional that your proof will talk about. End section.

Section. Starting a Proof. But where do you even start? You've been given something to prove, so this should be the last thing that is mentioned in the proof (you can, obviously, announce that you're going to prove it at the beginning, but you don't want to use it as an assumption). Write what you are trying to prove at the bottom of a fresh sheet of paper—this way you don't lose sight of your goal. Next, you may have some assumptions that you are able to use (this will be made clearer when we talk about the type of proof you are doing in the next section). Write these at the top of the page and make sure to flag that they are assumptions (that is, if you are assuming claim p , write “assume that claim p ,” or “suppose that claim p ”). Finally, there might be some definitions in the question that you need to know. You might be told to use a specific definition, or there might be various definitions in the assumptions or conclusion that you are working towards. Write these down and ensure that you understand what they mean. How you set up your proof will also be dependent upon the form of the question. The next section provides details on how to set up your proof based on the type of sentence. End section.

Section. Using Definitions. We mentioned that you must be familiar with all definitions that may be used in the proof, and that you can properly apply them. This is a really important point, and it is worth looking at in a bit more detail. Definitions are used to abbreviate properties and relations so we can talk about them more succinctly. The introduced abbreviation is called the definiendum, and what it abbreviates is the definiens. In proofs, we often have to go back to how the definiendum was introduced, because we have to exploit the logical structure of the definiens (the long version of which the defined term is the abbreviation) to get through our proof. By unpacking definitions, you're ensuring that you're getting to the heart of where the logical action is. We'll start with an example. Suppose you want to prove the following: Proposition. For any sets A and set B , the union of set A and set B equals the union of set B and set A . End proposition. In order to even start the proof, we need to know what it means for two sets to be identical; that is, we need to know what the “ set equality ” in that equation means for sets. Sets are defined to be identical whenever they have the same elements. So the definition we have to unpack is: Definition. Sets A and set B are identical, set A equals set B , if and only if every element of set A is an element of set B , and vice versa. End definition. This definition uses set A and set B as placeholders for arbitrary sets. What it defines—the definiendum —is the expression “ set A equals set B ” by giving the condition under which set A equals set B is true. This condition—“every element of set A is an element of set B , and vice versa”—is the definiens. Footnote. In this particular case—and very confusingly!—when set A equals set B , the sets A and set B are just one and the same set, even though we use different letters for it on the left and the right side. But the ways in which that set is picked out may be different, and that makes the definition non-trivial. End footnote. The definition specifies that set A equals set B is true if, and only if (we abbreviate this to “if and only if”) the condition holds. When you apply the definition, you have to match the set A and set B in the definition to the case you're dealing with. In our case, it means that in order for the union of set A and set B equals the union of set B and set A to be true, each z is an element of the union of set A and set B must also be in the union of set B and set A , and vice versa. The expression the union of set A and set B in the proposition plays the role of set A in the definition, and the union of set B and set A that of set B . Since set A and set B are used both in the definition and in the statement of the proposition we're proving, but in different uses, you have to be careful to make sure you don't mix up the two. For instance, it would be a mistake to think that you could prove the proposition by showing that every element of set A is an element of set B , and vice versa—that would show that set A equals set B , not that the union of set A and set B equals the union of set B and set A . (Also, since set A and set B may be any two sets, you won't get very far, because if nothing is assumed about set A and set B they may well be different sets.) Within the proof we are dealing with set-theoretic notions such as union, and so we must also know the meanings of the symbol union in order to understand how the proof should proceed. And sometimes, unpacking the definition gives rise to further definitions to unpack. For instance, the union of set A and set B is defined as the set of all z such that z is an element of set A or z is an element of set B . So if you want to prove that x is an element of the union of set A and set B , unpacking the definition of union tells you that you have to prove x is an element of the set of all z such that z is an element of set A or z is an element of set B . Now you also have to remember that x is an element of the set of all z satisfying the indicated condition involving z if and only if the indicated condition involving x . So, further unpacking the definition of the the set of all z satisfying the indicated condition involving z notation, what you have to show is: x is an element of set A or x is an element of set B . So, “every element of the union of set A and set B is also an element of the union of set B and set A ” really means: “for every x , if x is an element of set A or x is an element of set B , then x is an element of set B or x is an element of set A .” If we fully unpack the definitions in the proposition, we see that what we have to show is this: Proposition. For any sets A and set B : (a) for every x , if x is an element of set A or x is an element of set B , then x is an element of set B or x is an element of set A , and (b) for every x , if x is an element of set B or x is an element of set A , then x is an element of set A or x is an element of set B . End proposition. What's important is that unpacking definitions is a necessary part of constructing a proof. Properly doing it is sometimes difficult: you must be careful to distinguish and match the variables in the definition and the terms in the claim you're proving. In order to be successful, you must know what the question is asking and what all the terms used in the question mean—you will often need to unpack more than one definition. In simple proofs such as the ones below, the solution follows almost immediately from the definitions themselves. Of course, it won't always be this simple. Exercise. Suppose you are asked to prove that the intersection of set A and set B is not equal to the empty set . Unpack all the definitions occurring here, that is, restate this in a way that does not mention “ intersection ”, “ the equality sign ”, or “ the empty set ”. End exercise. This exercise remains unsolved. End section.

Section. Inference Patterns. Proofs are composed of individual inferences. When we make an inference, we typically indicate that by using a word like “so,” “thus,” or “therefore.” The inference often relies on one or two facts we already have available in our proof—it may be something we have assumed, or something that we've concluded by an inference already. To be clear, we may label these things, and in the inference we indicate what other statements we're using in the inference. An inference will often also contain an explanation of why our new conclusion follows from the things that come before it. There are some common patterns of inference that are used very often in proofs; we'll go through some below. Some patterns of inference, like proofs by induction, are more involved (and will be discussed later). We've already discussed one pattern of inference: unpacking, or applying, a definition. When we unpack a definition, we just restate something that involves the definiendum by using the definiens. For instance, suppose that we have already established in the course of a proof that set D equals set E (a). Then we may apply the definition of set equality for sets and infer: “Thus, by definition from (a), every element of set D is an element of set E and vice versa.” Somewhat confusingly, we often do not write the justification of an inference when we actually make it, but before. Suppose we haven't already proved that set D equals set E , but we want to. If set D equals set E is the conclusion we aim for, then we can restate this aim also by applying the definition: to prove set D equals set E we have to prove that every element of set D is an element of set E and vice versa. So our proof will have the form: (a) prove that every element of set D is an element of set E ; (b) every element of set E is an element of set D ; (c) therefore, from (a) and (b) by definition of set equality , set D equals set E . But we would usually not write it this way. Instead we might write something like, Quotation. We want to show set D equals set E . By definition of set equality , this amounts to showing that every element of set D is an element of set E and vice versa. (a) and so on (a proof that every element of set D is an element of set E ) and so on (b) and so on (a proof that every element of set E is an element of set D ) and so on End quotation. Section. Using a Conjunction. Perhaps the simplest inference pattern is that of drawing as conclusion one of the conjuncts of a conjunction. In other words: if we have assumed or already proved that claim p and claim q , then we're entitled to infer that claim p (and also that claim q ). This is such a basic inference that it is often not mentioned. For instance, once we've unpacked the definition of set D equals set E we've established that every element of set D is an element of set E and vice versa. From this we can conclude that every element of set E is an element of set D (that's the “vice versa” part). Section. Proving a Conjunction. Sometimes what you'll be asked to prove will have the form of a conjunction; you will be asked to “prove claim p and claim q .” In this case, you simply have to do two things: prove claim p , and then prove claim q . You could divide your proof into two sections, and for clarity, label them. When you're making your first notes, you might write “(one) Prove claim p ” at the top of the page, and “(two) Prove claim q ” in the middle of the page. (Of course, you might not be explicitly asked to prove a conjunction but find that your proof requires that you prove a conjunction. For instance, if you're asked to prove that set D equals set E you will find that, after unpacking the definition of set equality , you have to prove: every element of set D is an element of set E and every element of set E is an element of set D ). Section. Proving a Disjunction. When what you are proving takes the form of a disjunction (that is, it is an statement of the form “ claim p or claim q ”), it is enough to show that one of the disjuncts is true. However, it basically never happens that either disjunct just follows from the assumptions of your theorem. More often, the assumptions of your theorem are themselves disjunctive, or you're showing that all things of a certain kind have one of two properties, but some of the things have the one and others have the other property. This is where proof by cases is useful (see below). Section. Conditional Proof. Many theorems you will encounter are in conditional form (that is, show that if claim p holds, then claim q is also true). These cases are nice and easy to set up—simply assume the antecedent of the conditional (in this case, claim p ) and prove the conclusion claim q from it. So if your theorem reads, “If claim p then claim q ,” you start your proof with “assume claim p ” and at the end you should have proved claim q . Conditionals may be stated in different ways. So instead of “If claim p then claim q ,” a theorem may state that “ claim p only if claim q ,” “ claim q if claim p ,” or “ claim q , provided claim p .” These all mean the same and require assuming claim p and proving claim q from that assumption. Recall that a biconditional (“ claim p if and only if (if and only if) claim q ”) is really two conditionals put together: if claim p then claim q , and if claim q then claim p . All you have to do, then, is two instances of conditional proof: one for the first conditional and another one for the second. Sometimes, however, it is possible to prove an “if and only if” statement by chaining together a bunch of other “if and only if” statements so that you start with “ claim p ” an end with “ claim q ”—but in that case you have to make sure that each step really is an “if and only if.” Section. Universal Claims. Using a universal claim is simple: if something is true for anything, it's true for each particular thing. So if, say, the hypothesis of your proof is set A is a subset of set B , that means (unpacking the definition of the subset relation ), that, for every x is an element of set A , x is an element of set B . Thus, if you already know that z is an element of set A , you can conclude z is an element of set B . Proving a universal claim may seem a little bit tricky. Usually these statements take the following form: “If x has property P , then it has property Q ” or “All property P s are property Q s.” Of course, it might not fit this form perfectly, and it takes a bit of practice to figure out what you're asked to prove exactly. But: we often have to prove that all objects with some property have a certain other property. The way to prove a universal claim is to introduce names or variables, for the things that have the one property and then show that they also have the other property. We might put this by saying that to prove something for all property P s you have to prove it for an arbitrary property P . And the name introduced is a name for an arbitrary property P . We typically use single letters as these names for arbitrary things, and the letters usually follow conventions: for example, we use n for natural numbers, formula A for formulas, set A for sets, function f for functions, etc. The trick is to maintain generality throughout the proof. You start by assuming that an arbitrary object (“ x ”) has the property property P , and show (based only on definitions or what you are allowed to assume) that x has the property property Q . Because you have not stipulated what x is specifically, other that it has the property property P , then you can assert that everything with property P has the property property Q . In short, x is a stand-in for all things with property property P . Proposition. For all sets A and set B , set A is a subset of the union of set A and set B . End proposition. Proof. Let set A and set B be arbitrary sets. We want to show that set A is a subset of the union of set A and set B . By definition of the subset relation , this amounts to: for every x , if x is an element of set A then x is an element of the union of set A and set B . So let x is an element of set A be an arbitrary element of set A . We have to show that x is an element of the union of set A and set B . Since x is an element of set A , x is an element of set A or x is an element of set B . Thus, x is an element of the set of all x such that x is an element of set A or x is an element of set B . But that, by definition of union , means x is an element of the union of set A and set B . End proof. Section. Proof by Cases. Suppose you have a disjunction as an assumption or as an already established conclusion—you have assumed or proved that claim p or claim q is true. You want to prove claim r . You do this in two steps: first you assume that claim p is true, and prove claim r , then you assume that claim q is true and prove claim r again. This works because we assume or know that one of the two alternatives holds. The two steps establish that either one is sufficient for the truth of claim r . (If both are true, we have not one but two reasons for why claim r is true. It is not necessary to separately prove that claim r is true assuming both claim p and claim q .) To indicate what we're doing, we announce that we “distinguish cases.” For instance, suppose we know that x is an element of the union of set B and set C . the union of set B and set C is defined as the set of all x such that x is an element of set B or x is an element of set C . In other words, by definition, x is an element of set B or x is an element of set C . We would prove that x is an element of set A from this by first assuming that x is an element of set B , and proving x is an element of set A from this assumption, and then assume x is an element of set C , and again prove x is an element of set A from this. You would write “We distinguish cases” under the assumption, then “Case (one): x is an element of set B ” underneath, and “Case (two): x is an element of set C halfway down the page. Then you'd proceed to fill in the top half and the bottom half of the page. Proof by cases is especially useful if what you're proving is itself disjunctive. Here's a simple example: Proposition. Suppose set B is a subset of set D and set C is a subset of set E . Then the union of set B and set C is a subset of the union of set D and set E . End proposition. Proof. Assume (a) that set B is a subset of set D and (b) set C is a subset of set E . By definition, any x is an element of set B is also is an element of set D (c) and any x is an element of set C is also is an element of set E (d). To show that the union of set B and set C is a subset of the union of set D and set E , we have to show that if x is an element of the union of set B and set C then x is an element of the union of set D and set E (by definition of the subset relation ). x is an element of the union of set B and set C if and only if x is an element of set B or x is an element of set C (by definition of union ). Similarly, x is an element of the union of set D and set E if and only if x is an element of set D or x is an element of set E . So, we have to show: for any x , if x is an element of set B or x is an element of set C , then x is an element of set D or x is an element of set E . Quotation. So far we've only unpacked definitions! We've reformulated our proposition without the subset relation and union and are left with trying to prove a universal conditional claim. By what we've discussed above, this is done by assuming that x is something about which we assume the “if” part is true, and we'll go on to show that the “then” part is true as well. In other words, we'll assume that x is an element of set B or x is an element of set C and show that x is an element of set D or x is an element of set E . Footnote. This paragraph just explains what we're doing—it's not part of the proof, and you don't have to go into all this detail when you write down your own proofs. End footnote. End quotation. Suppose that x is an element of set B or x is an element of set C . We have to show that x is an element of set D or x is an element of set E . We distinguish cases. Case one: x is an element of set B . By (c), x is an element of set D . Thus, x is an element of set D or x is an element of set E . (Here we've made the inference discussed in the preceding subsection!) Case two: x is an element of set C . By (d), x is an element of set E . Thus, x is an element of set D or x is an element of set E . End proof. Section. Proving an Existence Claim. When asked to prove an existence claim, the question will usually be of the form “prove that there is an x such that the indicated condition involving x ”, that is, that some object that has the property described by “ the indicated condition involving x ”. In this case you'll have to identify a suitable object and show that it has the required property. This sounds straightforward, but a proof of this kind can be tricky. Typically it involves constructing or defining an object and proving that the object so defined has the required property. Finding the right object may be hard, proving that it has the required property may be hard, and sometimes it's even tricky to show that you've succeeded in defining an object at all! Generally, you'd write this out by specifying the object, for example, “let x be and so on ” (where and so on specifies which object you have in mind), possibly proving that the indicated omitted material in fact describes an object that exists, and then go on to show that x has the property property Q . Here's a simple example. Proposition. Suppose that x is an element of set B . Then there is an set A such that set A is a subset of set B and set A is not equal to the empty set . End proposition. Proof. Assume x is an element of set B . Let set A equals the singleton set containing x . Quotation. Here we've defined the set A by enumerating its elements. Since we assume that x is an object, and we can always form a set by enumerating its elements, we don't have to show that we've succeeded in defining a set A here. However, we still have to show that set A has the properties required by the proposition. The proof isn't complete without that! End quotation. Since x is an element of set A , set A is not equal to the empty set . Quotation. This relies on the definition of set A as the singleton set containing x and the obvious facts that x is an element of the singleton set containing x and x is not an element of the empty set . End quotation. Since x is the only element of the singleton set containing x , and x is an element of set B , every element of set A is also an element of set B . By definition of the subset relation , set A is a subset of set B . End proof. Section. Using Existence Claims. Suppose you know that some existence claim is true (you've proved it, or it's a hypothesis you can use), say, “for some x , x is an element of set A ” or “there is an x is an element of set A .” If you want to use it in your proof, you can just pretend that you have a name for one of the things which your hypothesis says exist. Since set A contains at least one thing, there are things to which that name might refer. You might of course not be able to pick one out or describe it further (other than that it is is an element of set A ). But for the purpose of the proof, you can pretend that you have picked it out and give a name to it. It's important to pick a name that you haven't already used (or that appears in your hypotheses), otherwise things can go wrong. In your proof, you indicate this by going from “for some x , x is an element of set A ” to “Let object a is an element of set A .” Now you can reason about object a , use some other hypotheses, etc., until you come to a conclusion, claim p . If claim p no longer mentions object a , claim p is independent of the asusmption that object a is an element of set A , and you've shown that it follows just from the assumption “for some x , x is an element of set A .” Proposition. If set A is not equal to the empty set , then the union of set A and set B is not equal to the empty set . End proposition. Proof. Suppose set A is not equal to the empty set . So for some x , x is an element of set A . Quotation. Here we first just restated the hypothesis of the proposition. This hypothesis, that is, set A is not equal to the empty set , hides an existential claim, which you get to only by unpacking a few definitions. The definition of set equality tells us that set A equals the empty set if and only if every x is an element of set A is also is an element of the empty set and every x is an element of the empty set is also is an element of set A . Negating both sides, we get: set A is not equal to the empty set if and only if either some x is an element of set A is is not an element of the empty set or some x is an element of the empty set is is not an element of set A . Since nothing is is an element of the empty set , the second disjunct can never be true, and “ x is an element of set A and x is not an element of the empty set ” reduces to just x is an element of set A . So x is not equal to the empty set if and only if for some x , x is an element of set A . That's an existence claim. Now we use that existence claim by introducing a name for one of the elements of set A : End quotation. Let object a is an element of set A . Quotation. Now we've introduced a name for one of the things is an element of set A . We'll continue to argue about object a , but we'll be careful to only assume that object a is an element of set A and nothing else: End quotation. Since object a is an element of set A , object a is an element of the union of set A and set B , by definition of union . So for some x , x is an element of the union of set A and set B , that is, the union of set A and set B is not equal to the empty set . Quotation. In that last step, we went from “ object a is an element of the union of set A and set B ” to “for some x , x is an element of the union of set A and set B .” That doesn't mention object a anymore, so we know that “for some x , x is an element of the union of set A and set B ” follows from “for some x , x is an element of set A alone.” But that means that the union of set A and set B is not equal to the empty set . End quotation. End proof. Source anomaly note. Source variable caveat. In the existence discussion, the printed conclusion says that x is not equal to the empty set, although the surrounding derivation and the next sentence concern set A being nonempty. The formula and prose are preserved rather than silently changing x to A. Original source remains available in Source view. End note. It's maybe good practice to keep bound variables like “ x ” separate from hypothetical names like object a , like we did. In practice, however, we often don't and just use x , like so: Quotation. Suppose set A is not equal to the empty set , that is, there is an x is an element of set A . By definition of union , x is an element of the union of set A and set B . So the union of set A and set B is not equal to the empty set . End quotation. However, when you do this, you have to be extra careful that you use different x apostrophe s and y apostrophe s for different existential claims. For instance, the following is not a correct proof of “If set A is not equal to the empty set and set B is not equal to the empty set then the intersection of set A and set B is not equal to the empty set ” (which is not true). Quotation. Suppose set A is not equal to the empty set and set B is not equal to the empty set . So for some x , x is an element of set A and also for some x , x is an element of set B . Since x is an element of set A and x is an element of set B , x is an element of the intersection of set A and set B , by definition of intersection . So the intersection of set A and set B is not equal to the empty set . End quotation. Can you spot where the incorrect step occurs and explain why the result does not hold? End section.

Section. An Example. Our first example is the following simple fact about unions and intersections of sets. It will illustrate unpacking definitions, proofs of conjunctions, of universal claims, and proof by cases. Proposition. For any sets A , set B , and set C , the union of set A with the intersection of set B and set C equals the intersection of the union of set A and set B with the union of set A and set C End proposition. Let's prove it! Proof. We want to show that for any sets A , set B , and set C , the union of set A with the intersection of set B and set C equals the intersection of the union of set A and set B with the union of set A and set C Quotation. First we unpack the definition of “ set equality ” in the statement of the proposition. Recall that proving sets identical means showing that the sets have the same elements. That is, all elements of the union of set A with the intersection of set B and set C are also elements of the intersection of the union of set A and set B with the union of set A and set C , and vice versa. The “vice versa” means that also every element of the intersection of the union of set A and set B with the union of set A and set C must be an element of the union of set A with the intersection of set B and set C . So in unpacking the definition, we see that we have to prove a conjunction. Let's record this: End quotation. By definition, the union of set A with the intersection of set B and set C equals the intersection of the union of set A and set B with the union of set A and set C if and only if every element of the union of set A with the intersection of set B and set C is also an element of the intersection of the union of set A and set B with the union of set A and set C , and every element of the intersection of the union of set A and set B with the union of set A and set C is an element of the union of set A with the intersection of set B and set C . Quotation. Since this is a conjunction, we must prove each conjunct separately. Lets start with the first: let's prove that every element of the union of set A with the intersection of set B and set C is also an element of the intersection of the union of set A and set B with the union of set A and set C . This is a universal claim, and so we consider an arbitrary element of the union of set A with the intersection of set B and set C and show that it must also be an element of the intersection of the union of set A and set B with the union of set A and set C . We'll pick a variable to call this arbitrary element by, say, z . Our proof continues: End quotation. First, we prove that every element of the union of set A with the intersection of set B and set C is also an element of the intersection of the union of set A and set B with the union of set A and set C . Let z is an element of the union of set A with the intersection of set B and set C . We have to show that z is an element of the intersection of the union of set A and set B with the union of set A and set C . Quotation. Now it is time to unpack the definition of union and intersection . For instance, the definition of union is: the union of set A and set B equals the set of all z such that z is an element of set A or z is an element of set B . When we apply the definition to “ the union of set A with the intersection of set B and set C ,” the role of the “ set B ” in the definition is now played by “ the intersection of set B and set C ,” so the union of set A with the intersection of set B and set C equals the set of all z such that z is an element of set A or z is an element of the intersection of set B and set C . So our assumption that z is an element of the union of set A with the intersection of set B and set C amounts to: z is an element of the set of all z such that z is an element of set A or z is an element of the intersection of set B and set C . And z is an element of the set of all z satisfying the indicated condition involving z if and only if and so on z and so on, that is, in this case, z is an element of set A or z is an element of the intersection of set B and set C . End quotation. By the definition of union , either z is an element of set A or z is an element of the intersection of set B and set C . Quotation. Since this is a disjunction, it will be useful to apply proof by cases. We take the two cases, and show that in each one, the conclusion we're aiming for (namely, “ z is an element of the intersection of the union of set A and set B with the union of set A and set C ”) obtains. End quotation. Case one: Suppose that z is an element of set A . Quotation. There's not much more to work from based on our assumptions. So let's look at what we have to work with in the conclusion. We want to show that z is an element of the intersection of the union of set A and set B with the union of set A and set C . Based on the definition of intersection , if we want to show that z is an element of the intersection of the union of set A and set B with the union of set A and set C , we have to show that it's in both the union of set A and set B and the union of set A and set C . But z is an element of the union of set A and set B if and only if z is an element of set A or z is an element of set B , and we already have (as the assumption of case one) that z is an element of set A . By the same reasoning—switching set C for set B — z is an element of the union of set A and set C . This argument went in the reverse direction, so let's record our reasoning in the direction needed in our proof. End quotation. Since z is an element of set A , z is an element of set A or z is an element of set B , and hence, by definition of union , z is an element of the union of set A and set B . Similarly, z is an element of the union of set A and set C . But this means that z is an element of the intersection of the union of set A and set B with the union of set A and set C , by definition of intersection . Quotation. This completes the first case of the proof by cases. Now we want to derive the conclusion in the second case, where z is an element of the intersection of set B and set C . End quotation. Case two: Suppose that z is an element of the intersection of set B and set C . Quotation. Again, we are working with the intersection of two sets. Let's apply the definition of intersection : End quotation. Since z is an element of the intersection of set B and set C , z must be an element of both set B and set C , by definition of intersection . Quotation. It's time to look at our conclusion again. We have to show that z is in both the union of set A and set B and the union of set A and set C . And again, the solution is immediate. End quotation. Since z is an element of set B , z is an element of the union of set A and set B . Since z is an element of set C , also z is an element of the union of set A and set C . So, z is an element of the intersection of the union of set A and set B with the union of set A and set C . Quotation. Here we applied the definitions of union and intersection again, but since we've already recalled those definitions, and already showed that if z is in one of two sets it is in their union, we don't have to be as explicit in what we've done. We've completed the second case of the proof by cases, so now we can assert our first conclusion. End quotation. So, if z is an element of the union of set A with the intersection of set B and set C then z is an element of the intersection of the union of set A and set B with the union of set A and set C . Quotation. Now we just want to show the other direction, that every element of the intersection of the union of set A and set B with the union of set A and set C is an element of the union of set A with the intersection of set B and set C . As before, we prove this universal claim by assuming we have an arbitrary element of the first set and show it must be in the second set. Let's state what we're about to do. End quotation. Now, assume that z is an element of the intersection of the union of set A and set B with the union of set A and set C . We want to show that z is an element of the union of set A with the intersection of set B and set C . Quotation. We are now working from the hypothesis that z is an element of the intersection of the union of set A and set B with the union of set A and set C . It hopefully isn't too confusing that we're using the same z here as in the first part of the proof. When we finished that part, all the assumptions we've made there are no longer in effect, so now we can make new assumptions about what z is. If that is confusing to you, just replace z with a different variable in what follows. We know that z is in both the union of set A and set B and the union of set A and set C , by definition of intersection . And by the definition of union , we can further unpack this to: either z is an element of set A or z is an element of set B , and also either z is an element of set A or z is an element of set C . This looks like a proof by cases again—except the “and” makes it confusing. You might think that this amounts to there being three possibilities: z is either in set A , set B or set C . But that would be a mistake. We have to be careful, so let's consider each disjunction in turn. End quotation. By definition of intersection , z is an element of the union of set A and set B and z is an element of the union of set A and set C . By definition of union , z is an element of set A or z is an element of set B . We distinguish cases. Quotation. Since we're focusing on the first disjunction, we haven't gotten our second disjunction (from unpacking the union of set A and set C ) yet. In fact, we don't need it yet. The first case is z is an element of set A , and an element of a set is also an element of the union of that set with any other. So case one is easy: End quotation. Case one: Suppose that z is an element of set A . It follows that z is an element of the union of set A with the intersection of set B and set C . Quotation. Now for the second case, z is an element of set B . Here we'll unpack the second union and do another proof-by-cases: End quotation. Case two: Suppose that z is an element of set B . Since z is an element of the union of set A and set C , either z is an element of set A or z is an element of set C . We distinguish cases further: Case twoa: z is an element of set A . Then, again, z is an element of the union of set A with the intersection of set B and set C . Quotation. Ok, this was a bit weird. We didn't actually need the assumption that z is an element of set B for this case, but that's ok. End quotation. Case twob: z is an element of set C . Then z is an element of set B and z is an element of set C , so z is an element of the intersection of set B and set C , and consequently, z is an element of the union of set A with the intersection of set B and set C . Quotation. This concludes both proofs-by-cases and so we're done with the second half. End quotation. So, if z is an element of the intersection of the union of set A and set B with the union of set A and set C then z is an element of the union of set A with the intersection of set B and set C . End proof. End section.

Section. Another Example. Proposition. If set A is a subset of set C , then the union of set A with the difference of set C and set A equals set C . End proposition. Proof. Suppose that set A is a subset of set C . We want to show that the union of set A with the difference of set C and set A equals set C . Quotation. We begin by observing that this is a conditional statement. It is tacitly universally quantified: the proposition holds for all sets A and set C . So set A and set C are variables for arbitrary sets. To prove such a statement, we assume the antecedent and prove the consequent. We continue by using the assumption that set A is a subset of set C . Let's unpack the definition of the subset relation : the assumption means that all elements of set A are also elements of set C . Let's write this down—it's an important fact that we'll use throughout the proof. End quotation. By the definition of the subset relation , since set A is a subset of set C , for all z , if z is an element of set A , then z is an element of set C . Quotation. We've unpacked all the definitions that are given to us in the assumption. Now we can move onto the conclusion. We want to show that the union of set A with the difference of set C and set A equals set C , and so we set up a proof similarly to the last example: we show that every element of the union of set A with the difference of set C and set A is also an element of set C and, conversely, every element of set C is an element of the union of set A with the difference of set C and set A . We can shorten this to: the union of set A with the difference of set C and set A is a subset of set C and set C is a subset of the union of set A with the difference of set C and set A . (Here we're doing the opposite of unpacking a definition, but it makes the proof a bit easier to read.) Since this is a conjunction, we have to prove both parts. To show the first part, that is, that every element of the union of set A with the difference of set C and set A is also an element of set C , we assume that z is an element of the union of set A with the difference of set C and set A for an arbitrary z and show that z is an element of set C . By the definition of union , we can conclude that z is an element of set A or z is an element of the difference of set C and set A from z is an element of the union of set A with the difference of set C and set A . You should now be getting the hang of this. End quotation. the union of set A with the difference of set C and set A equals set C if and only if the union of set A with the difference of set C and set A is a subset of set C and set C is a subset of the union of set A with the difference of set C and set A . First we prove that the union of set A with the difference of set C and set A is a subset of set C . Let z is an element of the union of set A with the difference of set C and set A . So, either z is an element of set A or z is an element of the difference of set C and set A . Quotation. We've arrived at a disjunction, and from it we want to prove that z is an element of set C . We do this using proof by cases. End quotation. Case one: z is an element of set A . Since for all z , if z is an element of set A , z is an element of set C , we have that z is an element of set C . Quotation. Here we've used the fact recorded earlier which followed from the hypothesis of the proposition that set A is a subset of set C . The first case is complete, and we turn to the second case, z is an element of the difference of set C and set A . Recall that the difference of set C and set A denotes the difference of the two sets, that is, the set of all elements of set C which are not elements of set A . But any element of set C not in set A is in particular an element of set C . End quotation. Case two: z is an element of the difference of set C and set A . This means that z is an element of set C and z is not an element of set A . So, in particular, z is an element of set C . Quotation. Great, we've proved the first direction. Now for the second direction. Here we prove that set C is a subset of the union of set A with the difference of set C and set A . So we assume that z is an element of set C and prove that z is an element of the union of set A with the difference of set C and set A . End quotation. Now let z is an element of set C . We want to show that z is an element of set A or z is an element of the difference of set C and set A . Quotation. Since all elements of set A are also elements of set C , and the difference of set C and set A is the set of all things that are elements of set C but not set A , it follows that z is either in set A or in the difference of set C and set A . This may be a bit unclear if you don't already know why the result is true. It would be better to prove it step-by-step. It will help to use a simple fact which we can state without proof: z is an element of set A or z is not an element of set A . This is called the “principle of excluded middle:” for any statement claim p , either claim p is true or its negation is true. (Here, claim p is the statement that z is an element of set A .) Since this is a disjunction, we can again use proof-by-cases. End quotation. Either z is an element of set A or z is not an element of set A . In the former case, z is an element of the union of set A with the difference of set C and set A . In the latter case, z is an element of set C and z is not an element of set A , so z is an element of the difference of set C and set A . Section. Proof by Contradiction. In the first instance, proof by contradiction is an inference pattern that is used to prove negative claims. Suppose you want to show that some claim claim p is false, that is, you want to show not claim p . The most promising strategy is to (a) suppose that claim p is true, and (b) show that this assumption leads to something you know to be false. “Something known to be false” may be a result that conflicts with—contradicts— claim p itself, or some other hypothesis of the overall claim you are considering. For instance, a proof of “if claim q then not claim p ” involves assuming that claim q is true and proving not claim p from it. If you prove not claim p by contradiction, that means assuming claim p in addition to claim q . If you can prove not claim q from claim p , you have shown that the assumption claim p leads to something that contradicts your other assumption claim q , since claim q and not claim q cannot both be true. Of course, you have to use other inference patterns in your proof of the contradiction, as well as unpacking definitions. Let's consider an example. Proposition. If set A is a subset of set B and set B equals the empty set , then set A has no elements. End proposition. Proof. Suppose set A is a subset of set B and set B equals the empty set . We want to show that set A has no elements. Quotation. Since this is a conditional claim, we assume the antecedent and want to prove the consequent. The consequent is: set A has no elements. We can make that a bit more explicit: it's not the case that there is an x is an element of set A . End quotation. set A has no elements if and only if it's not the case that there is an x such that x is an element of set A . Quotation. So we've determined that what we want to prove is really a negative claim not claim p , namely: it's not the case that there is an x is an element of set A . To use proof by contradiction, we have to assume the corresponding positive claim claim p , that is, there is an x is an element of set A , and prove a contradiction from it. We indicate that we're doing a proof by contradiction by writing “by way of contradiction, assume” or even just “suppose not,” and then state the assumption claim p . End quotation. Suppose not: there is an x is an element of set A . Quotation. This is now the new assumption we'll use to obtain a contradiction. We have two more assumptions: that set A is a subset of set B and that set B equals the empty set . The first gives us that x is an element of set B : End quotation. Since set A is a subset of set B , x is an element of set B . Quotation. But since set B equals the empty set , every element of set B (for example, x ) must also be an element of the empty set . End quotation. Since set B equals the empty set , x is an element of the empty set . This is a contradiction, since by definition the empty set has no elements. Quotation. This already completes the proof: we've arrived at what we need (a contradiction) from the assumptions we've set up, and this means that the assumptions can't all be true. Since the first two assumptions ( set A is a subset of set B and set B equals the empty set ) are not contested, it must be the last assumption introduced (there is an x is an element of set A ) that must be false. But if we want to be thorough, we can spell this out. End quotation. Thus, our assumption that there is an x is an element of set A must be false, hence, set A has no elements by proof by contradiction. End proof. Every positive claim is trivially equivalent to a negative claim: claim p if and only if not not claim p . So proofs by contradiction can also be used to establish positive claims “indirectly,” as follows: To prove claim p , read it as the negative claim not not claim p . If we can prove a contradiction from not claim p , we've established not not claim p by proof by contradiction, and hence claim p . In the last example, we aimed to prove a negative claim, namely that set A has no elements, and so the assumption we made for the purpose of proof by contradiction (that is, that there is an x is an element of set A ) was a positive claim. It gave us something to work with, namely the hypothetical x is an element of set A about which we continued to reason until we got to x is an element of the empty set . When proving a positive claim indirectly, the assumption you'd make for the purpose of proof by contradiction would be negative. But very often you can easily reformulate a positive claim as a negative claim, and a negative claim as a positive claim. Our previous proof would have been essentially the same had we proved “ set A equals the empty set ” instead of the negative consequent “ set A has no elements.” (By definition of set equality , “ set A equals the empty set ” is a general claim, since it unpacks to “every element of set A is an element of the empty set and vice versa”.) But it is easily seen to be equivalent to the negative claim “not: there is an x is an element of set A .” So it is sometimes easier to work with not claim p as an assumption than it is to prove claim p directly. Even when a direct proof is just as simple or even simpler (as in the next examples), some people prefer to proceed indirectly. If the double negation confuses you, think of a proof by contradiction of some claim as a proof of a contradiction from the opposite claim. So, a proof by contradiction of not claim p is a proof of a contradiction from the assumption claim p ; and proof by contradiction of claim p is a proof of a contradiction from not claim p . Proposition. set A is a subset of the union of set A and set B . End proposition. Proof. We want to show that set A is a subset of the union of set A and set B . Quotation. On the face of it, this is a positive claim: every x is an element of set A is also in the union of set A and set B . The negation of that is: some x is an element of set A is is not an element of the union of set A and set B . So we can prove the claim indirectly by assuming this negated claim, and showing that it leads to a contradiction. End quotation. Suppose not, that is, set A is not a subset of the union of set A and set B . Quotation. We have a definition of set A is a subset of the union of set A and set B : every x is an element of set A is also is an element of the union of set A and set B . To understand what set A is not a subset of the union of set A and set B means, we have to use some elementary logical manipulation on the unpacked definition: it's false that every x is an element of set A is also is an element of the union of set A and set B if and only if there is some x is an element of set A that is is not an element of set C . (This is a place where you want to be very careful: many students' attempted proofs by contradiction fail because they analyze the negation of a claim like “all set A s are set B s” incorrectly.) In other words, set A is not a subset of the union of set A and set B if and only if there is an x such that x is an element of set A and x is not an element of the union of set A and set B . From then on, it's easy. End quotation. So, there is an x is an element of set A such that x is not an element of the union of set A and set B . Since x is an element of set A , we have x is an element of the union of set A and set B . This contradicts the assumption that x is not an element of the union of set A and set B . End proof. Section. Reading Proofs. Proofs you find in textbooks and articles very seldom give all the details we have so far included in our examples. Authors often do not draw attention to when they distinguish cases, when they give an indirect proof, or don't mention that they use a definition. So when you read a proof in a textbook, you will often have to fill in those details for yourself in order to understand the proof. Doing this is also good practice to get the hang of the various moves you have to make in a proof. Let's look at an example. Proposition. Absorption. For all sets A , set B , Displayed expression. the intersection of set A with the union of set A and set B equals set A. End displayed expression. End proposition. Proof. If z is an element of the intersection of set A with the union of set A and set B , then z is an element of set A , so the intersection of set A with the union of set A and set B is a subset of set A . Now suppose z is an element of set A . Then also z is an element of the union of set A and set B , and therefore also z is an element of the intersection of set A with the union of set A and set B . End proof. The preceding proof of the absorption law is very condensed. There is no mention of any definitions used, no “we have to prove that” before we prove it, etc. Let's unpack it. The proposition proved is a general claim about any sets A and set B , and when the proof mentions set A or set B , these are variables for arbitrary sets. The general claims the proof establishes is what's required to prove identity of sets, that is, that every element of the left side of the identity is an element of the right and vice versa. Quotation. “If z is an element of the intersection of set A with the union of set A and set B , then z is an element of set A , so the intersection of set A with the union of set A and set B is a subset of set A .” End quotation. This is the first half of the proof of the identity: it establishes that if an arbitrary z is an element of the left side, it is also an element of the right, that is, the intersection of set A with the union of set A and set B is a subset of set A . Assume that z is an element of the intersection of set A with the union of set A and set B . Since z is an element of the intersection of two sets if and only if it is an element of both sets, we can conclude that z is an element of set A and also z is an element of the union of set A and set B . In particular, z is an element of set A , which is what we wanted to show. Since that's all that has to be done for the first half, we know that the rest of the proof must be a proof of the second half, that is, a proof that set A is a subset of the intersection of set A with the union of set A and set B . Quotation. “Now suppose z is an element of set A . Then also z is an element of the union of set A and set B , and therefore also z is an element of the intersection of set A with the union of set A and set B .” End quotation. We start by assuming that z is an element of set A , since we are showing that, for any z , if z is an element of set A then z is an element of the intersection of set A with the union of set A and set B . To show that z is an element of the intersection of set A with the union of set A and set B , we have to show (by definition of “ intersection ”) that (i) z is an element of set A and also (ii) z is an element of the union of set A and set B . Here (i) is just our assumption, so there is nothing further to prove, and that's why the proof does not mention it again. For (ii), recall that z is an element of a union of sets if and only if it is an element of at least one of those sets. Since z is an element of set A , and the union of set A and set B is the union of set A and set B , this is the case here. So z is an element of the union of set A and set B . We've shown both (i) z is an element of set A and (ii) z is an element of the union of set A and set B , hence, by definition of “ intersection ,” z is an element of the intersection of set A with the union of set A and set B . The proof doesn't mention those definitions; it's assumed the reader has already internalized them. If you haven't, you'll have to go back and remind yourself what they are. Then you'll also have to recognize why it follows from z is an element of set A that z is an element of the union of set A and set B , and from z is an element of set A and z is an element of the union of set A and set B that z is an element of the intersection of set A with the union of set A and set B .
